Uniform Title: Tripurārahasya Māhātmyakāṇḍa Main Title: Tripurārahasyam Māhātmyakāṇḍam Description: Part 2 of Gurumaṇḍala Granthamālā, Volume 28, Part 2; comprising chapters 51 to the end.
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: September 18, 2010.
Country of publication: India.
Fifty-first Chapter:
The Manifestation of the Auspicious Goddess Śrī Devī, preceded by her appearance after being gratified by the sacrifice, within the *Lalitāmāhātmya*.

O Pot-born one! Listen to that description of his wondrous form: by him the immortals were thus driven away from all sides, and they became distressed in the forests, in mountain caves, and within subterranean caverns.
In the bowers by the rivers, the daughters of the Daityas dwelt for a very long time, unobserved by the Daityas and terrified of them; at times, however, they were discovered by the Daityas.
Just as servants perform service when they are dragged about or beaten,
so too two thousand years passed away.
Then, on one occasion, the Lord of the Gods beheld his preceptor Aṅgiras;
having bowed to him, Śakra then spoke with his palms joined in reverence.
O Guru! Behold me, who am grieving and have taken refuge in You, the Lord of Gods.
You have been seen by me after a long time; show compassion toward me, Your disciple. (5)
"O Lord, I am not able to endure such hardship as this;
for even though Brahmā was previously entreated by me, he himself spoke again [to the contrary]. (6)
O Lord of the Gods, listen: this is not the time for a remedy against him;
wait for the right time, for without time our desired goal cannot be accomplished.
Today, countless years consisting of yugas have passed for him;
I do not perceive even a fraction of that time as bringing any happiness. (8)
Behold me, soiled, wretched, and with emaciated limbs, fearing danger on every side;
yet this thorny grove is indeed the celestial Nandana garden.
And here are Sudharmā, Maśakas, Gandharvas, Svaramaṇḍalas, Vandins, Karaṭas—these are the Śālūras who recite hymns of praise. || 10 ||
Rambhā and others are the swarms of fireflies; the swan’s down is the stone slab; the pillow is the cluster of shrubs; the invocation by mantra is the path of Śiva. (11)
The assembly consists of cranes, herons, and the like; the garments are the dust of the earth;
the chowries are the thorny branches of trees shaken by the whirlwind. || 12 ||
Seeing him thus endowed with such conduct, his mind was immediately moved;
saying, "Surely this is my own good fortune," he fell into a swoon. (13)
Seeing him fainting from grief, the Guru, the Lord of the Immortals, was moved by compassion; having comforted him, he spoke the words of Aṅgiras.
Listen, O bull among gods! The wise do not grieve for anything;
they are filled with joy in times of adversity and have attained equanimity in times of prosperity. (15)
Those of pure intention do not undergo transformation at all; having conquered sorrow through reflection and steadfastness, such great persons remain unshaken. (16)
They prevail for the sake of merit alone, awaiting only the proper time;
listen, for I shall now declare to you the resolve that brings forth fruit. (17)
Having propitiated the Lord of Beings through ascetic penance, he obtained fearlessness from all sides;
for him, death—whether born of a womb or from the mind—was warded off by Śiva. (18)
There is no duality whatsoever anywhere in the world;
nor has death been proclaimed for him by gods, men, or anyone else. (19)
Therefore, accompanied by the hosts of immortals, go for refuge to the supreme goddess Tripurā; there is no other protector whatsoever.
Having spoken thus to the god Māruta, the preceptor of the gods then meditated;
as soon as he was meditated upon, the Life-breath of the universe prostrated himself and appeared before him.
Then Vācaspati said to him: "Listen to my words, O Māruta!
You are the refuge of all and the life-breath of all, O one of great strength. (22)
"Lead Śakra from the path of the sky to a peak of the Snowy Mountain,
and quickly lead all the other gods as well, headed by Pāvaka."
Then, being completely unobserved by the hosts of Daityas, he was brought here;
for in this matter, every desired objective is achievable through the application of human effort.
Having uttered "Om," he brought all the gods together in the blink of an eye;
Śakra and all the immortals assembled from every direction upon the peak of Himavat. (25)
Then, having dispatched Vāyu, he brought back the lords of the Guṇas,
having resolved upon the desired plan for the victory over the demon Bhaṇḍa.
"Without Tripurā, the Supreme Sovereign, there is no way out here anywhere.
Thus did the gods, led by Brahmā, [speak] regarding Tripurā, the Supreme Goddess.
Restraining the winds of their senses, they meditated upon the Sustainer of the entire world;
thus, for those established in meditation, a hundred years passed by.
Then the gods, having consulted together for the sake of pleasing Tripura,
performed a great sacrifice (mahāyāga) against the Triple City according to the path of Tantra.
Then, when the great sacrifice was completed, well-provided with mantras and materials,
Brahmā himself became the Brahmā-priest, the officiant, and the preceptor.
At that sacrifice, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others were the officiating priests when the final day arrived,
which was manifested through the state of pure consciousness.
In the sacrificial fire of the nature of consciousness, kindled within the great pit,
the Guru performed the sacrifice with a full oblation while meditating upon the Supreme Mother.
Then, while the gods were offering praise with devotion, Tripurāmbikā appeared from the midst of the pit, from within the blazing fire of consciousness.
When the final oblation had been offered into the sacrificial pit, the fire blazed forth;
its flame, rising to a height of one yojana, increased immensely. (34)
There arose a great sound, like a mountain being split asunder;
it was like the falling of a hundred thunderbolts, piercing the ears of the gods.
Then, stealing the eyes of the immortals with his mature splendor,
he possessed a luster like the simultaneous flashing of ten million streaks of lightning.
Then, within the midst of the flames of fire, a great light arose along with a mighty sound and a corresponding brilliance; so it was perceived by the wise at that time. (37)
All were made deaf and blind; they fell to the ground in a swoon.
Except for the Guru, all of them fell from the three forms [of the Lord]. (38)
From the midst of that splendor, the venerable Mother Tripurā appeared,
her body possessing a luster like a mass of fresh, rising sunbeams.
Her slender body was raised like a flash of lightning, her delicate creeper-like form shimmering;
her face was like a full moon blooming amidst the lightning-creeper and the lotus.
Possessing a beautiful luster reddened by vermilion rising from the mass of darkness in her braid,
she is adorned with the jewels of her braided hair like a cluster of stars in the sky.
With her tongue-like parting-line emerging from her mouth like a long, coiling serpent, she casts the courtyard of the sky—
her hair— into shadow by the crimson glow of her vermilion-dyed eyes. (42)
Her forehead was marked with a half-moon, she was distinguished by royal insignia,
her hair was strewn with swarms of bees, and her lotus-face was in full bloom.
Her eyes were like blue lotuses in a lake of facial beauty;
her glance was a mantra that generates ten million gods of love.
Her side-glances are as beautiful as the waves arising from ten million oceans of milk;
her exquisite nose nourishes the splendor of the Campaka buds. 45.
The expanse of her cheeks shone with the splendor of kuruvinda gems like mirrors, while the lotuses of her earrings emerged from the rivers of her outer corners of the eyes.
The earring, shaped like a lotus, and the pearl necklace are the bow of beauty and the continuous flight of arrows of her sidelong glances; they serve as ornaments for her ears. (47)
Her lips were as red as the seeds of a ripe pomegranate, and her inner luster was like the filaments within a blooming red water-lily. || 48 ||
With her bud-like teeth emerging from lips as fresh as young shoots, she was like a milky ocean with its white swans and coral-colored lips. 49.
Her chin was radiant like the stalk of a lotus made of rubies;
her neck was as beautiful as a lotus, shining with jeweled necklaces and golden chains. 50.
Her two breasts were like lotus buds with stalks of lotus-fiber hands;
she was beautiful with her ruby-like body-vine adorned by the clusters of her breasts.
The *kucakokī* birds [her breasts] have hidden away out of fear of the radiance of her moon-like face;
the *marālikā* swans [her breasts] sport in the overflowing river of her gentle smile. (52)
With her hand-stalks raised like slender creepers and branches, reddened by the coral-tips of her fingers,
she was adorned with the buds of the *japā* flower at the tips of her finger-branches.
Her four arms shine with a spear, a noose, a bow, and arrows;
her arms are further adorned with bracelets, armlets, jeweled rings, and upper-arm bands.
Resplendent with a pearl necklace like a lotus stalk shining from her lotus-face,
she possesses two bud-like breasts upon a slender stalk of body-hair.
The line of body hair is a creeping vine rooted at the hollow of her navel;
the lake of her navel has the creeper of body hair as its floating moss.
A woman with shapely hips, clothed in garments dyed saffron-red and adorned with jewels, attains the middle state merely by the practice of holding her limbs erect. (57)
She wore fine silken garments with the luster of thin clouds, adorned with stars visible within them;
her rounded thighs were encircled by a girdle made of rubies and plantain stalks.
Her pair of shanks was beautifully adorned with quivers made of rubies, and her forefeet were endowed with the splendor suggestive of the back of a female tortoise.
Resplendent with jeweled anklets and the beautiful tinkling of small bells,
her lotus-like feet were generous with the fortune of blooming lotuses.
Adorned with the swan-like jewels shimmering upon her lotus feet,
she dispels the constant heat of suffering by the flow of nectar from the moons of her toenails. (61)
Her pair of feet are the preceptors of the swan-like, slow gait;
they are the tender mango sprouts for the fulfillment of the desires of her devotees. 62.
Seeing her thus manifesting herself, Brahmā and the other gods then prostrated themselves like a staff and cried out to her, "Victory, O Goddess! (63)
There, Vācaspati, having bowed again to that Supreme Goddess and rising up,
gazed upon her, submerged in an ocean of joy born from that vision.
With his two hands raised in the gesture of a cupped lotus, he was completely drenched by the flood of tears of joy flowing from his lotus-eyes. || 65 ||
With his voice faltering and slow due to the weight of supreme devotion,
he praised the Mother of Tripura, gladdening her with the joys of his poetic artistry.
I have no power to describe the splendor of your majesty; even that which has been spoken by me is not truly my own power, but yours alone.
For there is no loss of my status as Lord of Speech from that; if there were such a loss, then there would be a loss of your grace. || 67 ||
O Mother, I, the preceptor of the gods, speak thus: that which is reality is you alone; "you," "I," and "this"—all this is you alone.
Therefore, in this matter, neither loss nor gain exists for me, any more than the sweet and bitter tastes of waves are distinct from the ocean of milk.
If one of deluded vision perceives here that which has various divisions, appearing like the variegated forms shining upon the surface of a mirror—
then even this divine form displayed here before us [is likewise so perceived] through our compassion.
Just as before, by means of illusion alone.
O Mother, the deluded-minded sectarian, regarding himself as superior to the assembly of the wise, was infatuated by your playful charms;
not knowing you, he attempted to describe your boundless power through fallacious arguments based on the distinctions of the perceptible world.
O Mother of the World, for those who are intent on disputing with nets of various words through positions such as "it exists" or "it does not exist," time passes in vain;
whereas those who remain for even a moment contemplating Your digit of pure consciousness within their own hearts [attain the goal].
For they are indeed blessed. || 71 ||

O Mother, those yogis who behold that [divine] form within their own selves—within their inner being which is free from the latent impressions of craving for sense objects, stainless like a pure mirror, and motionless—are established in the state of supreme bliss;
indeed, they are blessed and victorious. (72)
Thus, having contemplated Your true nature within the inner field for a very long time, they become firm in their disposition and natural in their innate being;
thereafter, contemplating Your entire external form, they indeed find supreme delight in You.
They are worthy of worship by the lords of yogis. || 73 ||

O Lalitā, having attained some slight acquaintance with your lotus feet, I always and in every way perceive nothing at all within my compositions of speech or even my reflections, apart from you; therefore, I bow to you in truth.
Having thus praised her, the preceptor of the gods prostrated himself on the ground like a staff;
and even the creators headed by Brahmā, whose very nature is virtue, offered praise to Ambikā.
Victory, victory, O Mother, whose nature is consciousness, who possesses the power of the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe;
though Your body is the manifestation of all things, it is pervasive, having as its sole essence the unsurpassed consciousness.
This skill of yours is like a mirror; it is most wonderful even in the superimposition of existence.
Victorious is this great being of yours—the power to bring about the impossible. (77)

O Sovereign, though Your own form is all-pervasive, You make it appear limited through Your power of the impossible; having created all the various distinctions between the seer and the seen, You cause them all to shine forth.
Thus, you who possess a limited form perceive your own manifold nature; by inwardly reflecting upon consciousness with effort, you shine forth again as you truly are.
O Goddess, by Your own sovereignty, You manifest this vast play within the mirror of Your own Self;
having seen this as imagined and yet Your own, You eternally rejoice—salutations to You! 80.
O Maheśvarī! whoever, through their spiritual power, should understand that Your divine play is continuous, he too, like You, rejoices as a god who beholds the play of the worlds. (81)
Those wretched ones who were not able to behold your secret form, full of grace,
have now had this supreme form revealed before their eyes, producing its fruit for them.

We bow again here to that pair who are crimson with saffron, whose breasts are heavy and drooping, who are enriched by the crescent moon, and whose form is exceedingly beautiful; they bear the goad, the arrow, the bow, and the noose. (83)
Having praised her in this manner, Brahmā and the others prostrated themselves at her feet. Then the Supreme One said to them: "O children, arise quickly!"
"Here I am, having donned my armor, arrived for the sake of slaying your enemies.
O Lords of Virtue, what more do you desire? Accept it! || 85 ||
"O descendant of Aṅgiras, you too speak; what desired thing shall I give to you?
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Brahmā and the others then spoke.

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Blessed Lalitā," in the *Lalitāmāhātmya* of the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* within the glorious *Tripurārahasya*, the best of histories. || 4233 ||
Fifty-second chapter:
For the sake of showing her true form to the gods who had been comforted, at the request of Bṛhaspati.

The description of the manifestation of Tripura, preceded by a detailed account of the procedure for the recitation of the Śrīsūkta, as well as the consultation with the ministers and the preparation for terrifying the hosts of gods through the medium of Anubhaṇḍa.
Listen, O sage born from a jar! Then the words of Brahmā and the other gods were heard;
with their bodies bowed low in devotion, those headed by Brahmā spoke to the Goddess. (1)
Furthermore, even in great calamities, you must remain intent on protecting the worlds and carry out the destruction of the enemies and foes of the immortals.
O Mother! Listen, how was the demon Bhaṇḍa slain by you once again?
Surely he had attained immortality from all sides through the grace of the Three-eyed Lord.
"How can the work of the immortals be accomplished, and how can the destruction of the asuras be achieved?
Having heard these words of the leaders headed by Dhātṛ, Śaṅkarī spoke.
O Lotus-born One, do not entertain doubt here regarding the non-slaughter of the Asura;
nor am I born from a womb, even in my mind, of anyone whatsoever.
"Born from the sacrificial fire-pit, I am of extraordinary form in the likeness of a woman;
with an unknown weapon, I shall slay this great asura."
Having heard these words of Lalitā, the lords of qualities abandoned their anxiety;
then the preceptor of the immortals, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Supreme Power.
O Goddess! May Śakra and the other gods behold you, the Great Sovereign, the Mother of all beings, in this form; by that, may they become purified.
Having heard the words of Aṅgiras, the Mistress of Tripura said:
"Listen, O Jīva, Śakra, and the others; the body composed of Śakti is not like this. (9)
"These alone are worthy even to behold me; this form has not been seen by others.
Indeed, no ordinary person beholds one of such a form. (10)
"You are my devotees of this body and are always intent upon its meditation;
therefore, this has been shown to you, and it has never been seen by others."
Let the wielder of the thunderbolt behold that limited form in its various aspects;
then the Guru again entreated her in many ways.
"Show this to Śakra," she said to her guru;
"Listen, I shall tell you what would happen if Śakra were to see me in such a state. (13)
Let him propitiate me according to the ritual of the Śrīsūkta;
then I shall undoubtedly reveal this form of mine to him.
Having spoken thus, she awakened the unconscious gods with her glance of nectar and vanished right there while Brahmā and the others were looking on.
Then all the gods, headed by Śakra, having heard from Bṛhaspati about the manifestation of the illustrious Goddess Tripurā, rose up; thereafter, Vṛṣa [also arose].
Accompanied by the gods, having learned the sequence of worship from his preceptor,
he was filled with an abundance of devotion and faith according to the ritual procedure for the Lakṣmīsūkta.
He propitiated the supreme Goddess Tripurā, the Supreme Sovereign.
As he was thus worshipping her, five or six months passed by.
In the meantime, the preceptor of the Daityas, having learned of the activities of the immortals,
informed Bhaṇḍāsura of that entire occurrence in its entirety. (19)
Listen, O Lord of Daityas: the enemy, the Lord of the Gods, is currently on the Himavat mountain, worshipping the Supreme Śakti with devotion. (20)
Once she is provoked, in an instant she will destroy you along with your sons and kinsmen,
just as a forest fire consumes heaps of grass and wood.
Strive for it only so long as you do not meet with destruction;
for no other means of worship is seen here than the Sāman when one has taken refuge in the powerful.
Having swiftly surrendered heaven and earth, along with their wealth and all their appurtenances,
to Indra, she remained as the sovereign of the entire world, ruling over the realm of Pātāla alone.
"Go for refuge to the Goddess, otherwise you shall meet with destruction.
Having spoken thus and being honored by him, he departed to his desired destination.
Then the Daitya Bhaṇḍāsura, attended in the city of Śūnyaka, consulted with his ministers who were experts in counsel.
Commanded by the king, those ministers spoke according to their respective opinions;
one spoke of conciliation, another of sowing dissension, and yet another spoke of giving gifts.
"Some say it is punishment"; thus was the assembly distracted.
In that interval, there was the son of Viśukra, who was considered equal to Śukra.
The one renowned as Śrutavarman, having bowed to the Lord of the Gods, said:
"Listen, O King, to these words concerning the science of polity (Arthaśāstra), together with its established boundaries. (28)
The external vision is faulty and inherently fickle;
one should examine action with the vision known as the intellect, which is of the nature of *sattva*. (29)
One who acts without reflection perishes like a moth in a fire;
but he who acts with thorough reflection is fully embraced by prosperity.
The minister is stubbornly persistent, possesses clear vision, and is quick to grasp; the king speaks with a mind free from fear and is constantly intent upon his own self-interest. (31)
It would destroy the king along with his kingdom; of this there is no doubt, just as a boat with holes in its seat destroys both the traveler and the sailor in the water.
Therefore, a king who desires to rule his kingdom must abandon evil counselors;
listen, for I shall tell you what the subsequent action should be.

O Great King! In the past, you thought that the immunity from fear granted by the gods when they were gratified by your ascetic penance was insufficient regarding women, and thus you acted in vain. (34)
Therefore, there is no reason for confidence here; for in the past, the powerful Dānava Mahiṣa, having obtained sovereignty over the three worlds, was slain by a woman. (35)
We have heard that in former times, the two powerful and exceedingly valiant Śumbha and Niśumbha were slain in battle along with their armies by Caṇḍikā. (36)
In victory, the *liṅga* is not the cause; rather, the intellect and prowess are the instrumental factors.
Furthermore, I shall explain another matter to you, for this has indeed existed for a long time. (37)
Whosoever among the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas was most excellent,
Viṣṇu uproots each one of them, like a thorn standing in the path.
That was heard by us; indeed, by that Hari, the enemy of the Daityas, the Supreme Śakti was propitiated and manifested for your destruction.
She did not arise from the sacrificial fire-pit or from the mind;
she was not born of a womb, yet you did not choose immortality for her.
O Lord of the Daitya hosts! That which the venerable preceptor Śukra—the best among all the wise—has spoken is by no means insignificant. (41)
Therefore, it appears appropriate to me that only what has been spoken by the Guru should be followed here;
a wise person should, with every effort, cast off the fear born of time.
Valiant effort is best when there is no fear, but when fear arises, peace alone is best;
for one who understands, the root cause must be eliminated by force in every way.
When the root is cut, what hope is there for fruit? When the root is protected, there is the arising of fruit.
O King, hear here my considered opinion, reflected upon with wisdom. (44)
Having brought about complete pacification according to the method taught by the Guru, he again,
through austerity as before, [propitiated] the gods and dispelled the remaining fear. (45)
"Then, O one of noble prowess, bring the three worlds under your control once more!
This mantra has been imparted to you; without it, there can be no security anywhere. (46)
"Having reflected, do that which is desired by you; it shall not be long for you.
Having heard the words of Śrutavarman, Bhaṇḍa, the lord of the Daityas, spoke these words: || 47 ||
Having entered the assembly of the Daityas, he spoke while indeed disparaging that position;
yet it did not please him, just as medicine does not please one who desires to die.
In the meantime, a Daitya intoxicated with pride spoke to the king:
"O Lord of Daityas, listen to what I have said, which brings great happiness here. (49)
Fools who have fallen into a state of cowardice should not be admitted to the assembly of mantra-practitioners;
this boy does not know anything at all of the strength of your arms.
"Because of the words of the timid Brahmin Uśanas, this man has become excessively [timid].
What mindset could a Brahmin possibly have regarding the occasions of war for kings? (51)

What recourse is there in battle for those Brahmins who are presiding priests over the sacrificial fires, who are experts in the knowledge of the Vedas, and who know the rules for formal invitations? (52)
Heroes who possess the sharp-edged knowledge of the Vedas are those who spread the *kuśa* grass and sacrificial fuel;
they do not know the edge of a sword, nor are they heroes when strewn with arrows. (53)
Alas! If even Brahmins can conquer in battle by means of mantras,
then these elephants, terrified by the village lion, would surely discharge their urine.
If Brahmins were also to know how to perform fierce deeds of war, then jackals would have torn open the temples of intoxicated elephants. 55.
Arise, O King! This is the moment; it does not deserve rest.
Whether it be a woman or a man, one who has become an enemy must not be overlooked. (56)
Alas! Today this woman, O Lord of Daityas, shall conquer you—whose prowess uprooted Mount Meru and whose majesty scorched the three worlds like the sun—with her own splendor. (57)
Then even a mountain might be pierced by the petals of blue lotuses, and even a solid mountain of iron might be perforated by the tips of kusha grass. (58)
Alternatively, remain right here, devoted to the enjoyment of your desires and living happily; command me, your servant, and I shall go and [subdue] them in the twinkling of an eye.
"Having bound or even slain those [gods] beginning with Brahmā, I shall offer them to you.
Upon hearing these words of the Daitya, the Dānava Bhaṇḍa was greatly delighted.
Having fallen under the sway of Time, he laughed and said to Śrutavarman:
"Child! Why indeed are you so needlessly afraid of these reports of battle?"
(533) "In our family, no one has ever been born, nor will anyone ever be, who is as cowardly as a eunuch, terrified by the mere talk of war with women. (62)
"You are a fool; go, for you ought to speak endearments to your beloveds. Fie on me, who appointed one such as you as a minister—a destroyer of counsel! (63)
"Even for the wise, the skill of speech is like a thunderbolt to the mountain of their fortitude; [it destroys] the wicked.
Having said this, he rose up with sword in hand to harm the gods.
Accompanied by crores upon crores of heroic asuras armed with various weapons,
he went to where the gods, headed by Śakra, had assembled at Tripura.
Hearing that Bhaṇḍa, the lord of the Daityas, had arrived, the gods, led by Śakra, became utterly terrified and cried out loudly to the Goddess of the Gods, "Protect us! (66)
Perceiving that they were terrified, Tripurā spoke to Nityā Caturdaśī:
"Go, O Jvālāmālinī; protect the frightened gods immediately! (67)
Since the Daityas, intent on harming the immortals, had been thus commanded,
the auspicious Jvālāmālinikā blocked them forcefully with her flame.
Seeing the region enveloped in flames and perceiving that the gods had been overwhelmed by the forest fire and destroyed, the Daitya Bhaṇḍa departed once more in great joy. (69)
And the gods, hearing the intense clamor of the Daitya armies, became terrified and, desiring death, cut off their limbs on all sides. (70)
For the pleasure of the deity, they each offered oblations into the fire-pit;
having thus sacrificed all their limbs, they finally offered their bodies as the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Desiring to offer a distinguished oblation, they recited the mantras in a low voice;
in that interval, Tripurā, who is solely devoted to the protection of her devotees, [appeared].
From the middle of the sacrificial pit there appeared a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
and a loud, towering crackling sound arose from within the pit.
The flames of that fire increased exceedingly, and the gods beheld within the midst of those flames the Great Goddess, the embodiment of all beauty.
Overjoyed, they prostrated themselves like staffs and cried out loudly, "Victory! Victory!
Then, rising up, Indra and the others offered praise to that Great Goddess.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, as well as sages and seers, arrived;
a rain of flowers fell from the sky, and the celestial drums resounded.
The winds blew with pleasant touch, fragrant and moving gently;
Brahmā and all the other gods performed her worship according to the prescribed rites from every side.
Especially with great offerings such as garlands and other articles of worship,
and with various kinds of food— both solid and soft— as well as intoxicating drinks and even meat. (78)
Having thus worshipped the Goddess of the Gods, they greatly gratified her with songs, dances, instrumental music, and numerous festivals. (79)

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Tripurā in Response to the Distressed Prayer of the Devas," within the Lalitopākhyāna of the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories. || 4312 ||
Fifty-third Chapter:
[Concerning] the Śrīdevī’s manifestation of all the gods for the purpose of being seen, when she was gratified by the sacrifice in the *Lalitāmāhātmya*.
Description of the Establishment of the Self-Abiding Power on the Auspicious Mount Meru:
Now, having beheld that Supreme Goddess, the gods, headed by Śakra, spoke to the creators led by Brahmā for the purpose of establishing the Goddess’s abode. (1)
Having heard the words of the gods, those headed by Brahmā bowed down to that Sovereign of the Universe and made a request; hear what it was, O Pot-born One! (2)
O Supreme Goddess! Your abode has been sought after by Śakra and the other gods, so that we may eternally behold you, the Great Sovereign (Maheśvarī), within this world. (3)
We are eternally lords of virtues because our greatness has been attained through your grace;
having reached your world, we behold your lotus feet.
These gods, Śakra and the others, are constrained by destiny for you;
though they desire to behold you, they are not permitted to break through the cosmic egg.
"Therefore, having fashioned a world here, you ought to make it your dwelling.
Thus was the Great Goddess Tripurambā entreated by the faces of Brahmā.
In that auspicious city on the peak of Mount Meru, fashioned by Viśvakarman,
she dwelt with her retinue just as she did in her own world.
Then, out of desire, Ambikā made Kāmeśvara her husband, who had been designated by the division of half of her own portion; she became wedded to him. (8)
Having thus heard what was spoken by Hayagrīva, the one born from a jar (Agastya),
filled with great curiosity regarding the supreme hearing of the Vibhavas, questioned him.
O Hayagrīva! O ocean of compassion! Where indeed is that city situated? Of what nature is it, and what is its extent, wherein she who is supreme dwells? (10)
How indeed did the Architect of the Universe come to know that place which is inaccessible even to Indra and the other gods? What is its name, and what is its configuration like? (11)
Moreover, when she was propitiated by Śakra and the other gods according to the ritual of the Śrīsūkta, that Mother Tripurā indeed became pleased. (12)
What is its ritual procedure, and of what nature is its hymn? What is the greatness of this hymn? You should tell me this. (13)
"O Hayānana! Show mercy to me, your devoted disciple!
Thus was that best of sages, the horse-faced one, questioned.
Considering that to be appropriate and having heard it, he spoke joyfully:
"Listen, O Pot-born One; I shall speak, for you are endowed with devotion and faith. (15)
This is not fit to be told to one who lacks faith, nor to one who is devoid of devotion, nor to a rogue;
you are in every way blessed upon this earth. (16)
O Sage, I know the reason why such enthusiasm for hearing this narrative is seen in you; this is not of small fruit! (17)
Devotion to all the embodiments of the qualities may be common to everyone;
however, devotion to the feet of Tripurā is difficult to attain in every respect. (18)
Wherever there may be devotion to Tripurā, that birth shall be the final one;
devotion to Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others is proclaimed here as merely the gateway. (19)
By gradually propitiating Viṣṇu and the other deities and attaining service at the feet of Śrī, a living being is liberated in every respect; not otherwise, even in tens of millions of kalpas.
I shall explain the reasoning here, so that you may have no doubt:
in this world, those who are followers of one endowed with universal sovereignty exist in varying degrees of excellence. (21)
Superior, middling, and inferior, they are satisfied with their own respective stations;
moreover, they point out the path for attaining the state above them without obstruction.

O Pot-born One! Just as at the beginning, Dvāraka, being pleased, granted unimpeded access through the gates and the attainment of the status of a Prāṅgaṇeśa, so indeed does he bestow [these fruits]. || 23 ||
Brahmā and the others are born from the gunas and are their worshippers;
you should have no doubt about this, for it is already well known to you. (24)

Even though there is non-duality of reality, from the perspective of worldly experience, the distinction between primary and secondary is clearly established by its regulation, just as, for example, among bodies, the head [is distinguished]. (25)
There is no confidence here for those who have committed evil deeds or for the blind who look on,
nor for those gods born from his feet who are ever intent upon service.
O Brahmin, you are highly fortunate that you have reached Śrī Parāra;
such is the greatness of this association—oh, what fortune! Oh, what austerity! (27)
Listen, O Brahman, to that which causes supreme devotion in you:
she who is dear to you, the virtuous princess named Lopāmudrā. (28)
Formerly, while she was staying in her father's house, she attained supreme devotion to the Supreme Being;
I shall tell you the cause of that, which no one else knows. (29)
The principal power of Tripura is named Bhagamālinī;
the king was always devoted to her service with his whole being. (30)
From her childhood, this pure-minded woman was devoted to the service of her father;
having observed the sequence of her father’s worship, she followed it exactly according to the proper order.
While he was performing the duties of kingship, he propitiated her;
thus, through long-term propitiation, as well as by devotion and meditative cultivation. (32)
That Blessed Lady was pleased and granted him a boon;
he chose the service of the feet of her who is worshiped by all the world.
She too, being pleased, perceived that true knowledge of Tripura;
and she, in turn, perceived that knowledge which was overflowing with an ocean of speech. (34)
Like a jewel being pulled from the ocean, through his grace the Vidyā attained the status of a Ṛṣi; she became clearly known by his name. (35)
"By the power of her association, devotion has arisen within you.
Having heard this detailed account of his wife's prosperity, Agastya (the one born from a jar) [spoke].
Being pleased, he honored his wife who was devoted to the feet of Śrī;
then, being likewise pleased, Hayāsya spoke to the one born from a jar (Agastya).
Listen, O son of Kalaśī! Being self-restrained, I shall fully declare to you the most purifying ritual procedure of the Śrīsūkta, which you have asked about. (38)
This should not be spoken to one who is not a devotee, nor to one who is devoted to other deities;
like a secret lore (vidyā), it must be guarded, kept most strictly concealed in all circumstances. (39)
The Śrīsūkta consists of sixteen verses; originating from the Veda, it was formerly beheld by Śrī and properly extracted from the ocean of the Vedas.
By propitiating the supreme Śakti Tripurā according to the prescribed rites, she attained the status of Mother of the World and became worthy of worship by all. || 41 ||
Having been propitiated for twenty-one billion years,
the supreme Tripurā, being pleased, invited him to choose a boon.
And having been chosen by her for that union (*sāyujya*), the Supreme Mother then said:
"O child! Without you, Viṣṇu is incapable of protecting [the world]. (43)
If this were not protected by him, it would fall apart in the blink of an eye;
therefore, there would be a violation of my destiny, which you ought not to permit now.
Therefore, I now grant this: I shall always bear your name and your very form; I will tell you how, so listen. (45)
I am proclaimed as Śrīvidyā; let my city be Śrīpura.
Let my wheel be the Śrīcakra; let my lineage be the Śrīkrama. || 46 ||
May this Śrīsūkta become mine; may it be the sixteenfold Vidyā of Śrī.
Known as Mahālakṣmī, I abide in a state of identity with you. 47.
And you, established in four forms, shall receive worship in my presence;
whatever is dear to you in this world shall also be dear to me. (48)
On the day of the descendant of Bhṛgu (Venus), you are worshipped by devotees according to the prescribed rites;
there, I too shall be especially worshipped by those devotees. (49)
There, she who is worshipped with hymns and mantras,
as well as with ritual services and various sacrificial substances, being pleased, bestows the desired objects.
And when consecrated with waters, milk and other substances, and the juices produced from fruits, she grants all desires within the yantra, or even in the image and so forth. (51)
In the daily,
occasional, and optional worship, as well as in other rites of mine,
one should recite the sixteen-verse Lakṣmī-sūkta during the bathing ritual of the Goddess. (52)
By reciting it even once, Lakṣmī shall dwell forever in his house;
or, if unable to perform the full worship, he who should always recite merely this hymn at its conclusion.
"Everything performed by him shall become complete, and I myself shall be pleased;
furthermore, through union with you, my Vidyā shall also become dear to me. (54)
Since I am the essence of knowledge, that seed-syllable of yours is entirely auspicious;
by means of it, I am designated as the Great Śrī-Ṣoḍaśākṣarī, the sixteen-syllabled [mantra] of perfection.
During the ritual services, one should recite the mantras originating from the Sūktas;
that worship shall become a Great Worship (Mahāpūjā), and because of it, I shall quickly become pleased.
In the hymn (sūkta), I am hidden in the form of its meaning, and my seed is also concealed;
I, in my full form, was prayed for by the seers from my father, the Purifier (Agni).
Nothing else anywhere in the world is more dear than your well-spoken words;
you are I, O Goddess, and I am you—there can be no difference between us two. (58)
"Whoever perceives a difference within her shall meet with supreme calamities.
Having thus granted this boon to Ramā, the supreme Tripurā [bestowed it].
"O Pot-born one (Agastya), as soon as this greatness of the Śrīsūkta was spoken, he immediately attained the state of the sky; therefore, you should never speak of this to anyone. (60)
Regarding those who are undevoted, deceitful, and inwardly devoid of faith—I shall now describe the extraordinary history of Śrīpura; listen. (61)
Merely by hearing it, one is liberated from all sins;
when that supreme goddess was entreated by the foremost of the gods, such as Brahmā.
"O Pot-born One! Remain here for the sake of being seen by Śakra and the other gods.
She, assuming a playful form, consented to that stationing.
Then, having summoned Tvaṣṭṛ to the exceedingly lofty peak of Mount Meru,
the Creator (Brahmā) commanded him regarding the construction of the city of Śrī for the Goddess.
Then Viśvakarman, bowing down to his great-grandfather, spoke thus:
"O Blessed One, I did not know where that city was situated."
"What is its measure, what is its form, what is its essence, and of what kind does it abide?
Tell me this, O Blessed One; having heard it, I shall act accordingly. (66)
Then the Creator of the World said: "Listen, O Architect of the Universe; I shall describe the dimensions, the configuration, and the nature of Śrīpura."
Listen also with a very clear and attentive mind to the form [of Tripurā], by hearing which one shall attain auspicious devotion to the feet of Tripurā. (68)
The golden mountain named Sumeru is the wondrously variegated body of the universe;
in its center is a great peak that measures four hundred yojanas.
"In that place, build a city for the goddess Śrī Tripurā for the sake of the world;
having heard what has been instructed by me, it must be carried out according to the proper ritual rules. (70)
Listen as I describe that which is captivating, exceedingly beautiful, and adorned with various types of ramparts, according to the established tradition of the world. (71)

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Arrangement of the Śrīcakra, Preceded by the Ritual of the Śrīsūkta," in the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories, within the dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya. || 4383 ||
Chapter Fifty-Four:
Description of the Auspicious City (Śrīpuravarṇana)
Situated outside the cosmic egg,
extending upwards for an infinite number of leagues, lies the ocean of nectar numbering many millions.
With its dancing waves and billows rising as high as Mount Sumeru,
in its center lies a jewel-island that dispels the mass of darkness with its radiance.
Extending for hundreds of millions of yojanas, it was exceedingly enchanting;
the ground was adorned on all sides with variegated groves of wish-fulfilling trees.
Situated there was her city, resplendent with all kinds of jewels,
extending for four hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
Of that same extent stood his palace, made of the essence of iron,
square, auspicious in every respect, and illuminating the horizons on all sides.
It rises four thousand yojanas high, is surrounded by a rampart,
and is adorned on the outside with four gates and a moat.
Within that, situated at a distance of seven thousand yojanas,
stands a wall made of bell-metal, of the aforementioned dimensions and exceedingly brilliant.
In that interval, it was crowded with hundreds of groves of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) and resplendent with hundreds of ponds, each ten yojanas in extent.
In the eight directions, it is joined with lakes of blooming lotuses extending for a hundred *yojanas*, situated on the outer half of the earth made of iron.
In the inner courtyard, which was fashioned of bell-metal and filled with various birds and deer,
there were eight houses made of bell-metal constructed within the grounds of the lotus-pool.
Adorned with many variegated designs and graced by fivefold enclosures,
it was one hundred yojanas in extent and height, and exceedingly beautiful.
On the great throne is Mahākāla, his body embraced by Kālī,
overflowing with the good fortune obtained through service at the feet of Tripurāmbā.
Having divided himself eightfold, he resides separately in the eight abodes;
constantly present, he is served by hosts of innumerable attendants.
Beyond the inner rampart made of bell-metal, at a distance of the aforementioned yojanas,
there is a wall constructed of copper, possessing a luster like that of the rising sun.
The ground in the middle of the house, including the doors, windows, and ponds, should be measured as prescribed;
it should be made of bronze or copper both inside and out, with a central area [specifically] of stone.
In the interval between those, as previously described, there was a forest of Kalpa trees;
within those dwellings, the exceedingly beautiful spring season shone forth.
Serving the Supreme Mother together with Madhumādhava and Śakti,
and joined by his own retinue, he prospers through his own glory.
The gate, the ponds, and the lotus-pond grounds, each measuring one *sāla*, are to be understood according to the method already stated; the specific details are now declared in due order. (18)
Then there was a palace made of silver, adorned with a grove of *santāna* trees;
it stood like the summer season, surrounded by the pure power of the planet Venus.
The rampart there is made of brass and contains groves of yellow sandalwood;
the rainy season shines there through the months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada.
The palace, made of the five metals and adorned with a grove of Mandāra trees,
shines there with two spears that possess the power of the autumn season and the month of Īśa.
Beyond that is the silver wall, indeed surrounded by the Pārijāta grove;
there the Himanta [season] shines with thousands upon thousands of Śaktis.
The trunk was made of refined gold and possessed the radiance of a hundred rising suns;
there stood a grove of Kadamba trees, thickly perfumed with the fragrance of wine.
Sweet with the humming songs of bees, crowded with the splendor of dance and song,
and beautiful with the sweet sounds of the flattering cries of flocks of parrots.
There resides that queen Mantriṇī, who deludes the world;
she is the goddess Saṅgītamāṭṛkā, renowned as Mātaṅgī. (25)

The *śaukā* and others are dark-complexioned (*śyāmalā*), while another, the *śārikā* and others, is a *hasantikā*; likewise, the *vīṇāveṇumukhā* and others are dark-complexioned and preceded by the syllable *la*. (26)
Śyāmalā, preceded by Rāja, and she who is herself considered the Mantriṇī, as well as Śrīmātṛkā and her other beloved—thus they are situated in the eight directions. (27)
Surrounded by tens of millions of Mātaṅga maidens, there then stood a rampart made of topaz, as previously described. (28)
There, the Lord of Siddhas, surrounded by Siddhas, dwells in that supreme [abode];
its rampart is made of rubies, and its edge is as red as a flame of fire.
Devotees of Tripurā, accompanied by young women, dwell at Caraṇa;
there, the Sāla tree is filled with Gomedaka gems by the Bhairava leaders.
The goddess Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī is surrounded by a multitude of Vaṭukas;
she is formidable, possesses the luster of a dark cloud, and holds a sword as her weapon.
She is eternally served by the lords of the eight crores of Bhairavas, by the eight Subhairavas, and accompanied by thirty-two crores of Baṭukas.
Meditating upon the lotus feet of the Great Queen, she shines with great splendor;
thereupon stands a Sāla tree made of vajra, and there flows the river Vajrā.
Surrounded by a moat that enters the ocean of nectar,
it shines brilliantly with its two banks composed of gold, gems, and diamonds.
There, the goddess Vajraśvarī is resplendent with vajra-ornaments, satisfied by the bestowing of the vajra, and worshipped by those headed by the Vajrin. || 35 ||
Within that [palace] is a beryl grove; there dwell the Nāgas, the sons of Diti, who are ceaselessly meditating upon the lotus feet of the Supreme Mother. (36)
Then there would be a palace made of sapphire; mortals are situated there, and within it are the guardians of the quarters, each stationed in their respective directions in due order.
Then there was the emerald Sāla tree, joined by groves of golden palm trees, which produced an abundance of the fragrance of intoxication from the flowing sap of the palm trunks. || 38 ||
There, the goddess Śrīdaṇḍinī appears in a dream surrounded by these [attendants], well-established and inflicting punishment upon those who have committed offenses. (39)
Then, overflowing with the ocean of internal bliss awakening through the service of honey, there stands within that enclosure a coral *sāla* tree. (40)
It was surrounded by numerous perfected sages and yogis;
moreover, its rampart was made of the nine precious gems, exceedingly beautiful and auspicious.
There, Viṣṇu shines with his feet served by his attendants and others; beyond that is a most radiant rampart composed of a multitude of various jewels.
There, the three-eyed Śiva, who is served by the Pramathas, resides;
beyond that is the Manomaya wall, which is vast and has a luster like the rising sun.
In the middle of that [area] there should be a pool of nectar (amṛtavāpī), situated in the central third of the ground, surrounded by a moat-shaped enclosure and filled with blossoming lotuses. (44)
It was beautifully adorned with swans, kāraṇḍava ducks, ruddy geese, and cranes;
in its center, it shone brightly upon a boat richly furnished with the nine gems.
Tārā, the savior of the multitude of devotees, is seated upon a lotus throne,
surrounded by Śaktis stationed on innumerable jeweled boats.
The staff-bearer never carries anyone across anywhere without an order;
however, the Sala tree, consisting of wisdom, is as clear as the orb of the moon.
There, the Ānandavāpikā (Pool of Bliss) is entirely beautiful as previously described;
there resides Amṛteśī, situated upon the sun and surrounded by Śaktis.
Within that [lotus], there is an inner space filled with fragrance, consisting of the bliss of wine;
no one drinks this without the command of Amṛteśānī. (49)
One should not cross the pond protected by Amṛta and Aiśvaryā;
therefore, the gatekeeper Ahaṅkāra is dark-complexioned in form.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, within it is also a pond named Mimarsā,
which is cool and still, carrying the essence of knowledge.
There, the goddess Kurukullā, the Great Sovereign, resides upon a boat; without her command, one cannot obtain that nectar there. (52)
Having drunk even a mere drop of that [nectar], which arises from the cessation of ignorance,
they abandon all suffering and behold the reality of the world unobscured.
Then the Sāla tree, whose essence is the sun and which is a mass of light, stood there;
and within it, the Sun was seated upon a lotus throne.
Accompanied by Mārtaṇḍabhairava and others, the twelve-fold forms of the Sun,
he is praised by his devotees whose bodies resemble the sun. (55)
Then King Soma, the one who covers the moon, possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons, stood there, scattering nectar with his rays.
In that interval, however, was the Śṛṅgārasāla, exquisitely variegated, fashioned from a multitude of gems known as Kaustubhas, and possessing a beautiful form. (57)
In the midst of that [ocean],
there was a ship named Śṛṅgāra, filled with the clear sentiment of erotic love (śṛṅgārarasa), wherein the Kaustubha gem had been fashioned as the mast.
Kandarpa himself was present there with Rati, joined by many millions of groups of Kandarapas, Ratīs, and Prītis. || 59 ||
The crest-jewel of the devotees of Śrī Tripurā rejoices while being served there;
beyond that, however, lies the Mahāpadma forest, thick with fragrance.
I shall now describe to you their terrestrial lotus-forest— their stalks, petals, filaments, and even their extremely long pericarps.
Their trunks are one thousand yojanas in length and thick as a gavyūti;
the length of their leaves is proclaimed to be twenty yojanas.
O son of Kalaśī! The petals are thirty yojanas long, and the filaments are fifteen yojanas in length.
The pericarps are proclaimed to be ten yojanas in extent;
there they stand, resembling bumblebees and jewels, reaching the height of mountain peaks.
The abode of the goddess Śrī Tripurā is exceedingly radiant within;
it is fashioned from the finest wish-fulfilling gems and adorned with various wonders. (65)
Therein, it is provided with four gates and well-sustained by a divine foundation;
the foundation consists of the form of fire, circular and endowed with its [respective] kalās.
It is five hundred yojanas in width and half that in height;
therein is the vessel consisting of the sun, endowed with twelve digits (kalās).
It is one thousand yojanas in width and one and a half [yojanas] in height;
there, it is filled with the nectar of immortality, delicious and sweetly fragrant.
There, the Moon, whose form is like nectar and who is joined on all sides by his digits,
remained upon the boat, sporting in the waves of the wine-nectar.
This is prepared for the drinking of those powers (śaktis) who reside within the Śrīcakra,
as well as for those stainless powers who dwell in the forest of the Great Lotus (mahāpadmāṭavī).
Having obtained the grace of the primary power (mukhya-śakti), they rejoice perpetually;
there is the great sacrificial pit (mahā-kuṇḍa) belonging to Agni, garlanded with the flames of the fire of consciousness (cidagni).
It is one thousand yojanas in length and likewise deep, possessing three ridges;
each ridge is one hundred yojanas high and wide.
There, the progenitor of the illustrious Goddess Tripurā is the fire consisting of consciousness (cinmaya),
surrounded by a garland of flames rising two thousand yojanas high.
Situated to the west of the house was a chariot consisting of the syllable *cakra*,
strewn with various clusters of jewels and extending for a thousand yojanas. (74)
Exalted by four virtues, exceedingly beautiful with its nine stages, it is equipped with the ten sense-faculties as horses and joined with the mind as its charioteer. (75)

And there stands the wheel of tradition (Āmnāyacakra), the charcoal (Aṅgāra), the ray of yoga (Yogaraśmi), the banner of the wind (Marudhvaja), the sky (Nabhas), the great canopy (Vitāna), which consists of all the worlds. || 76 ||
In the center of that palace of wish-fulfilling gems is the Lord of the Śrīcakra,
most beautiful, accompanied by the goddesses of the nine enclosures.
In the midst of that, upon the throne consisting of the five Brahmans, the Goddess Tripurā,
seated upon the lap of Kāmeśvara, shines resplendent in the form of light.

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Auspicious City," within the *Śrīpurāpākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Auspicious Tripurā) in the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* (Section on Greatness) of the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of sacred histories. || 54 ||
Having heard this wondrous account, Viśvakarman was greatly amazed;
immediately thereafter, he addressed these words to the Grandfather of all the worlds. (1)
O Grandfather, O Blessed One, this doubt has arisen within me in many ways; I ask about it here, and you ought to explain it to me.
By whom was this place created, when, and for what reason?
It has been heard that others who are not born of [divine] qualities have no access there.
Furthermore, the immortals, mortals, nāgas, and others are described there;
how is this situated, O God? O Lord, have mercy upon me. (4)
Thus questioned, the Lord of the World spoke to that architect of the universe:
"O Tvaṣṭṛ! Listen, I shall relate this well-guarded account."
At that time, we were devoted to the activities and forms at the beginning of creation;
Ambikā was propitiated by us with hearts always filled with agitation.
Tripurā is the supreme Śakti, whose nature is pure consciousness;
she is partless in the form of space, the auspicious one who consists solely of the syllable *vaṃ*. (8)
"O children, what is desired by you? Having heard these words of the incorporeal voice, we bowed and spoke thus: (9)
Having praised her with various hymns and joined our palms in reverence,
O Great Goddess, we too are constantly engaged in this task of the world.
"Indeed, directed by you, we do not find anyone superior to the descendant of Niṣadha;
having abandoned the state of abiding in your own true nature, nothing else pleases us. (11)
Just as those who have tasted the essence of nectar find no pleasure in consuming salt water, so please show us mercy, O Goddess of Gods! We find no delight in these ritual acts.
Thus addressed by the mouths of Brahmā, Tripurā spoke to us again: "O leaders headed by Brahmā, let this not happen to us in any way at this time."
"Destiny is extremely difficult to ward off; it was ordained by me alone in the past.
You should not think in this way; I shall grant you another desired boon."
Then we entreated that Tripurā, the creator of the worlds:
"If it is so, O Mother, then you are indeed the Great Goddess Maheśvarī, whose form consists of the qualities (guṇas) and the principles (tattvas). (15)
Having become the Queen of the Queens of all cosmic eggs in their governance, perform [this] there; we shall always [be present] through our attendance upon your form. (16)
"We shall find delight in this world even through the fulfillment of your command.
Having heard what we said, the supreme Tripurā spoke:
"Let it be so; for the sake of your welfare, I shall manifest a visible form.
However, I shall not abide within these [particular] cosmic eggs (aṇḍas), but rather among those who dwell in all cosmic eggs without exception. (18)
I create a common island of jewels in the ocean of nectar;
there, let the lords of the world worship me with a spirit of devotion. (19)
There, having kindled the fire consisting of consciousness within that sacrificial pit, when it blazes brightly and is pure,
meditate upon me as the auspicious one according to the nature of male and female, as desired.
Having become conformable to your meditative absorption (dhyāna), I shall govern the succession of cosmic eggs;
therein, for all those beginning with Brahmā who reside within the entire multitude of eggs, [I shall provide] continuous [guidance].
"I grant you the vision of a woman established in the state of grossness"; having spoken thus to us who were facing away, she vanished from sight.
Then, at her word, we emerged from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and,
having reached the ocean of nectar, [we traversed] the island of jewels on all sides.
Then, after searching for a long time, the Jewel Island was discovered;
it was composed of the nine precious gems and had filled the intermediate quarters of space with its own radiance. (24)
Having gone there and having fashioned an exceedingly beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of the prescribed dimensions, how indeed could the fire be joined therein? (25)
We fell into anxiety there, for there was neither fire nor fuel;
then the god Śiva fashioned fire from his own eye within the sacrificial pit.
Seeing him pure and facing toward tranquility, though lacking fuel, Viṣṇu himself, being well-aware, mentally provided the sacrificial wood.
Then, when the fire was kindled, I performed the ritual according to the rules: I made the mind the sacrificial animal, the intellect the clarified butter, and the ego the oblation.
And having purified the ritual implements and vessels for the supreme deity,
I meditated within my own internal fire upon such a form of the Goddess as a woman.
As soon as she had meditated upon the oblation being offered, that Supreme Goddess emerged from the fire of the sacrificial pit, manifesting in accordance with the form visualized in meditation.
This supreme power (Parāśakti), the most beautiful woman in the three worlds, having been praised by us there, emerged from that fire and went outside.
Then the Supreme One said to me, "Point out a seat for me.
Thus instructed, I prepared a supreme seat.
By the mere touch [of his hand], that seat instantly crumbled away; yet that very seat, fashioned from various excellent materials, appeared once more, shattered by the touch. (33)
Even those hundreds of seats provided with every possible comfort for me then fell apart, and at that time I was filled with shame.
Then, by her mere will, Sadāśiva—the god of all—manifested from the blink of an eye; and he, being in the fourth state (turya), along with her, both bowed down to that Goddess.
The supreme goddess said to them both, "Prepare a seat.
Having heard her words, Sadāśiva then meditated for a moment.
Countless millions of Sadāśivas and Īśvaras, who are the embodiments of all virtues, arrived from all of them. || 37 ||
Having extracted the essence, he fashioned five exceedingly beautiful forms;
among them, by a portion of Sadāśiva, was one as red as a mass of vermilion.
He fashioned for him an auspicious seat (phalaka) composed of the forms of the fourfold assembly of Īśa, Rudra, Hari, Vidhi, Śakti, and Saṅgha.
Then that Sadāśiva fashioned his feet from the materials constituting those [limbs],
and thereafter a bed-strewn with the essence of the entire earth.
Upon his head was spread a cushion, as soft as a cluster of swan-down feathers,
fashioned from a collection of the finest peaks of Mount Meru.
Having fashioned the cushion, Sadāśiva, the God of gods, bowed and said to that Goddess: "It is ready, O Mother; please ascend!"
In their midst, having paid homage to Sadāśiva, the Lord of the Guṇas, they said: "O God, this temple is indeed not a suitable seat. (43)
"Therefore, build a beautiful mansion supported by the sky.
Sadāśiva, considering that to be appropriate, constructed an auspicious dwelling.
Strewn with clusters of wish-fulfilling gems and adorned with various jewels,
that king of palaces was two thousand yojanas in extent.
It has four gates, consists of the four Vedas, and is adorned with the sacred traditions (Āmnāyas);
it is exceedingly resplendent with a vast canopy made of the ether.
Then, perceiving that excellent and enchanting mansion,
he created a beautiful great forest of lotuses all around it.
By him, that temple shone, possessing the characteristics as they have been fully described.
Thus, in that temple, the Sovereign Lady sat upon a throne of jewels.
Tripurā ascended, illuminating everything all around;
that Great Goddess was seated upon that jeweled lion-throne. 49.
Praised in many ways by countless Brahmās, Viṣṇus, Īśas, and Sadāśivas who constitute the fourfold forms, the Sovereign Lady spoke to Sadāśiva.
O Sadāśiva, perform for me the wondrous narration of the Ineffable (Anākhyā),
by which I may become known in the world as one whose form is fully understood.
Thus enjoined by her, Sadāśiva, the God of gods,
then reflected in his mind upon her narrative.
At that time, he was entreated by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the others:
"O Lord, this [plan] does not appear suitable; Parāmbikā is not [to be approached] in this manner. (53)
Consciousness, eternal and consisting of the seer, is the cause of both the existent and the non-existent;
through compassion, it has assumed the form of an object of meditation and thus become visible.
We consider that the Goddess, assuming the form of a woman without the support of a male, does not shine exceedingly because it is a source of public censure. (55)
Neither in this world nor in the next does a woman exist without reliance upon a man,
just as on earth a creeper cannot exist without a tree.
Therefore, find for this mother of the world a suitable and auspicious husband, so that everything we desire may be fulfilled. (57)
Having heard this speech from those embodiments of virtue, Lord Sadāśiva reflected for a long time and, with a resolute mind, spoke these words.
O you who possess a multitude of virtues, listen with concentrated minds to these words of mine:
this Goddess is higher than the highest, whose essential nature is pure consciousness alone. (59)
There was one alone at the very beginning, bestowing the nature of sovereignty;
for there existed nothing whatsoever that was either existent or non-existent, nor undivided or divided. (60)
By the very weight of the manifestation of her own inherent nature,
she illumines this variegated wheel of the world within herself, like the play of a mirror.
(561) No one equal to her has ever been made, nor could anyone be superior;
who here could be the husband of this mother of all the worlds? (62)
"Indeed, I would have no power to do anything at all here;
Śiva always speaks thus to us as we look on. (63)
Having understood our intention, that supreme goddess Tripurā offered a slight smile, radiant as ten million full moons.
Then there arose a great sound that shattered the multitude of cosmic eggs,
tearing through the networks of ears and deafening the horizons of the quarters.
He of great splendor blazed forth, devouring the entire circle of the quarters;
possessing a brilliance like the rising of ten million lightning bolts, he robbed all eyes of their sight.
By that great sound and splendor on all sides, they were deafened and blinded; wondering "What is this? they gathered there in amazement.
Then, in an instant, we beheld that Supreme Goddess,
resplendent upon a jeweled couch, her limbs as beautiful as his own.
Just as a reflection assumes the form of those who have united in union, so too [the Goddess], seeing herself adorned by the embrace of a man identical to her own, [became jealous]. (69)
O Creator of the World, they attained incomparable joy through the fulfillment of their own desires,
merely by beholding one another’s physical beauty, gracefulness, and ornaments.
As if casting aside that couple who were intensely absorbed in the pleasure of their embrace, the Supreme Lord then said to us: "O gods, your desired goal is accomplished. (71)
Indeed, for the sake of your desire, I have manifested in two forms; let our names be told so that we may attain renown here in this world. (72)
Having heard this, Lord Sadāśiva, seeing us bewildered regarding our name and ritual action, bowed to that Goddess and spoke for the sake of fulfilling our desires.
You are Kāmeśvarī and the god is likewise Kāmeśvara;
you are now the sovereign even over us, who are the souls of the kings of kings.
You are indeed the Queen of the Kings of Kings, and he is the King of the Kings of Kings;
you are indeed Tripurasundarī, and he is Tripurasundara.
Then, having praised that Supreme Goddess through the gateways of the elements, we further entreated her,
perceiving her to be standing there all alone.
"O Mother, you, the sovereign lady, ought to remain here with your retinue;
O Auspicious One, seeing you alone, we do not rejoice at all. (77)
Thus requested by us, she instantly created from her own body a power resembling herself, like a reflection. (78)
Thus he invoked that Śakti, Mahātripurasundarī:
"Create for me an excellent wheel of Śaktis that is suited to my purpose. (79)
Having said "Om," that goddess [bestowed] a retinue desired by all the world, born from a portion of herself, along with a most wonderful circle of powers (śakticakra).
By the power of the illustrious Mahādevī, he created a wondrous enclosure;
meanwhile, in the midst of that, the Great Goddess herself became eighteenfold.
Then the Goddess herself became the seventeenth, exceeding them;
in that interval, she was Mahātripurasundarī. 82.
She created nine powers from her own body, and having created them, she spoke to them:
"Each of you should separately create beautiful powers corresponding to yourselves. (83)
Having been addressed as "Mahāsundarī," they each separately brought them forth;
thus was the Greatly Auspicious Mother Tripurā created with her entire retinue. 84.
Having quickly fashioned their abode as the wheel of the world, she was served by those powers stationed in their respective places. || 85 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Location of the Śakticakra in Śrīpura, together with Kāmeśvarī and Kāmeśvara," in the Dialogue between Brahmā and Viśvakarman within the Lalitāmāhātmya, in the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories. || 4546 ||
The fifty-sixth chapter:
A description of the determination of the deities of the Śrīcakra, in the dialogue between Brahmā and Viśvakarman.
Having heard this wonderful account, Viśvakarmā, the architect of the universe, bowed down again and, filled with great curiosity, questioned him once more. (1)
O Blessed One, tell me the names, forms, and locations of those Śaktis who were created by the goddess Tripurāmbā, numbering as many as kings.
Tell me of those who were created by Mahātripurasundarī; describe their forms, how many in number they are, and also explain those whom she created.
And what is the nature of that abode which resembles the wheel of the universe?
By whom was it created—by the power of Śrī Tripurā? And where do which powers reside? (4)
"Tell me all of this; it is my desire to hear it.
Thus questioned by the Creator of the Universe, the four-faced one (Brahmā) spoke with joy.
Listen, O Tvaṣṭṛ, with an attentive mind, to this most secret [teaching]:
thus was she, the Great Tripurasundarī, first emanated.
She created nine powers for the purpose of emitting the flood of powers;
commanded by her, they addressed Tripurasundarī.
"O Mother, how shall we create, since your powers have been thus invoked? Having heard this, Mahātripurasundarī spoke again: (8)
"Relying upon your own power, create quickly; do not delay!
Having spoken thus, Adya created ten very red Śaktis.
Then, they became the bestowers of the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) and others in the world;
they held nooses, lotuses, and goads in their hands, and wore crescents of the moon as crests.
Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, īśitva, then vaśitva, prākāmya, bhukti, icchā, and prāpti follow in sequence. (11)
Desiring success, the ten goddesses emerged;
then those nine Śakris spoke to their mother, the Goddess.
"O Mother, quickly grant us a name; from that we shall create power.
Having heard them, Mahātripurasundarī spoke to those great Śaktis: 13.
"By means of yoga, through creation and the rest, you shall become yoginīs.
Then Ādyā, having prostrated before Tripureśī, made this request: || 14 ||
"O Mother, quickly prepare a place for the assembly of the Śaktis.
Thus entreated, the Supreme Śakti created a wonderful abode.
There is a single square terrace, two yojanas in height,
constructed with a width of two hundred yojanas.
Above that, leaving a space of four yojanas on each of the four sides,
there was a most beautiful inner enclosure with four gates.
It is twenty yojanas in width, exceedingly beautiful, and six yojanas in length; it is connected to that [city] at its edge. (18)
Rising for two yojanas, it has beautiful square terraces;
then, inside that, it is again two yojanas wide and one yojana high.
Thus, within its sixteen yojanas, there are three tiers;
the platform is sixteen yojanas high and resembles a sixteen-petaled lotus.
Rising twenty yojanas high from its base, it has the form of a lotus with eight petals;
its foundation is exceedingly beautiful for a span of twenty yojanas.

The ground-platform is one yojana in width, equal to the sun's [diameter], and it rises one yojana high from within that; it has the brilliance of Indra’s peak, and its interior depth is likewise the same.
The ground is ten-cornered and lusterless; within it is the union with Śiva.
It is as high as a yojana, and its radiance is equal to that of the ten corners, as before.
In the interval, there stands a ground ten yojanas in extent,
consisting of eight corners and beautified by a height of one yojana.
Its upper part is triangular in shape, measuring one *rasa* (six) *yojanas* across;
rising upwards from that base for one *yojana*, it is beautiful with a height equal to its width.
The ground of the *bindu* is perfectly circular, measuring one *yojana* in length and breadth; having thus prepared the site, she herself stands upon that circular ground. (26)
Seated upon the fivefold Brahma-throne, she graces the lap of Kāmeśvara;
from her own body have emerged the Śaktis, equal to herself, numbering eighteen. (27)
These [energies], having been sequentially deposited from their own level onto the level three levels below, are the presiding deities of the lunar digits, the fortnights, and the days. (28)
I shall tell you their names according to the reason for which they are called "eternal" (nityā):
the first eternal goddess is Kāmeśvarī, and the second is Bhagamālinī.
Nityaklinnā and Bheruṇḍā, then Vahnivāsinī; after that Mahāvidyeśvarī, and beyond that Śivadūtī. (30)
Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākikā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā, and Jvālāmālā after that. (31)
In the [mandala] named Citra, they are placed respectively on the left, the back, and the right;
by means of the application of the fivefold sequence, they are established upon the triangular ground.
She herself, the seventeenth eternal one who was previously described as the sixteenth,
has attained union through the conjunction of austerity and power.
Then, having placed before himself that goddess Mahātripurasundarī who presides over the ground of the Bindu, he should seat her there at the beginning of the [mantra].
The nine Yoginīs previously mentioned were also created by her; and by them, too, names were obtained according to their respective functions in due order. (35)
Then there is the Manifest, the Secret, the More Secret, and the Supreme;
the Oral Tradition, that which Transcends the Akula, the Partless, and the Esoteric. (36)

In that very same way, the one called the "Great Secret" (Atirahasyā) and the "Secret of the Higher and Lower" (Parāpararahasyā) have been sequentially established within the wheels (cakras) of the Goddess; listen to that. (37)

In the square [mandala], there are eight petals for the kings and then eight for the nāgas; subsequently, [the syllables] are placed individually in the directions, intermediate directions, the nāga-points, the fire-corner, and above.
Then that Yoginī, known as Prakaṭā, sequentially established ten Śaktis created by herself below the earth.
Furthermore, having created the eight powers consisting of Brāhmī and the other Mātṛkās,
he established the powers of the [eight] classes in the second stage.
Then he created a group of ten Śaktis known as the Prakaṭās and established them in succession upon the third level.
Then, although she was named Guptā, upon seeing the king's residence, she created that many Śaktis; thereafter, she whose name was Guptatarā [created more].
Transcending the various traditions and being indivisible yet distinct from one another, He created diverse powers according to the arrangement of His own state. (43)
He manifested seven secret powers (śaktis),
and he indeed created one power whose name was most secret.
Aṇimā and the others also separately created hundreds upon hundreds of Śaktis, each possessing a form identical to her own, complete with weapons, garments, and ornaments. (45)
She who is the Mistress of the Bindu-cakra is Mahātripurasundarī;
she has been appointed by the Root Goddess to provide the names and forms for the Śaktis.
He gave individual names to each of those ten goddesses created on the third level, according to their respective actions. (47)
Knowing the rules for the reality of mudrās, and having bodies whose essence is all mudrās, the goddesses bring forth joy; therefore, they are called "mudrā-samā" (equal to mudrās). 48.
Having produced joy, she excessively agitates the worlds;
she causes them to melt, attracts them, brings them under her control, and even intoxicates them. (49)
The Sovereign Goddess sows, causes to sprout, and likewise moves within the sky; she divides into three parts and brings forth the nature of the womb.
Thus, these powerful mudrās are known as Saṅkṣobhiṇī (the Agitator), Vidrāviṇī (the Dissolver), Ākarṣaṇī (the Attractor), and thereafter Vaśaṅkarī (the Subjugator). || 51 ||
Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Trikhaṇḍā, and Khecarī—these, along with Bīja and Yoni, are [to be placed] respectively in the cardinal directions, the corners, and above and below. (52)
In this same way, there are three stages: Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and Kaumārī; then Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, and thereafter Māhendrī. (53)
Cāmuṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī—these and others such as these are established here;
they possess limbs, weapons, ornaments, and garments identical to those of Brahmā and the other [deities]. || 54 ||
The mudrās, however, have a reddish luster and are joined with the noose (pāśa) and goad (aṅkuśa) mudrās;
they hold red goads and are beautifully adorned with rubies. || 55 ||
Then, created by the one named Guptā for the sake of attracting the desires of devotees,
there is first Kāmākarṣiṇikā, and the next is Buddhyākarṣiṇikā.
Then there is Ahaṅkārākarṣiṇī, and likewise Śabdākarṣiṇikā;
similarly, Sparśākarṣiṇikā, and after that Rūpākarṣiṇikā. || 57 ||
The attractor of tastes is preceded by scent; the attractor of mind is preceded by resolve;
the attractor of speech is preceded by courage; the attractor is preceded by mindfulness. || 58 ||
The first is the Attractor of Names, and the next is the Attractor of Seeds;
likewise, there is the Attractor of the Self, and after that, the Attractor of Nectar.
Thus, the sixteen petals of power, beginning with Śarīrākarṣiṇī,
have been meditated upon by Guptayoginī and are situated starting from the left of the front petal.
Resplendent, resembling white silken garments, and graced with the beauty of full youth,
they are adorned with the noose, the goad, and the vessels of nectar for bestowing gifts as their weapons.
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgapūrvikā, Madanā, Anaṅgamadanā, Aturā, and Anaṅgādyarekhikā. (62)
Aṅgaveśinī, Anaṅgā, Anaṅgāṅkuśā, and Anaṅgādyamālinī—these, known as the most secret [mantras], arose from Akhyā; they did not enter the dwellings. || 63 ||
Red in color and resembling silk garments, they are stationed in the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions;
a noose, a blue lotus, a vessel, and a goad are held in their hands. (64)
Saṃkṣobhiṇī, Vidrāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Āhlādinī, Sammohinī, Stambhinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, and Vaśaṅkarī. || 65 ||
Then there are Rañjinī, Unmādinī, and likewise Arthasādhinī; then Sampattipūraṇī, Mantramayī, and Dvandvakṣayaṅkarī. || 66 ||
Established in various corners according to the tradition,
they are seated starting from the front and proceeding counter-clockwise, possessing a reddish luster and adorned with red garments and ornaments.
With four arms, they shine, holding a noose, a jar of nectar, a mirror, and a goad;
they are the bestowers of supernatural powers (siddhis) and prosperity, and thereafter [comes] Priyaṅkarī.
Then she is remembered as the performer of auspiciousness and the fulfiller of desires;
likewise, she is the liberator from suffering and the pacifier of death. (69)
Then Aṅgasundarī, who wards off obstacles, and Saubhāgyadāyinī are likewise situated in the corners of the rows as before. (70)
Holding a noose, a casket of ornaments, and a goad with their four hands,
they possess radiant forms and are adorned with garments and jewelry.

The Śaktis who have transcended the family (kula), who are fully manifest and endowed with youth, bestow the power of knowledge and sovereignty; therefore, they are remembered as being composed of knowledge (jñānamayī). || 72 ||
Then follows Vyādhivināśinī, then Ādhārā and the others who possess the nature of the vowels;
then Pāpaharā, Anandamayī, and Rakṣāsvarūpī. (73)
And [the goddess] Īpsitādya; these are situated in the ten-spoked [cakra] as before, holding nooses, gifts, and the axe in their hands, with red limbs and ornaments. (74)
The pure Śaktis known as Nigarbhā have been meditated upon;
they are Vaśinī, Modinī, likewise Vimalā, and then Aruṇā. (75)
Jayinī, Sarveśvarī, and Kaulinī are the Śaktis;
born of the secret Yoginīs, they possess a radiance like that of a ruby.
In the corners of the bow, those with hands adorned with red ornaments are beautifully situated in the previously mentioned order.
And one Śakti, called Atirahasyā, arose in the south-eastern corner;
thus were those Śaktis created in the wheel by the Prakṛti-Śaktis. (78)

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deities of the Śrīcakra," in the *Śrīlalitāmāhātmya*, within the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* of the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of glorious histories. || 4624 ||
The fifty-seventh chapter:
A description of the determination of the deities of the Śrīcakra.
