Having heard what was spoken by the Creator Tvaṣṭṛ, he again asked respectfully:
"O Grandfather, this Śrīcakra, the maṇḍala of Śakti, has been heard. (1)
Tell me, as I ask you, the reason for the perfection of the powers;
likewise, why is there a place devoid of power in the eight-spoked wheel and the triangle?
"By what means did that great eternal Ṣoḍaśī attain union [with him]?
Thus questioned by Tvaṣṭṛ, the four-faced one then spoke with joy.
O Viśvakarman, listen to this great secret that has been concealed:
the sixteen eternal [energies] were created by the Greatly Auspicious Tripureśānī.
The other powers were created by Mahātripurasundarī; their individual names have been defined solely according to their respective functions. (5)
That power which is the Great Goddess, known as Tripurā and most exalted—
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is her eternal manifestation.
Abiding as a partial manifestation within the forms of Brahmā and the other gods, that Great Goddess,
consisting of pure consciousness, carries out the entire cycle of activity of the world.
Although she is the Mother who is an indivisible single essence and whose body is pure consciousness alone,
she manifests in manifold ways through the radiance of her own sovereignty. (8)
Just as the sun with its thousand rays, the swan, or the jewel of the sky, though single, appears manifold; or as the ocean remains [vast] even when standing alone.
Just as a single mirror exists with a thousand reflections, so does that which consists of waves, crests, and foam exist as many through its manifold nature. 10.
Likewise, this supreme state also exists as consisting of both difference and non-difference;
its powers, whose nature is that of parts, are proclaimed as Aṇimā and the others.
Through the power of her autonomy, she assumes a gross form;
that which is her power and the cause of her activity remains established in that very manner.
Thus created, those powers, deluded by the great illusion (mahāmāyā), vied with one another for their positions due to their respective high status and pride. || 13 ||
Seeing that dejection had arisen within her circles of power (śakticakra),
Mahātripurasundarī spoke at the command of Mahādevī.
Listen now, all you Śaktis, to my words:
there is no place here in the presence of the Goddess for those whose minds are possessed by rivalry and anger. (15)
"That state is difficult to attain; you shall find it through the practice of austerity, and not otherwise.
Having said this, he himself first performed a most great and wonderful penance.
Having seen Mahātripurasundarī devoted to asceticism,
all the others as well performed penance with restrained minds. (17)
While the host of Śaktis was thus engaged in ascetic penance there, a very long time passed; then Parā, being pleased, spoke.
"O children, I am pleased with your penance; I shall grant you a suitable abode.
Having spoken thus, Mahātripurasundarī assigned them their place.
Then the Supreme Goddess, who had bestowed upon her the sovereignty over all the wheels,
established the Nityās and the powers of the Self within the triangular ground.
Then, on each side of the group of five, there was a constant group of sixty-four;
although they were situated facing him as prescribed, he did not consider that to be much.
Furthermore, she performed an extremely difficult penance;
likewise did Kāmeśvarī and Bhagamālinikā as well. (22)
Considering that place not sufficient, the two performed supreme austerity;
while Śakti and Maṇḍalaka were thus engaged in penance, Śivā [remained there].
Not seeing his own [consort] alone, he did not consider that to be right;
then, having recognized her as the beloved Mahātripurasundarī, [he rejoiced].
He dispatched ten Śaktis from Tripurā’s limbs and weapons;
once released, they took their positions around Mahātripurasundarī.
They asked her, and the goddess said, "Seek a place through austerity.
Having spoken thus, they first performed intense austerity together with their powers (śaktis).
Furthermore, the Goddess, considering herself to be alone, gazed around her.
From that gaze, powers (*śakti*) as numerous as the Vedas were born. (27)
Having seen the entire host of Śaktis, who possessed the luster of gold, held lotuses, and were adorned with white garments and ornaments, always devoted to ascetic penance; || 28 ||
They too set their minds upon asceticism and departed; Tvaṣṭṛ likewise did so.
He then beheld again the four Śaktis born all around him.
Holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and a goad, with red limbs and ornaments,
possessing three eyes, and devoted to asceticism— thus they beheld their ancestors.
Furthermore, others were created, holding nooses, books, and rosaries, as well as goads; they were adorned with red-colored ornaments. || 31 ||
Furthermore, that same number of Śaktis were created again, possessing the luster of crystal;
they stood performing austerities, holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, the boon-granting gesture, and a goad.
Furthermore, having created those two [Śaktis], he saw them standing before him, adorned with red ornaments and devoted solely to ascetic penance. || 33 ||
Then, seeing her advanced in asceticism, the Goddess of Tripura said to that Nityā Ṣoḍaśikā: "O child, choose the boon you desire."
Considering all other states to be insignificant, she chose union (sāyujya) alone;
and there she attained the supreme sixteenth state, the highest union.
Those four goddesses who were born from her own limbs became fivefold; having herself become the fifth, she remained there, satisfied and equanimous toward them. (36)
By that, those five attained the state of being a pentad and the name-pentad;
[they became] the primordial Ratneśvarīs, and after that, the possessors of desire (Kāmadhuk).
Likewise, [he attains] the lordship of Kalpalatā, then the station of Kośeśvarī,
the state of Lakṣmīśvarī, and the station on the seat of the multitude of Śaktis for those who are at the end.
And Śivā bestowed upon each of them the sovereignty over a thousand Śaktis,
along with jewels that grant all desires and treasuries named Kalpalatākośa.
Know those powers, O Tvaṣṭṛ, to be individually designated by the name Lakṣmī;
they are twenty-five thousand in number, each distinct from the others.
Each serving their own respective lord, there are one thousand for each;
thus, the powers (śaktis) of the Root Goddess (Mūladevī) number five thousand.
There, Sidhalakṣmī is the first, Rājamātaṅginī is the second, Bhuvaneśānī is the third, and Vārāhikā is considered the fourth. || 42 ||
These have been declared as the Ratneśvarīs; now hear of the Kāmadughās:
the first is Sudhāpīṭheśvarī, and after her is the supreme Sudhāsūḥ.
The third is Amṛteśānī, and the fourth is Annaprapūraṇī;
then there are the Kalpalatās, and beyond those, the five Kāmas.
Pārijāteśvarī, and Kumārī after her;
then Pañcabāṇeśvarī, and Paraṃjyoti after that. || 45 ||
Parā, Niṣkalā, Śāmbhavī, Ajapā, Mārṭkā, and Parā—these are declared to be the Kośeśvarīs; now hear of the Lakṣmīśvarīs.
Then Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and the supreme one beginning with Triśakti, as well as Sāmrājyalakṣmī and Ramā—these are the five deities. (47)
Thus, gratified by the ascetic penance of the five goddesses,
she granted them positions in proximity, one after another, above the Binducakra.
In the corners beginning with the southeast (Āgneya), due to the excellence of his ascetic penance,
he bestowed incomparable prosperity upon Mātaṅginī and Vārāhī.
The state of being a minister, the cause for deliberating upon the affairs of all the worlds;
and the state of being a female staff-bearer for Vārāhī, the cause for the punishment of the wicked. || 50 ||
Then, after some time, the goddess, being pleased by his service, granted a central position to Hemaharin and Maṇisuvapraya.
Thus, pleased by his specific austerity, Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśī, and Bhagamālinī once again granted him a station.
Having granted them the status of Samaya-devis, he assigned places for the goddesses in front of him, behind him, and on his left and right sides. (53)
But that goddess who was manifested under a most secret name attained, through the excellence of her asceticism, a place upon the earth within the Vajrasālā grove.
Because she possesses sovereignty on the banks of the Vajra River, resides in a temple, and is the Mistress of Vajraratna, she is therefore considered Vajreśvarī. || 55 ||
Furthermore, due to the excellence of her asceticism, Kāmeśvarī and the others obtained a place at the corners of the triangle; likewise, Kāmeśvarī once again [attained it].
And by the power of her asceticism, she attained the second station among the eight spokes;
likewise, there is another power, Mahātripurasundarī.
And by that goddess, having been established in the stations in due order,
she was thus distributed and installed within the nine wheels.
She herself manifested in nine ways as the presiding deity of each, becoming Tripurā, Tripureśī, and likewise Tripurasundarī. (59)
Then there is Tripuravāsinī, then the glorious Tripurā, then the supreme one;
then Tripuramālinī, Tripurā Siddhā, and Tripurāmbikā. || 60 ||
And the ninth is Mahātripurasundarī herself, the sovereign of the Tantra;
she stands at the forefront of each respective enclosure, possessing a form identical to that [of the central deity].
All the Śaktis stood facing Mūladevī;
likewise, Brahmā and the others beheld everything surrounded by the host of Śaktis.
Thinking that this was not correct, the Lord of Desire (Kāmeśa) made this request:
"O Lord of Desire, O Blessed One, O God, you too must create [beings] from a portion of yourself. (63)
Since it is not appropriate for the retinue to have the form of Śiva,
we consider the host of powers alone to be the poison. || 64 ||
Then the god Kāmeśvara, from his own portion, from the portion of Śakti,
from both portions, and from another [portion], created those numbered as the Vedas.
Then [he saw] those named Mitrīśa, Ṣaṣṭhīśa, Auḍḍīśa, and Caryānātha, possessing crystal-like luster and holding a book, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a lotus, and consciousness (cit).
[Visualize them] as wearing white garments and ornaments, possessing three eyes, with red Śaktis, seated upon lotus-thrones, and having serene faces and eyes. || 67 ||
He made those preceptors of the Śakti-mantras peaceful in form, and he said to them, "You yourselves must create the preceptors of the various Vidyās. || 68 ||
Then he created there the groups known as the Divyas, followed by those known as the Siddhas; the third, known as the Mānavas, he created in due order.
Then the Fourth [Lord] created nine highly effulgent protectors, the masters of all sciences, who were as numerous as the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and who were the embodiments of Time.
Having thus created the maṇḍala of the Guru and performed most intense austerity,
Tvaritā attained her station upon the back [of the deity]. (71)
There, indeed, the temples of the divine, the perfected ones (siddhas), the multitudes of humans, and the gurus are situated in three rows in successive order.
There they attain the state of the supreme goddess Tripurā,
having worshipped her through the yoga of complete devotion according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
"Awakened by their gurus, they subsequently attain the supreme state.
Thus has that which you asked—the most profound and great secret—been explained to you. (74)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Definition of the Deities of the Divine Current and Others in the Śrīcakra," within the Lalitāmāhātmya of the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories. 4689.
p.582) Then Tvaṣṭṛ again respectfully questioned the four-faced one:
"O Creator of the World! I ask you; you are the gurus, appearing in the form of the multitude [of deities]."
Why did they not become equal in number?
Tell me that, as well as the names of all of them, and then the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) of Agni shall be described. || 2 ||
In that regard, describe also by whom that fire was produced;
and for what reason did you all assume female forms in that sacrificial pit?
O All-pervading Lord, Parāśakti has reflected upon this cause;
I am not satiated even by hearing this wondrous narrative repeatedly.

Who indeed could ever be satiated while drinking the nectar of the stories of the Supreme Power, who is the very form of one's own Self—unless, being struck by fate, one were like a withered stump? 5.
Tell that to me, O Blessed One, if it be something I may hear;
having heard what was spoken by the Creator of the Universe, the Grandfather became pleased.
Being composed, listen to the ancient and wonderful story of Tvaṣṭṛ;
being pleased, I shall relate to you how Pārvatī was protected on all sides.
Those who were created by the Lord of Kings of Kings, beginning with Mitreśa,
are all masters of the science of speech (vāgvidyā), whose nature is that of pure consciousness. (8)
Paśyantī, Madhyamā, Vaikharī, and likewise Parā—
the fourfold Power consisting of sound thus unfolds.
I shall explain that sequence to you, which is well-guarded in all respects.
For that power known as Tripurā consists of pure self-awareness.
Therein, neither the organs of speech nor the mind exist in any way;
she is the Supreme Goddess, whose form is the Self, the essence of all that exists. 11.
Neither dharma nor the possessor of dharma exists, because of the relinquishing of all dharmas;
it is the consciousness that is the support of all, pure, solitary, and beyond the range of speech.
And its consciousness is the Self; nothing more exists than that. That very [consciousness] is absolute sovereignty, and is therefore called Māyā. (13)
Possessing an inconceivable and unassailable majesty, and being the refuge of all,
it itself repeatedly conceptualizes its own stainless self in manifold ways.
By mere play, this very conceptualization, whose essence is sound, having been set in motion, [manifests] as the entire web of the world through its divisions of gross, subtle, and intermediate. (15)
It is established that [speech] is fourfold by way of its subtle and causal distinctions.
Among these, that which is gross in form is proclaimed as *vaikharī*. (16)
In that regard, it is said that the essence of sound is unmanifest, while its nature as phonemes is manifest;
being both worldly and transcendental, it exists everywhere in two ways. (17)
Therein, the unmanifest is sevenfold, consisting of the sprout of the Brahman-sound:
Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and [Niṣāda]. (18)

These seven notes, beginning with Niṣāda, are produced from the strings, the throat, and other sources; they are distinguished by the numbers six, four, five, three, two, and eight, which correspond respectively to the oceans, elements, fires, eyes, and serpents. (19)
However, when further divided in this way, they become innumerable.
This very celestial configuration consists of seven preceptors.
By him, Mitrīśa, the divine currents were proclaimed;
the manifest, extraordinary, and knowledge-filled tetrad of peak-syllables (kūṭa) is [thus established]. 21.
The hosts of Siddhas have that as their support; therefore, these are said to be equal in number to the Vedas.
They are declared to be the lineage-gurus of the multitude of Siddhas, having been manifested by Ṣaṣṭhīśa.
The worldly *mātṛkā* should be the self consisting of the eight *kuṭeśvarīs*; human beings are dependent upon them, and therefore they are eight in number.
Thus, nineteen [disciples] stood in the three currents;
these men, originating from Auḍḍīśa, were eight in number. (24)
Every sound consists of time, having as its ultimate limit three measures (mātrās);
it is joined with a mass of resonance and the eightfold group of veils (varaṇas).
Therefore, there shall indeed be nine protectors born from Caryanātha;
they are the delimiters of time and take refuge in the fourth state (turiya).
Then there is Prakāśa (the Light), then that called Vimarśa (Reflective Awareness), then Ānanda (Bliss) known as Jñāna (Knowledge);
then Satya (Truth), Pūrṇa (Fullness), Svabhāva (Essential Nature), Pratibha (Intuition), and the one named Subhagā (the Auspicious One). || 27 ||
Thus, these nine lords of mine are the presiding leaders of the currents (oghāḥ);
the current is fourfold, according to the divisions of the Vidyās and the divisions of the Yugas. (28)
Because they are mixed together, the gurus are established as being mixed with the Śaktis;
furthermore, there may be a fifth current (ogha), which is the initiator of the Guru-vidyā.
Those who travel outside the wheel are twelve or eleven *rasa*s (yojanas) in measure;
we are perfected ones (*siddhas*) of divine nature, as are the Kumāras and other human beings.
Thus have been declared the gurus, beginning with Nṛsiṃha, who have arisen from the Ogha.
Now, I shall describe to you the nature of Agni as consisting of consciousness; listen in due order.

He who is Mahādeva Maheśvara, the third [form] in the embodiment of the qualities (guṇamūrti), consists of darkness (tamas) and action (kriyā); yet he is the embodiment of goodness (sattvamūrti), blossoming and inwardly composed of consciousness (cinmaya).

Situated within the bodies of embodied beings is the threefold path that is free from ailment, located respectively on the right, the left, and in the middle— namely, the Piṅgalā, the Iḍā, and the Suṣumṇā.
Therein, the two [aspects] consisting of will, action, and knowledge exist as distinct;
the wise, the noble ones, know the middle path to be bound by Rāhu. (34)
Having the nature of the vibration of consciousness, she emerges upward from the two sides that have been obstructed;
she makes the desire for action conscious, and for that reason mortals are indeed sentient beings (cetana).

Associated solely with the desire for action due to the obstruction of the path of knowledge, these conscious beings [experience] the upward flow of the pure consciousness that has become their substratum. 36.
Because they obstruct the upward path of those moving horizontally and remain fixed in a horizontal state,
they do not perceive any past or future within themselves at any time.
Therefore, all those animals are indeed equal to insentient things;
such being the case, Mahādeva, who possesses three eyes, is superior even to that.
Within us, the central channel (madhyamā-nāḍī) is interpenetrated and is the locus of consciousness;
therefore, our internal consciousness is perceived as full. || 39 ||
Within Mahādeva, however, due to the overflow of knowledge,
the central channel (madhyamā nāḍī), which is of the nature of consciousness, was split open above that in the region of the forehead.
Consciousness itself, existing as fire, possesses the state of an internal abundance of darkness;
therefore, it is renowned as the "Fire of Consciousness" (cidagni) produced from that eye.
Now I shall explain that to you, since it is conceived in the form of woman;
listen, O Viśvakarman, for whatever happiness exists in the world is of the nature of consciousness (cidātman).
Therefore, the delight of even animals is established in pleasure with their whole being;
for that which brings happiness and is beautiful in this world is evident through direct perception. (43)

Whatever form is beautiful and is always beheld by people in the world, that is the form of women, due to their nature of concealing happiness. Furthermore, I shall tell you of that other [form] which is supreme and consists of consciousness.
The universe, which is of the nature of one's own majesty, is manifested through absolute freedom. || 45 ||
Indeed, everything is strictly determined by destiny and by one's own inherent power;
yet, out of delusion, the vain conceit "I am the doer" persists.
If the agent acts by himself, why is anything else observed? Even so, tell me, how could there be the attainment of what is undesired? (47)
Therefore, everything beginning with creation is but her manifestation;
thus, meditation upon her as consisting of womanhood has been revealed by her alone.
All the manifold variety of the universe is based upon His sovereignty;
thus did the Great Queen then abide within the palace of the wish-fulfilling gem.
Having beheld that king of palaces situated within the great lotus-abode,
Mahādeva Sadāśiva realized that even this was not the ultimate reality.
Having received the command of the Śrī Devī, he constructed the city as described;
and all those who dwell within the cosmic eggs—the gods, the Daityas, mortals, and others—[were established there].
Having worshipped Tripureśānī, they attained liberation in the state of *sālokya*;
they dwell there, each separately, in their respective locations. (52)
Indra, Brahmā, and others likewise do not dwell for long in that city;
rather, having attained perfectly pure sovereignty over various regions within its interior, they reside there.
Having departed from there for ten million times the duration of each respective period of time,
they indeed enter the supreme state that is beyond the reach of speech and mind.
In the meantime, however, Brahmā, Indra, Candra, and the others arrived;
having previously attained union (sāyujya), they remained present everywhere. || 55 ||
Now, joined with that very rite which exists there,
they have reached other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), numbering sixty thousand.
Six hundred and sixty-three *sāyujya*s have been traversed by Brahmā;
thus has the entire measurement situated within Śrīpura been recounted to you. (57)
"Build a beautiful city here on Mount Meru according to the method described, wherein the Sovereign of the Auspicious City, Tripurāmbā, shall reside. (58)
"Wherever we remain, we constantly behold her who is beautiful to the eye.
Hearing these words of the Creator (Dhātṛ), Viśvakarmā was greatly amazed. (59)
With his heart overflowing with joy and contemplating what was ordained by the Creator, he set his mind upon constructing Śrīpura for the Goddess on the peak of Mount Meru. (60)

Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Siddhis up to the State of Union (Sāyujya), preceded by the Description of the City of Śrī," within the *Māhātmya-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-lalitā-māhātmya*, in the *Tripurā-rahasya*, the most excellent of glorious histories. || 4749 ||
Chapter Fifty-Ninth: A Description of Nārada’s Awakening of Bhaṇḍa, in the Dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya.
Having thus heard the exceedingly beautiful words of Hayagrīva,
Agastya (Kumbhodbhava), eager to hear more of that narrative, spoke again.
O Blessed One, the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, who has the face of a horse, has arrived;
he desires to create obstacles to the penance of the gods, who are surrounded by fire.
Having observed the gods turning away, he departed for the empty city;
tell me that in great detail—what did he do there? (3)
As I listen to you recounting the story of Laliteśānī, my desire to hear it again truly increases all the more. (4)
Thus questioned by Kumbhaja, the horse-faced sage said:
"Listen, O Pot-born one, to this wondrous and most marvelous tale."
When the demon Bhaṇḍa had departed, the divine sage Nārada then returned from the sky like an autumnal cloud to Śūnyaka.
As that divine sage was approaching through the sky, playing upon his auspicious lute, the demon Bhaṇḍa beheld him resembling a rain-bearing cloud.
Having approached and brought the Sage there, the Daitya honored him;
and having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, he spoke these words with palms joined in reverence: (8)
"O celestial sage, welcome! It has indeed been a long time since I have desired to see you.
Out of compassion, look upon your disciple; a compassionate glance from you is difficult to obtain."
"Tell me, O twice-born ones, the firm state of those who are free from old age and whose [karmic] existence is exhausted;
for brahmins are generally timid, and my preceptor is bewildered by fear. (10)
"O gods, you have not known the strength of my arms, which brings fear even to the asuras; if you were to worship Śakti, she would become gracious. (11)
"Your defeat will be certain; therefore, create an obstacle.
Having been told this by the hosts of Daityas, I arrived there with the intent to slay him.
Seeing those gods, including Indra, consumed by the flames of fire,
I returned to my place delighted and asked about the matter at hand.
How did the gods, seized by forest fires, come to be reduced to ashes? Was anyone there liberated? O Lord of Sages, explain that to me.
Thus questioned, the divine sage smiled and said to the lord of the Daityas:
"I must never harbor envy toward the lords of the Daityas."
"We never speak untruth anywhere, for we rely solely on truth;
why then do you speak like one who is deluded, even though you are a learned man? (16)
Is it not indeed a perverse rule that your intellect is such as this,
since you were seen by me filled with joy at a time for sorrow? (17)
O Great Goddess, those enemies of yours have become exceedingly powerful through your support;
they have manifested for the sake of slaying you, having been gratified by the foremost of the Śakras and others.
Emerging from the fire-pit of consciousness is the Supreme Goddess Lalitā,
the sovereign of all worlds, possessing a divine form and extraordinary, great power.
Equipped with all weapons and surrounded by multitudes of spears, she will come to slay you; why indeed do you rejoice like a fool? (20)
Having heard what was spoken by Nārada, the king of the Daityas laughed and said:
"Surely I have said this before: Brahmins are by nature timid."
O Sage, you know that I am not directly terrifying to Death;
Viṣṇu is the most powerful among the gods, yet he was defeated by me in battle.
I am the powerful lord of one hundred and five eggs;
I am the creator of gods, asuras, and others, and of the entire succession of worldly weapons and missiles.
The lineage of gods headed by Brahmā and Viṣṇu abide under my control;
why then are you afraid of a woman? By nature, women are weak. (24)
In the meantime, within the inner apartments of the Daityas, the wives of Bhaṇḍa, led by Sammohinī,
brought the celestial sage along with groups of female companions.
Having honored the tiger among sages who had arrived with excellent seats,
water for the feet, respectful offerings, and abundant sacrificial materials, they bowed down and spoke with great reverence: (26)
O divine sage, by your grace and by the sight of you, we are blessed;
look upon us with eyes of profound compassion. (27)
Meanwhile, we shall serve the wives of our gurus with extreme reverence;
the goddess Lalitā has been born, and she is being worshipped by the gods. (28)
O Supreme Goddess, for the sake of our husband’s slaying and for the happiness of the gods, you must awaken him so that the lord of the asuras does not meet his destruction. (29)
We have come to you for refuge, submerged as we are in an ocean of suffering;
lift us up from this sea of misery and protect us, your attendants.
Having spoken thus and touched his feet, the wives of the Daityas wept;
and seeing their lamentation, his mind was overcome with compassion. (31)
Having summoned that king of the Daityas there, Nārada spoke to him:
"O Lord of the Daityas! Listen to my words, which are like nectar. (32)
Do not cause these weak women to grieve, nor lead your kinsmen to destruction;
for among people in this world, one who speaks what is beneficial is exceedingly rare.
One should recognize as an enemy in the form of a friend that person who speaks sweetly in one's presence without considering the gain or loss [to himself]. (34)
He who, having reflected with a superior intellect upon the arrival and departure [of fortune], speaks what is bitter like medicine— know that person indeed to be a friend. (35)
A teacher should be a poet, extremely patient, long-suffering, and devoted to the welfare of his beloved;
he is like medicine that is most wholesome for a sick person. (36)
Without abandoning what has been taught by the guru, one shall attain supreme good fortune;
O Lord of Daityas, listen as I declare that to you. (37)
Regarding that which you consider yourself to be the strongest of all, listen to this as well which I shall tell you: Kaiṭabha was the crest-jewel of the Daityas. (38)
From whose fat this earth, the sustainer of the world,
was formed— he who was peerless in strength and prowess, yet was slain in battle by Viṣṇu.
That you consider her to be a weak woman is something heard from long ago; for by this very supreme goddess,
Śumbha, Niśumbha, and Mahiṣa— who was arrogant in his strength— were all destroyed,
even though he was surrounded by the forces of the great Asuras.
Enough of your pride in strength with that enemy who destroys his own self;
do you not remember your previous defeat by Gaurī in battle?
This Lalitā Parameśvarī is distinguished by Gaurī and others;
she is served by many tens of millions of Śaktis, headed by Gaurī.
The entire circle of the universe is equal to a single toenail of this Śakti;
by her grace alone do you consider yourself the best among the powerful. (43)
Mahādeva himself was born from a portion of her pedestal-base;
therefore, enough of this obsession with destroying all the goals of your own self. (44)
Behold these beloved, virtuous women, grieving and fallen into a state of wretchedness;
I shall lead you there, to the presence of Parāśakti.
And I beg forgiveness from that goddess with every effort for your sake;
rule the kingdom in Pātāla, while Vāsava may govern heaven.
Protect the retinue of the Daityas; do not perish along with those dear to you.
When you do not act according to what I have said, then you shall perish.
O Lord of the Daityas, does anything that I have spoken find favor in your mind?
Reflect upon this means of self-protection with a sattvic intellect. (48)
Having heard these words of Nārada, the demon Bhaṇḍa laughed and, seizing the celestial sage by the hand, ascended to the pinnacle of the palace.
Resembling the peak of Mount Meru, he entered a golden palace atop a mansion,
where, at a jeweled window, he sat upon a soft seat.
Having seated the divine sage there upon a soft seat made of *tūla* fibers,
you ought not to direct your anger toward a disciple who embodies the divine sage. (51)
I know you: a great devotee who has taken refuge at the feet of the Supreme Power.
Whatever you say, all of that is known by me exactly as it is; it is not otherwise.
"You know my entire history; thus you speak to me with such ease."
"I am indeed Māṇikyaśekhara, the messenger of the goddess Ramā.
Once, she performed great penance for the sake of pleasing Tripurā. (54)
For three million years, a certain Kinnarī, filled with the nectar of youth, took her abode on the banks of the Jāhnavī. (55)
Rising up and sinking down, fallen into the waters of the Jahnavi and carried away by the currents, she found no protector.
Seeing this, overcome with compassion, he plunged into the waters of the celestial river;
placing her upon his back, he quickly ascended to the bank.
I entered into her there, and she became free from fever in an instant;
and I too, through the touch of her limbs and the sight of her beauty, [was likewise freed]. (58)
Deluded by desire, I spoke these words to her:
"O auspicious lady, you have been protected by me as if from the very jaws of death. (59)
"O Jāla, I am afflicted by passion due to contact with your body; protect me here!
One who is capable should personally perform a return-favor for what has been done, with all one's soul. (50)
By failing to return a favor, one destroys oneself by one's own hand;
therefore, I, who am afflicted by the fire of desire and have come to you for refuge, [am in this state]. 61.
"If you do not protect us now by giving yourself, I shall give up my life.
Having heard these words of mine, which were contrary to her own intent, that virtuous Kinnarī spoke these words:
She spoke these sweet and most virtuous words, flowing like nectar:
"O Kinnarī, who regards her husband as a deity, do not fall into confusion of mind. (63)
My husband, devoted to asceticism, dwells five *krośas* from here;
I am his beloved, staying close to him like the shade of a tree. (64)
I shall never transgress my husband under any circumstances, no matter what reason I might hear;
for he is the one who rescued me from calamities and the one who nurtured me in my childhood. (65)
"He is declared to be one's father according to the Dharma in the scriptures; therefore he is my father.
You are my daughter according to the Dharma, and I am yours; you ought not to speak to me in this manner. (66)
A person should restrain the mind, which is the enemy of one's own self, from its domain;
he whose mind is not under control must quickly destroy that very mind.
Reflect with a clear and steady intellect upon the conduct of the world:
the pleasure derived from women is indeed one and the same in every respect, for there is no distinction even among beasts. (68)
Therefore, direct your mind toward finding delight only in your own beloved wives and not elsewhere;
lest, upon encountering the fire of the wrath of those devoted to their husbands, you be reduced to ashes. (69)
Although I spoke such beneficial words in many ways, my soul was overwhelmed by the delusion of desire and, being afflicted, I failed to reflect upon them. (70)
Crying out, she came to the presence of Queen Ramā’s feet, saying "Save me! Save me! right before her.
With my eyes blinded by lust, I grasped her upper garment;
then, seeing this misconduct, the goddess Ramā became enraged and cursed me. (72)
"O fool! O ill-behaved one, this divine form is not suitable for you;
for this is indeed an asura deed of yours, so become an asura! (73)
Having heard that curse of terrible form, I was suddenly awakened by the force of passion and immediately became submerged in an ocean of grief.
Having been comforted, that Kinnarī went to her own abode;
then Ramādevī spoke again to me as I was submerged in an ocean of grief. (75)
"Fie on you, ignoble one! You are not fit to remain here in my presence; your body, which commits the violation of another's wife, is of a truly terrible form. (76)
"Go at once to invisibility, or else become one whose body is air!
Thus cursed by her, I was then terrified and sought the protection of the Goddess.
Though she was to be propitiated with various prayers and even by those bowing down,
Ambikā thus became gracious once again after a long time. (78)
When I requested her for the sake of release from the curse, she then said to me:
"O Maṇikyaśekhara! You have committed an utterly reprehensible act. (79)
"I see no other recompense for this, even the slightest;
my curse shall not be in vain, and you must certainly experience the fruit of what you have done. (80)
Having lost your body and become wind, remain for a long time as an asura;
however, out of compassion, you rescued her when she had fallen into the water. (81)
Through the ripening of that merit, having attained a wealth exceeding all else and the lordship over many cosmic eggs, he enjoyed pleasures according to his desire.
Slain by Mahādevī in battle, he attained his station in that world;
having reached it, he was honored there by the asuras for a long time.
"Having reached that state, you shall not be born again.
Having heard these words, I questioned the Mother of the World once more.
O Goddess! Who is that Great Goddess by whom I would have been slain in battle? Is she a goddess superior to you? I do not know anyone superior to you. (85)
"Tell me, who is she, and what is her greatness?"—
thus questioned by me, the Goddess Śrī Lokamātṛkā replied. (86)
O Māṇikyaśekhara, listen: that Goddess is supreme in every respect;
she is the nature of the Great Consciousness, from whose essential character the primordial nature (prakṛti) arises.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara are the embodiments of the qualities (guṇas) within every cosmic egg;
and Īśvara, the lord of the three qualities, is the one who performs the act of concealment (tirodhāna).
Even there, Sadāśiva is said to be the one who bestows grace;
by a mere fraction of whose glance, through his grace, he creates the entire universe. (89)
This Great Lord creates [the world] in order to bestow grace and liberate the multitudes of individual souls who have been bound by the snare of illusion since beginningless time. (90)
There is no liberation for atoms remaining in dissolution due to their state of emptiness;
having attained the state of a body in creation, they are empowered to know.
She too is a constituent part of Him; thus she is the very essence.
She is declared to be the supreme power of consciousness (citi-śakti), whose nature is the self of all. 92.
That very [consciousness] exists here as the world, comparable to a variegated mural or a mirror;
it is designated by the word "Brahman" because it is the expansion of the Self in its entirety.
She is neither woman, nor eunuch, nor man; she is the consciousness that constitutes the body of Tripurā.
Beyond the reach of speech and mind, she consists of pure consciousness, entirely free from the object of thought.
That seventeenth [power], however, is eternal and rests upon the Supreme Lord.
Of that Lord, there are two aspects: being the object of action and being the agent. (95)
The state of being an effect is sixteenfold, while the state of being an agent is of a single form.
Furthermore, there is the tenfold group of the senses and likewise the fivefold group of the elements.
Thus, the state of being an effect consists of sixteen aspects, namely the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
the seventeenth aspect would be the agency (kartṛtā) of the Great Lord, which is eternal. (97)
That consciousness, which is the sixteenfold substratum, is the cause of everything;
apart from it, there is no Śiva, nor even Brahmā or Sadāśiva.
Whether it be Īśvara, Śiva, Viṣṇu, or Brahmā, or the host of deities; men and women, the multitude of living beings, as well as the moving and the stationary—99.
Whether with breath or without breath, nothing whatsoever remains [of the self], just as there is no gold distinct from the ornaments, nor water distinct from the ocean and such. 100.
Just as emptiness exists in space, as touch exists in the wind, and as movement exists in that which is beyond;
just as heat exists in fire, as form in water, and as taste in moisture. (101)
Like fragrance and solidity in the earth, she is present everywhere;
she exists for the purpose of uplifting the worlds that are her own playful manifestations.
Having been empowered with the sovereignty over the city of the supreme Śrīcakra, we were born from her limbs as Vāk, Śrī, Gaurī, and the others. 103.
Kālī, born from wrath, was united with Mahākāla;
likewise, by his command, Tārā was born, united with Bhairava. (104)
Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, arose from valor;
she was born from the Praty-aṅgiras through his ferocity, accompanied by Mahāśarabha.
Śūlinī is born from the syllable Śā, and Mālinī arises from Vāk;
Caṇḍikā is produced by the sound Caṇḍa, and Dhūmrā by the cruel gaze.
Thus, all [the goddesses] arise from her limbs; indeed, none exists apart from her.
Through her playful descent in battle under the name Lalitā, [all others are surpassed]. (107)
"Once you have been slain and have dwelt for a long time in that world, you shall be liberated.
Having been told this by her, he then made another request.
"If it be so, O Mother, let it be; however, I pray to you once more:
may my state as an Asura come about without being through a connection by birth. (109)
May my birth come from the body of a principal devotee of the Supreme Power;
O Mother of the Universe, may this wisdom never forsake me! 110.
When Ramā had thus been petitioned, she replied, "So be it for you";
then I obtained birth from that foremost of devotees, Kāmāṅga.
He exercised sovereignty over one hundred and five eggs for a long time;
having enjoyed unsurpassed sense-objects constantly for a very long duration. (112)
"Disgusted with sense objects, I desire my own death;
having resolved upon it, I wish to dwell in her presence in that world. (113)
Constantly meditating upon the lotus feet of that Supreme Goddess,
I await the time when she will come and grace me. (114)
"Slain by her in battle along with my sons, grandsons, wife, and others, I shall dwell quickly in that world"—this is what my mind desires. (115)
"Go there, comfort my wife, and instruct her with the discernment of a horse.
Having heard these words of Bhaṇḍa, Nārada was delighted in his heart.
Having praised the lord of the Bhaṇḍa-demons and consoled his beloved wife,
Nārada, the best of sages, departed for his desired abode.
Thus, in the glorious *Tripurārahasya*, the best of histories, within the section on majesty (*māhātmyakhaṇḍa*), in the *Lalitāmāhātmya*,
during the dialogue between Śrī Nārada and Bhaṇḍa, [the account] of her who was overcome by the ripening of the karma performed in her own previous birth through the agency of Bhaṇḍa.
The fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Attaining the Abode of the Goddess through the Power of Compassion."
Chapter Sixty:
A Description of the Deliberation on Bhaṇḍāsura in the Dialogue between Nārada and Hāritāyana.
Having heard these words spoken by Hāritāyana, Nārada,
being pleased and thrilled by the description of his own experience, spoke as follows.
O Hāritāyana! You have spoken well regarding this long-accumulated mental [defilement] of mine, as well as that which was formerly external. || 2 ||

Because it was taught exactly as it is, I remember it according to the sequence in which it was spoken; even though it was separated by a long period of time, it is as if it were just today through your teaching.
Everything shines within your inner organ; you are truly blessed on this earth, for by the grace of another, all that is external and internal has been known by you.
I ask you about reality; tell me, for a long-standing doubt has remained within me.
You have indeed explained that which is past, both internal and external, and it has become known to me.
"O observer of noble vows, how do you know that which has neither been seen nor heard?
Having heard these words of Nārada, Hāritāyana laughed.
O divine sage, listen; I shall speak this which has been declared, whether it be much or little.
The proof for this will be fully established in another section.
Just as a person remembers what has been experienced, so indeed do I;
by the boon of Brahmā, [I remember] everything, whether external or internal. (8)
By your grace, she was conquered by me alone;
I remember this through the great favor of the Illustrious Goddess, though I am indeed unskilled.
Then the preceptor, having been honored, spoke to Rāma, whose mind was one-pointed:
"Listen, O Bhārgava! After that, you shall hear it from the one born from a jar (Agastya)."
Bhaṇḍa related the most wonderful account of the battle between the Asura and the Goddess;
listen, O sage Agastya, to this auspicious story born from the sacrificial fire.
Having seen Lalitā, the Supreme Goddess and the sole beauty of all the worlds, the gods, headed by Śakra, reflected within their minds: ||| 12 ||
"Indeed, this young woman, a temple of beauty for all the world, does not shine, being like a creeper deprived of its support—bereft of her husband. (13)
Having thus perceived the gods' anxiety, Brahmā and the others, who are the embodiments of the qualities (guṇas), meditated upon Kāmeśvara; and even as they did so, he emerged.
Seeing that the body of that great goddess was adorned with ornaments of identical form, they considered a husband who was a match for the goddess to be the best choice for her.

Intent on the aspiration, "May the marriage of these two take place," those who speak through the mouth of Brahmā learned of that [intention] and petitioned the Goddess, who is higher than the highest.
They performed the marriage according to the rites of a great festival. Then, that supreme goddess Lalitā was entreated by the gods. (17)
For the sake of the destruction of Bhaṇḍāsura, she fashioned his retinue;
by mere remembrance, she brought forth the entire multitude of his enclosures.
In the meantime, the celestial sage arrived at the feet of the Goddess;
having prostrated like a staff before her and praised her with various hymns of praise. (19)
With palms joined in reverence, humble and with his head bowed, he spoke to her:
"O Goddess, I have arrived in the presence of the demon Bhaṇḍa."
"The exceedingly powerful one is approaching, drawing along a great army;
therefore, sent by him, that lord of the asuras addresses you. (21)
"You are weak; by whose strength do you wish to fight with me?
O deluded one, do not go to your destruction now without first knowing my power. (22)
Come quickly to my side; abandon the gods headed by Brahmā, who have been repeatedly defeated by me and rely merely upon their illusory powers.
"Whoever here, whether woman or man, opposes me, shall by all means meet with death as if entering the very mouth of Death; let him not find happiness. (24)
Having said this, he properly gave orders for the supreme preparation for battle:
"I believe that you have now been largely conquered by that steadfast one."
"O Goddess! I ask you something; command me quickly regarding a secret.
Having heard those words of Nārada, she looked toward the minister's wife. (26)
Then the supreme minister, who understood gestures, perceiving the queen's intention,
took the divine sage by the hand and entered into a private place.
Then, seated there together, the Mistress of Mantras said to him:
"Ask, O Nārada! Whatever you have in your mind that ought to be asked."
I know you to be devoted to the worship of the feet of Parādevī;
indeed, nothing in this world remains unknown to you because of your refuge at the feet of Śrī. (29)
"Nevertheless, ask what you desire; I shall cut away the doubt you have harbored.
Thus commanded by the female counselor, the ascetic Suratapas bowed down.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these most elegant words of inquiry:
"O Goddess! The demon Bhaṇḍāsura has been seen by me and thoroughly examined. (31)
Surely he is the preeminent among all our devotees;
how could he, who takes refuge solely at the feet of the Supreme, be defeated in battle? (32)
Moreover, he declared: "I have been slain by the Goddess in battle;
after dwelling for a long time in the world of Śrī, I shall then go to her abode."
Why is one who causes harm to the world liberated even if his conduct is base? Why do we not attain the state of the world? Tell me that. (34)
Then Queen Śyāmalā, who was behind him, replied to Nārada:
"Listen now, O Nārada, to my words, even though they concern a secret. (35)
One who takes refuge at the feet of the Śrīpāda never falls anywhere;
his attainment of the supreme state will occur in every way and not otherwise. (36)
Just as a mother does not give even desired wholesome food to a sick child,
so too she does not give wholesome medicine that is not requested.
Thus, she who was intent on nourishing him gave [him food] by force;
having killed that crest-jewel of devotees, a vast evil deed has been committed. (38)
Listen as I describe how it likewise swiftly leads one to its own state, destroying even the most powerful [bondage] without the weapons of mere sight or conversation. (39)
Whoever single-mindedly desires a particular object with their own mind, Tripurā bestows that upon them quickly; of this there is no doubt. (40)
As long as that which is contrary to one's desire has not met its destruction, for that long it persists; thereafter, one shall attain one's own desired goal. || 41 ||
Listen: you are eternally liberated; liberation is not something to be sought by you.
Such a desire may belong to the ignorant, but how could it arise for the knower? (42)
For just as one who is bound desires liberation, so does one who is hungry desire food;
how could one who is satiated desire food? And how could anyone else cause him to eat? (43)
What attainment could possibly occur for that which has already been attained?
How and by what means could there be an attainment of that which is already full, like space? || 44 ||
"Therefore, liberation is to be attained by the ignorant; how can it be so for the wise?
Having heard these words spoken by the minister's wife, Nārada was delighted in his heart. (45)
Having bowed to that Tripurā, he, being liberated while living, departed.
Then the goddess Tripurā [set out] for the sake of slaying the demon Bhaṇḍa.
Requested by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, she set forth with her army of Śaktis upon a chariot consisting of nine joints,
which was identical in form to the King of Discuses (Cakrarāja).
On the upper level, which was like a mine of precious gems and beautifully adorned,
she stood, fully equipped with a vast array of war materials.
Clad in impenetrable armor, she was terrifying with her formidable attainments; equipped with a multitude of weapons and missiles, her eyes were bloodshot with rage.
Dhanurveda stood at his side in embodied form with palms joined in reverence;
likewise, weapons and missiles indeed stood there in personified forms.
p.610) All the various obstructive powers (āvaraṇa-śakti) are likewise taught in descending order,
well-adorned with diverse armor, weapons, and missiles. (51)
The Gurubhaṭṭārakas also stood ready, clad in armor and longing for battle;
to the south of that [place] was Mantreśī, resplendent with seven joints.
Stationed with her retinue, armored for the work of battle,
and attended by the dark-hued hosts led by Śuka and others, she went forth.
Her pair of lotus-eyes were rolling with the intoxication of the joy of divine drinks,
and she was surrounded by countless millions of young female elephants of that same kind.
They gratified the minister with gifts, instrumental music, dances, and clever, humorous remarks, as well as with playful gestures mixed with laughter.
She too, the minister of Queen Śrī Lalitā,
was skilled in mantras and remained constantly engaged in those spells that were agreeable to her mind.
Especially eager for song, instrumental music, jesting, and play,
there then appeared to her left the sovereign Daṇḍasāmrājñī with the face of a boar.
In the Kiricakra, which possesses five joints, she stands at the very top,
surrounded by her own many powers, such as Jambhinī and the others.
Embodied as wrath, she is exceedingly fierce, yet devoted to the forgiveness of others;
she stands ever ready, punishing all who are intent on transgression.
She is graced by a great buffalo and a lion standing at her two sides as her mounts, and by weapons such as a plow and a pestle held in her hands. (60)
Surrounded by crores of *baṭukas* and *yoginīs*, so too is the venerable Bālā Tripurasundarī, who is taught by Lalitā. 61.
The maiden is seated upon a chariot called the Small Wheel (laghucakra),
completely surrounded by her own retinue and the hosts of Great Powers (mahāśakti).
On her right side, however, was attained the Mistress of Prosperity (Sampadadhīśvarī),
amidst the most terrifying account known as Raṇakolāhala, which was divided into three parts.
Upon the lordly elephant, who resembled the great peak of the Vindhya mountain and was intoxicated by nature,
she stood firmly, wielding a massive goad.
Following her were countless intoxicated elephants, numbering more than millions upon millions.
Those originating from the Vindhya, those from Malaya, and those arising from Prāgjyotiṣa. || 65 ||
Well-trained, thoroughly acquainted with the maneuvers of battle, and sixty years of age,
they set forth accompanied by the powerful forces of Sampadī and Īśitrī.
Mounted upon swift horses, those skilled in weapons, missiles, and warfare took their positions on her left side; there the Great Goddess herself was seated, mounted upon a horse.
She mounted the horse-treasure named Aparājita, which was exceedingly tall,
born of the Gandharva race, and possessed the speed of the wind.
Adorned with all the auspicious marks that surpass even Uccaiḥśravas,
[he was decorated] with conch-shells, half-conches, gems, divine svastikas, and lotuses. (69)
Marked with auspicious signs such as the *gaṇḍikā* and others, and radiant like gold,
they could not perceive the contact of his hooves even with the keenest attention.
Knowing the disposition of his master’s mind and skilled in the methods of training horses,
he followed her with countless steeds born in Sindhu and Taṅkaṇa.
The Āradas, Pārvatīyas, Vārvaras, and Sutejanas;
those who are red, dark, white, yellow, tawny, and pale-red—likewise [these are the tribes]. (72)
Green, smoke-colored, dappled, and blue-red;
variegated, with all limbs beautiful, and adorned with thick manes.
They follow various modes of training, skilled in dance and in harmony with rhythm;
they are empowered by their mastery of diverse weapons, missiles, and powers.
Leaping forward like waves surging from all sides upon the ocean, they emerged as if tearing up the earth with the thrusts of their hooves. (75)
Accompanied by the "caṭa-caṭa" sounds produced by the stamping of hooves, joined with a multitude of snorting cries mixed with the trumpeting of elephants; || 76 ||
With the lion-roars of the Śaktis, the great sounds of the heroes' chest-clapping, the resounds of victory drums, and the noises of mṛdaṅgas, mṛdaṅgas, and jhallarīs; (77)
It was blended with the sounds of cow-horns, small drums, cymbals,
and kahalas, arising from the multitude of wheel-rims of the chariot of the illustrious King of Mandalas (Śrīcakrarāja).
Hearing the great sound of the auspicious procession of Goddess Lalitā, a mighty roar arose as if filling all directions.
The Daityas experienced extreme terror, as if from death itself;
meanwhile, the Daitya Bhaṇḍa [realized] that his own long-desired death had come at her hands.
Having heard that roar from nearby, they concluded it was certainly [the enemy];
then, beholding the Daityas terrified with their lotus-faces parched, [he acted]. (81)
Overcome by supreme compassion, he thought within himself:
"Surely these people, along with their kinsmen, are perishing for my sake. (82)
In this world, there is never any fear greater than death;
they will grieve for these sons, dear to them, who have been slain on my account. (83)
"Alas, such a slaughter of sisters and chief mothers!
Therefore, having gone before her and fought with the venerable Mother Lalitā," 84.
"Purified by the fire of that weapon, may I attain my desired goal;
why then do I grieve for these [beings], having separated them from their respective kinsmen? (85)
Therefore, enough of this wailing over my terrible death;
you were capable of protecting your own people from a cause for grief in some way or another. (86)
He should be known by people as a slayer of kinsmen, equal to a man-eater;
for thus, having brought about my death, he has incurred the queen's own calamity. (87)
For my kinsmen, who are now deprived of me, there will be nothing but sorrow;
how indeed will my relatives endure when I have been slain by the gods? (88)

Adorned with great supernatural power, they will be overcome by the gods and stripped of their majesty; thus, deprived of their splendor, they will fall into grief, yet even this is not considered desirable.
How could anyone, having attained the highest position, remain unvanquished?
Surely, when I am slain, the queen’s kinsmen—her brothers, sons, and others—[will be overcome].
But the brave ones, exalted by their valor and wrath at that very moment, would undoubtedly reduce their own selves—like moths—to ashes in the fire of battle. (91)
Then those who were cowardly and of little vigor fell to the ground;
like gods overcome by dejection, they were separated from their wives, sons, and other kin.
Thus grieving for one another, they would indeed become like the dead;
however, there is no weeping by relatives at all, under any circumstances. (93)
p.615) "Therefore, I think what is the use of this vain reflection? There is nothing better than this: first they were slain by the Goddess, and only then was I killed. (94)
For this appears to me superior, as there are many virtues herein:
purification by means of divine weapons and the attainment of the highest world. (95)
There is no possibility of being treated with contempt and the like, and one's fame in the world becomes very great;
yet even in this regard, I consider that there is no possibility for those who have the faces of women or children. 96.
This matter is indeed unfathomable; here, destiny is the ultimate resort.
Or rather, this was previously heard by me from the mouth of the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā).
She is the supreme Goddess Tripurā, the fulfiller of the desires of her devotees;
may that Supreme One not wither away this retinue of mine. 98.
"Even though I know this from the perspective of ultimate reality, O Goddess, she still sufficiently produces delusion in me. (99)
Therefore, my reflection was in vain regarding this worldly existence, whose essence is like a dream;
I have sought refuge in Him with my whole being. (100)
Therefore, employ me in that which you have commanded, and not otherwise;
protect me, O Supreme Goddess, O Refuge! who have come to you for shelter. (101)
"O Mahādevī Tripurā, you ought to lift me up here from this entanglement of the net of delusion. Having thus entreated her, the Dānava Bhaṇḍa—
Observing his kinsmen standing around him, who had fallen into a state of dejection, he spoke these words of valor, gladdening them. (103)
p.616) O Dānavas! Listen to my words with supreme faith.
There is no death for me from any source whatsoever, for I am the death of Death itself. (104)
In the presence of you all, I am the creator of weapons and missiles, even those of great illusionists, as well as of the worlds of moving and non-moving beings. 105.
"I am the lord of one hundred and five eggs and possess great strength;
knowing this woman to be powerless, I do not wish to kill her quickly. (106)
Seeing her intense passion for battle, he conquered her with ease,
brought her to his own inner apartments, and thoroughly delighted her with great joy.

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deliberations and Counter-arguments of the Asura Bhaṇḍa, Who Prepared for Battle with the Goddess," in the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrīlalitāmāhātmya*, within the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of sacred histories. || 4983 ||
The sixty-first chapter:
A description of the Daitya king’s dispatching of his own messenger in order to ascertain the military preparations of Śrī Lalitā.
Having spoken thus to his attendant charioteer Dīrghagrīva, the great asura, his eyes copper-red with rage, said: "Let the chariot be harnessed! (1)
Then the charioteer, having bowed down with great humility, presented the excellent chariot, ready at a mere blink of an eye, to the lord of the Daityas.
The powerful Bhaṇḍa Daitya ascended that best of chariots;
taking up his bow along with arrows, he set forth, filled with extreme rage.
Having seen and heard that the lord of the Daityas was departing for that reason,
the Daityas went forth quickly, fully armed and frantic with rage.
Surrounding him on all sides— in front, at his flanks, and from behind— the Daitya warriors, bearing their weapons, marched forth in great throngs.
All the sons of the Daitya Bhaṇḍa were equal to Bhaṇḍa in prowess;
among them, Kuṭilākṣa was the eldest, possessing immeasurable strength and valor.
Seated in chariots, well-armored, and never retreating in battles,
the Bhaṇḍa Daityas marched at the front, accompanied by hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs.
Viṣaṅga and Viśukraka, who constantly vie with one another in battle, each seeking to be first, stand at the two flanks of the king of the Daityas.
His two brothers, whose prowess was equal to that of Viṣṇu,
stood upon their chariots with great bows, their eyes reddened with rage.
As if devouring the enemy armies, the two advanced swiftly,
surrounded by a hundred akṣauhiṇīs each.
Ministers with fierce deeds and terrifying prowess followed that lord of the Daityas, accompanied by hundreds of akṣauhiṇīs. || 11 ||
Thus, as the lord of the Daityas set forth for the sake of battle,
the royal highway shone like a river in the rainy season.
The river had the Daityas for its water, was filled with chariots as its whirlpools,
had horses for its broken currents, elephants for its crocodiles, and swords for its turtles.
Rich with masses of foam that were the fluttering banners, resembling a series of waves, with great serpents that were the long swords, and variegated with fish that were the quivers; || 14 ||

The multitude of Dānavas was like a cluster of lotuses upon her; the swarm of her eyes was like a school of fish; and she was garlanded by rows of various parasols resembling swans and other water-birds.
The river of the army flowed along, turbid with swarms of high-leaping horses like great porpoises, and resounding with the mighty roar of chariots.
From the great jeweled gate of that city,
as water swiftly flows from the mouth of a canal into a field, [the sound] issued forth from the gateway. (17)
In an instant, that army issued forth from the city gate;
Vijaya, having reached the entrails of the city, quickly encountered the lord of the Daityas.
Having prostrated and placed his folded hands upon his head, the minister stood waiting; then, having received permission, he spoke these well-chosen words appropriate for the occasion. (19)
O Great King, Lord of the Daityas, your fame has spread everywhere;
and this sun of your majesty shines even above the cosmic eggs.
This Hari alone was perceived here as being exceedingly powerful;
yet even he, having come before you in battle, was utterly defeated. (21)
"The certainty that anyone might defeat you in battle is indeed futile;
nevertheless, at the proper time, the minister [should act] according to the authority of the treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra). (22)

Having reflected, one should speak to the king that which is beneficial and proportionate; for one who does not speak at the proper time and with what is appropriate does not deserve the title of a good counselor.
Only four means are proclaimed for the application of force;
even one among them, when employed at the proper time, is considered most powerful. (24)
At an improper time, following the counsel of foolish and wicked ministers, a king perishes after consuming what is unsuitable, just like a sick man who takes the wrong medicine. (25)
There, having observed everything through the eyes of spies and scouts, the wise should engage in battle; by doing so, one shall attain prosperity. (26)
Once they have given their consent, envoys and spies will quickly proceed against the enemies;
meanwhile, the army too shall be ready and free from apprehension. (27)
"The protection of the city must also be arranged according to the prescribed rules;
this should be reported by me to you, my lord, at the proper time. (28)
"What has been requested by you should be carried out at the appropriate time," [the king said], having heard those words of the minister, which were fitting and esteemed as skillful. (29)
He approved the counsel of his kinsmen for the sake of securing their support,
having stationed the army there in its various divisions under the command of generals.
For the purpose of protecting the city, the great asura Bhaṇḍa dispatched Kuṭilākṣa and spoke to his excellent minister Amitraghna.
Go, O Amitraghana; speak to her on my behalf, addressing her by the name Lalitā:
"I shall never, under any circumstances, take refuge with you, though you are a beautiful goddess worthy of being sought. (32)
I desire to fight; why then have you come here to fight me?
This desire for battle of yours is indeed entirely agreeable to me.
I do not fear a great battle; whence could there be fear in a battle for the truth?
However, having seen you, who possess a lovely form, I am suddenly overcome by the god of love.
"Abandoning the side of those gods, take refuge in me;
whether by means of conciliation or by war, I shall make you dependent upon myself. (35)
"By opposing me, you will surely suffer loss in this world; there is no doubt.
Reflecting upon this, quickly choose one side or the other. (36)
"Speak thus to her with conciliation, having ascertained her intention;
and having understood her entire strength and what must be done, return quickly. (37)
Then he spoke to Vidyunmālin, the best among illusionists:
"O Vidyunmālin, O highly wise one, leader of the family of illusionists! (38)
Having gone unobserved by others, he thoroughly ascertained the queen's army, its strength, its resolve, and its points of vulnerability through strategic means. (39)
"Having reflected, come here quickly; you are skilled.
Having been thus commanded, the other two Daityas went toward the army of Śakti.
Having somehow failed to cross that infinite army,
which resembled a vast ocean, the slayer of enemies entered it like a boat entering the sea.
Guarded by spears with blades drawn from their scabbards,
as soon as he had entered, that exceedingly powerful one was seized by a spear.
The attendant Kāñcanābhayā,
having swiftly struck Daṇḍanāthā with a slap, seized that asura by the throat.
He threatened him with words full of anger and terrifying:
"Who are you, that you [dare approach] this army well-guarded by the goddess Daṇḍarājñī? (44)
"You entered without having announced yourself, and you have entered this army while being watched by those led by us, without the command of Queen Daṇḍarājñī. (45)
"O Jīvana, even Death himself will come before you in person;
meanwhile, those appointed to protect the army have arrived. (46)
In an instant, hundreds of powers (śaktis), awaiting the command of Daṇḍin, violently dragged him away; he was struck down and fell unconscious. || 47 ||
Having heard of that meeting with the Daitya in the meantime, the Lord of Punishment brought him into his presence by means of his own secret agents and powers.
Having questioned that messenger who had arrived and having learned that he belonged to the Asura Bhaṇḍa,
she informed the queen and then brought him into her presence.
She too, having informed him that he had arrived, led him to the presence of Lalitā and questioned the messenger regarding the purpose of his coming there.
Having bowed down, the slayer of enemies said: "I have arrived by the command of Bhaṇḍa;
I am the messenger of that Daitya, and I shall speak what he has said. (51)
(623) There is no enmity between us; why have you come here to fight?
Whether you fight with us or not, O Goddess, may you become one who takes refuge in me. 52.
Tell me, how can I fight with you, who are the truth, dear to my soul, and beloved?
Therefore, abandon the gods entirely and become one who takes refuge in me. 53.
"You must go and ascertain the strength and weakness of the enemy's army"—
thus was I sent by him, like a messenger who is to be bound or censured.
"The wise do not prescribe the execution of a messenger in the scriptures.
Thinking thus, I entered, and was perceived by all the Śaktis.
"From the very moment he entered, he was seized by your Śaktis;
he has been brought before you—thus all this has been explained. (56)
"In the presence of the Goddess herself, there is no refuge; my death would be the only result.
Having heard these words of the messenger, [he considered] the opinion of Lalitā. || 57 ||
Having understood this, the minister, speaking with a beautiful and smiling voice, said:
"Do not fear, O Daitya; go in peace; you shall never be slain. (58)
Having heeded what I have said, you should speak to that Bhaṇḍa, lord of the Daityas:
"If you have any desire to live, come quickly and without fear. (59)
Seek refuge with the Goddess of the gods and completely abandon the three worlds;
O Indra, you shall become the lord of the three worlds and dwell in Pātāla.
Form an alliance with the breaker of mountain peaks (Indra), along with his sons, forces, and vehicles;
otherwise, there will be no liberation for you while you remain alive anywhere. (61)
O Empress of Punishment, do not show this army to him from all sides;
having shown it to him, then dismiss him outside the army.
Thus commanded, she showed him her own army, which had faces like crocodiles, and sent that son of Diti outside the military camp.
Then, feeling himself as if born again once he was released,
he went into the presence of the king with his inner self overwhelmed by fear.
Having observed that he had been struck down by the slayer of enemies,
the greatly illusory Vidyunmālin became terrified at night and assumed the body of a female owl.
Moving through the path of the sky, he observed the entire army;
having counted the whole host as it proceeded along the celestial route, he beheld it.
A certain night-roaming female demoness seized him with her power;
as soon as he was seized, the master of illusion flew up high into the sky.
At a distance of fifty yojanas, he fought fiercely with her;
after fighting for a long time, struck by her trident, he was somehow released by her.
With but a fraction of his life remaining, he went toward the lord of the Daityas and fell before him,
facing the rising sun.
Seeing the Daitya fallen before him, dying and severely struck,
Bhaṇḍāsura, while muttering a mantra, touched his limbs with his hand. (70)
Merely by the touch of the mantra, he was restored to life and freed from his agony;
rising up, he quickly prostrated before the king of the Daityas who stood before him.
Then, being questioned, Vidyunmālī related his own history in due order:
"O Great King, I went into the presence of Amitraghna."
I beheld that army, resembling the ocean at the time of universal dissolution;
then Amitraghna himself first entered the great host.
As soon as I looked, he was forcibly seized by the Śaktis in an instant;
then he was overwhelmed by those Śaktis, just as a bee is assailed by swarms of flies.
In an instant, though he was strong, he became devoid of wisdom;
unable even to move, what of battle and what of flight? (75)
"He shall not live by any means whatsoever; such is my resolve.
Thinking thus, though terrified, I became intent on fleeing from that wicked man. (76)
Out of respect for your command, I did not turn back out of fear of you;
therefore, at the end of the day, I assumed the form of a deceptive owl.
Moving higher and higher above the army and observing it,
I beheld that vast host, formidable and making a terrifying noise.
Like the ocean with its great waves agitated at the time of universal dissolution.
Merely by the sight of him, the Asuras flee from the army as if toward death.
There, all the great and terrifying Śaktis, possessing fearsome prowess, were at the outset eager to engage in battle, each vying for precedence, saying "I first, I first. (80)
There, a young girl who was the beloved daughter of Lalitā was surrounded by hundreds of millions of maidens.
Skilled and proficient in the use of weapons and missiles, she repeatedly cried out in the excitement of preparing for battle, "I shall slay the sons of Bhaṇḍa! (82)
Those maidens also said to Bhaṇḍa’s son Suvāhinī:
"Eager for battle and roaring loudly, we shall destroy you in an instant."
Then there was the Śakti leader named Saṃspharī, mounted upon a horse,
[surrounded by] countless elephants and horses occupied by great Śaktis.
Those two, powerful and fierce, were pulling [the chariot] while leaning against the sides of the young woman;
meanwhile, the young woman herself was seated behind the great chariot.
The illustrious Great Goddess Lalitā is surrounded by the nine encircling powers (navāvaraṇa-śaktis),
who are endowed with immeasurable strength, ferocity, and heroism.
On both her sides stand the Lords of Mantra, bearing staffs;
each is mounted upon a chariot and possesses most wonderful prowess. (87)
The minister’s wife stood there, surrounded on all sides by many millions of Mātaṅga maidens who were her own equals in appearance and possessed of wondrous prowess.
Vārāhī also, joined by Śaktis and Baṭukas and others bearing names of most terrifying and formidable forms, was filled with extreme wrath. (89)
(627) Throughout all the armies of Śakti, I have not observed anywhere that which is not already well-known in connection with the account of your slaughter. (90)
In this matter, it is my firm resolve, established upon careful deliberation, that even a single inferior power could destroy our entire army in an instant. (91)
O King of the Daityas! I tell you that this very army, consisting of hundreds of koṭyarbudas and parārdhas, is thus bristling with power. 92.
Their power, strength, vigor, and prowess are considered by you to be different;
yet it surpasses all of us Daitya hosts in every respect. (93)
Having spoken thus to the king of the Daityas and prostrating with palms joined in reverence,
Vidyunmālī remained silent within the assembly of the Daityas.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Spy's Words of Bhaṇḍa’s Messenger Vidyunmālin," in the Lalitāmāhātmya of the Śrī Tripurārahasya, the most excellent of glorious histories.
The sixty-second chapter: A detailed description by Amitraghna, a secret agent of the Rākṣasa king, regarding the queen’s armor.
Then, in an instant, the slayer of enemies (Viṣṇu) entered the interior of the Daitya assembly;
with his heart overwhelmed by fear, he fell at the feet of Bhaṇḍāsura.
Questioned by his ministers while trembling, Āśava told them what had happened:
"O Great King, commanded by you, I went to the great army of Śakti."
Having entered, he was seized by those Śaktis with great force in an instant;
neither my heroism nor my strength shone at all in the presence of the Śaktis.
Just as the brilliant light of a firefly is eclipsed when submerged in the radiance of the sun,
so too did I instantly lose consciousness upon seizing them.
Then, led into the presence of the Lord of Punishment, he stood like one dead;
she, with a face like a boar’s and a golden luster, was as lofty as a mountain range.
As if vomiting the fire of her wrath through her beautiful eyes with a gurgling roar,
she possessed such a host of Śaktis kindled by fury.
Having seen her, I was once again unable even to breathe, O Lord;
by her command, I have been sent from here along with the Śaktis and the ministers.
O Goddess, that female minister was seen, resembling the leaf of the *tāpiccha* tree;
she was a doe for the deer of beauty and lineage, and proud of her full youth. (8)
With a face of gentle smiles, she was intoxicated by the pride of drink and ever devoted to song and laughter, intent upon the playing of the lute.
Sustained by the rain of nectar from her lotus-like eyes of grace,
I gazed upon her, the sole refuge of all auspiciousness.
Questioned by her, I related everything you had said;
then, that great queen led me before her presence this very day.
That Queen Lalitā, who dwells in great opulence, was seen by me as she was delivering to me the message that you had given through the mouth of her minister.
"I shall speak; listen with an attentive mind, O Lord of Daityas!
If you have any regard for your life, O Lord of the Bhaṇḍa-daityas, you should say this to him. (13)
"Relinquish the three worlds to Indra and take refuge with your mother;
dwell together with your retinue in the abode of Pātāla."
May you be united with Indra, accompanied by your sons, ministers, and others;
for without doing this, there shall be no liberation for you even when you have gone to another world. 15.
"O Indraśatru, I shall bring you under my own protection.
Thus should you speak to that Bhaṇḍadānava when you have gone there.
In the meantime, a certain dark-complexioned Śakti, mounted upon a horse and with a formidable sword raised in her hand, arrived there. (17)
p.630) Having descended from her own vehicle and bowed to the Mother Lalitā, she,
being questioned by her, related the entire account of what had occurred. || 18 ||
My servants, having been dispatched to the army and in the city of the demon Bhaṇḍa, went there,
saw everything with their powers, and have now returned.
"By them, the entire army as well as the city itself was made visible;
thus she related everything that had occurred concerning our refuge. (20)
Among the Daityas and their soldiers,
there was nothing whatsoever— whether external or internal— that remained unknown to her in every respect.
All women are well known to us, as is everything they have spoken;
yet even this mantra that you have recited here is not known by us.
Then, having been addressed by her, he related the matter and the events separately and individually,
saying, "I consider it strange that, though I have lived here for a long time, I remained unknown."
Then she related everything exactly as it had occurred;
indeed, you have told us that which was not even known by you here. (25)
I consider that power of the Goddess to be unconquerable by the foremost of the Daityas;
even a single, inferior Śakti could destroy us all in an instant. (26)
"O Lord of Daityas, I am indeed not inferior to Bali in strength within your army;
even Indra and the other gods have been repeatedly defeated by me in combat. (27)
Indeed, as soon as I had entered, I was quickly seized by Hari with his power and his consort through mere sport, like a young deer.
Just as children snatch a toy held in another's hand and seize it for themselves, so too was I, though powerful, seized by them. (29)
I did not possess even the power to move, much less to effect liberation;
there is no doubt that it was impossible for the Daityas to conquer in any way whatsoever. (30)
Having spoken thus, the Daitya then fell silent before the Lord of the Daityas.
Having heard these words of the Daitya, Bhaṇḍa reflected within his own mind.
Surely that Tripureśānī, out of compassion for me who has sought refuge in her,
has today bestowed the grace I have long desired.
That which was spoken by you, O Lokamātā, has today been proven true;
I am blessed to have beheld the Mistress of Tripura and to have conversed with her in battle. (33)
With my limbs purified of all impurities by the great flames of the fire of that weapon,
I go to this world of Lalla, the abode of supreme bliss.
This body, born of great sins and a refuge for evil,
fashioned by the very nature of a demon, has indeed become a long-standing burden.
"Just as one seized by a demon flees after casting off his burden, so shall I cast off this body, which is a source of suffering, and depart. (36)
I shall flee to a place of safety; I feel no distress here.
Surely this fire will consume me for hundreds of thousands of years.

Even though I have attained extreme happiness, it does not please me; for those very same enjoyments, that kingdom, those women, and that association [with them]—[all these no longer hold my interest]. (38)
As I practiced this day after day, everything turned to distaste;
I am utterly weary of this stale self. (39)
I desire the destruction of this body, like one long afflicted by disease seeks its end;
however, these dear ones, separated from me, will grieve.
Likewise, being deprived by them as well, I do not find even a moment's happiness;
whether at the beginning or immediately thereafter, death shall bring only suffering. (41)
"This appears to be a difficult situation; how might my suffering not continue?
In this way, may the Goddess Tripurā grant me her desired grace. (42)
If she were not to slay them simultaneously, it would seem better for my peace;
for by her very nature, she bestows fruits exceeding the desires of her devotees. (43)
"How could she not fulfill the desire of my own feet, which are her very own?
