Having reflected thus in his mind and having paid homage to the Supreme Mother (Parāmbikā), [he proceeded].
Like an actor on the stage, he freely unleashed a great fury:
"Fie upon you, O base son of Diti! How can you [act thus] in my very presence? (45)
Even while uttering unpleasant words in praise of others, you feel no shame;
for such praising of others is the vow of a coward in this world. (46)
But knowing him to be strong, the hero never boasts;
whether he be strong or weak, heroes do not fear him there. (47)
Having spoken thus, he raised his sword like the great serpent Kāla in a rage,
as if vomiting from his eyes and mouth the fire of the crows of his wrath.
He emerged from the city gate as if from the mouth of a great cave,
so that the Daityas who were afraid might witness his prowess therein.
"Having encountered me in battle today, she shall no longer exist.
Even as the lord of the Daityas was speaking thus, the charioteer stood before him with the chariot.
Then he too, having mounted his chariot, arrived and proceeded;
people regarded him as Time itself, intent on the destruction of the world.
"Once the world has encountered his fire of wrath, it shall not exist again"—
thus all the foremost among the Asuras suddenly spoke, filled with fear.
The commanders of the armies and the ministers set forth with their respective forces;
so too did all the sons, grandsons, and brothers.
Terrified, they departed, taking the entire army with them;
then King Kuṭilākṣa was commanded by Viśukra.
With five *akṣauhiṇīs*, he established the defense of the city; having reported this to Viśukra, he drew forth that great army. (55)
He marched before Bhaṇḍāsura as if swallowing the very quarters of the sky;
thus did the king of the Daityas set forth with his entire army.
The Daityas, however, sounded their war-drums on all sides,
along with the sounds of kettledrums, drums, and large drums, accompanied by the roars of the demons.
With the slapping of arms and the rattling of wheel-rims mingled with the trumpeting of elephants, and with the clamor of bards and panegyrists along with the neighing and the braying of horses; (58)
Indeed, a great sound was produced by the crackling noises arising from the impact of the horses' hooves, combined with the thunderous calls and roars of the *huṃ* cries.
Upon hearing the roar of the army and the arrival of the demon Bhaṇḍa, he shone as if filled with the bold intent to tear asunder the veil of the universe.
Having learned this from the mouth of her spy and having resolved upon a great effort,
Daṇḍinī quickly approached the Mistress of Mantras and informed her.
"O ministers, this Bhaṇḍa has arrived accompanied by his army;
with his great array of armor and equipment, a major battle is at hand. (62)
Having informed Queen Lalitā, accompanied by her attendants and surrounded by them, follow the Great Queen while protecting her with the hosts of Śaktis.
"I shall go ahead, surrounded by my army, to stop him;
for this sound, filled with elephants and horses, is indeed being heard. (64)
I think that these children, eager for battle, have entered the fray;
endowed with excellent masters and accompanied by their steeds, they possess wondrous prowess. (65)
While she was speaking thus, a messenger arrived;
having greeted both the Commander-in-Chief and the Queen-consort, she spoke.
O Goddess, a very great battle has commenced with Bālāmbā;
the king of the Daityas has donned his armor and made a grand effort for war.
Surrounded by his entire army, including brothers, sons, and others, he arrived most cruelly, possessing exceedingly fierce prowess in battle. (68)
Thus, I have been appointed by Sampatkārī to make this representation;
what more can I say after going again to that goddess who rides upon an elephant? (69)
Having heard the words of the messenger, the illustrious Daṇḍanāyikā spoke words appropriate for that occasion, augmented by her valor.
"O leader of the army of elephants, go and speak to her what I have said; having heard my words, she must certainly fight with vigilance against the foremost of the Daityas. (71)
This young girl is constantly eager for talk of war;
she must be protected from all sides, and I too have arrived here in haste.
"O bull among the Daityas, you must fight after confining him in such a way that he cannot escape by means of illusion; this shall continue until my arrival. (73)
Then, before long, I destroyed his ancient faith in that [false doctrine] in a mere instant,
just as the rising sun destroys the darkness.
"Go quickly, taking this message to the elephant-mounted force. Having been thus commanded, that messenger Śakti departed. (75)
Then Daṇḍinī, mounted upon a chariot drawn by deer, went forth quickly, accompanied by countless armies of Śaktis and filled with rage. (76)
Naturally prone to anger, further incensed by the commencement of battle,
she seemed for a moment to wish to consume all the worlds with the fire of her wrath.
Accompanied by the great roar of chariot-rims, the immense clamor of the army entered through the path of the ears, piercing the hearts of the enemies.
With a great roar resounding in every direction and a terrifying form surging forth, thus did the illustrious Sovereign of the Staff (Daṇḍasāmrājñī) commence her victorious expedition. 79.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Goddess’s Daughter, Bālā, Preparing for Battle," in the *Śrīlalitāmāhātmya* within the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of glorious histories.
Chapter Sixty-three: A Description of the Girl’s Prowess in Battle.
Having heard the great clamor and tumultuous roar of Bhaṇḍāsura’s vast army,
he gazed toward the direction with extreme eagerness for battle.
Moving toward the north-east, that maiden, who was dear to the heart of Lalitā,
beheld the dust raised by the crushing of Daitya’s army.
Like a multitude of world-destroying fires arising at the time of reabsorption,
he perceived that the king of the Daityas had arrived, surrounded by his entire army.
Her mind eager for battle, that young maiden Tripurasundarī mounted the chariot of the swift wheel and urged on the driver of the chariot.
Then, suspecting an obstruction by the illustrious mother in the battle,
she went to the queen-consort, the minister, without even seeing the Great Goddess.
Desiring both the commander-in-chief and the army with great haste,
she advanced toward the Daitya host with the speed of the wind.
Like a great cloud in autumn driven by the wind across the sky, the chariot sped with such velocity that it seemed to fall directly before him. 7.
Seeing that perilous military expedition of Bālā,
she quickly mounted her horse and pursued her at great speed. (8)
With horses possessing lofty leaps like those of the ocean,
that army rushed from all sides as if to submerge the world in a conflagration.
And after her was Sampatkarī, stationed amidst the tumultuous clamor of battle,
swiftly followed by an army consisting of many millions of elephants.
For the sake of protecting the child, she who was skilled in the art of charioteering was urged on with speed; impelled for a swift journey, she pursued [him] with great force.
With a form resembling that of a young girl, she drove the chariot with speed;
like a river in the rainy season flowing toward the ocean, she plunged into the army of the Daityas.
Drawing her strung bow and raining down a shower of arrows,
she [pursued] that chariot like a boat upon the ocean split open by the force of a river's current.
Kuṭilākṣa, mounted upon an elephant, entered the army of the Daitya king at the head of the Daitya host, which had been shattered by a flood of arrows.
The exceedingly powerful commander of the Daitya army besieged Bālā with a vast host; he too, having seen the young maiden Bālā, [acted accordingly].
He perceived her, who was showering volleys of arrows and possessed of marvelous prowess, to be alone, mounted upon a chariot, with tender limbs, and only eight years of age. || 16 ||
"Oh, how truly marvelous this is! Who is this single maiden who, fearless, fights against us—the terrifying ones headed by Indra? (17)
"I consider this woman to be Lalitā based on signs praised by my spies; I perceive all the characteristics, yet she is not a young girl. (18)
How could this girl, who was previously heard of as someone's daughter, now be that very same daughter again, yet deprived of her army? (19)
"If she should somehow arrive alone in the battle, fully prepared for combat, it appears to me that she alone will surely conquer us all. (20)
He would observe who among them— whether Viśukra, or Viṣaṅga, or the king, or even I myself— would be capable of standing before him in battle.
"Where are the princes and the others, whether individually or gathered together? Our army is looking for them here and there. (22)
Within half a moment, he rendered [the enemy] feeble with a net of arrows;
millions of Daityas were slain, and our great army was terrified.
Some of these had their arms, feet, hearts, chests, and heads severed; others lay fallen and dead, while still others fled in great terror.
Unable to cross the flow of blood, trembling with fear,
they fell there by the hundreds and were submerged in the rivers of blood.
(540) "Having reached this point, she might pierce our army and enter in a mere moment.
She must be restrained by me with great effort; alas, that I am situated in such a state! (26)
"A young woman shall pierce my army in my very presence and enter;
this was never done before by Indra, nor by Marut, nor even by Vāyu. (27)
"This is indeed difficult for me, that she must be conquered by all means"—having thus resolved, he mounted a great elephant in order to restrain her. (28)
He rushed forward before her and showered her with nets of arrows;
the exceedingly powerful Daitya fought with Kuṣṭhilākṣī.
Skilled in battle and proficient in the weapons and missiles of illusion, Bāla showered a rain of arrows upon the girl who stood before him in combat.
Like the rising sun amidst a mass of snow,
that young girl, her limbs glowing with the hue of dawn, was struck by the exceedingly sharp rays of autumn.
In half a moment, he brought that entire year to utter destruction and afflicted the army of the Daitya with his sharpened arrows.
Due to her extreme swiftness, no one—not even an expert with eyes of extreme subtlety—could perceive her drawing and releasing the arrow. (33)
They withstood the continuous stream of arrow-clusters issuing from the bow,
like an unceasing torrent of water from the face of a mountain during the rainy season.
Having dispersed that great army within an eighth part of a muhūrta,
he approached Kuṭilākṣa and struck him with sharpened arrows.
That powerful one also fought with all his might in the battle;
he showered volleys of counter-weapons against his opponent’s nets of weapons and missiles. (36)
Having rendered those sharp arrows futile, he struck the leader of the Daityas;
with a single sharp crescent-headed shaft, he swiftly severed his bow.
Then, with a single arrow, he struck the elephant in the face; thus struck on the countenance, the elephant, who resembled the king of mountains, [fell]. || 38 ||
Uttering a cry and writhing on the ground, he fell down instantly, deprived of life;
for Kuṭilākṣa, the wielder of the mace, had recognized that the elephant was about to die.
In his wrath, he rushed to slay the child seated upon the chariot, like Rahu of swift motion swooping down to devour the reddish young sun. 40.
The gods and siddhas dwelling in the vault of the sky beheld her approaching with exceeding speed, observing that mace in her hand.
He pierced him in the center of the heart with an arrow drawn back to the ear;
being struck by that sharp shaft, he vomited profuse blood. (42)
He fell unconscious upon the ground like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt;
then the young girl, her face smiling, spoke to her friend Rathaneṭrī.
"Friend, quickly drive the chariot near the demon Bhaṇḍa!
Here comes behind me that woman with the staff and the boar-banner. (44)
"I am eager to fight with the Daitya Bhaṇḍa in battle;
having encountered me, O Mistress of the Staff (Yama), he will surely be thwarted. (45)
"Drive the chariot quickly so that she may not catch me," said the charioteer; then that young woman spoke to her friend. (46)
In the midst of the Daitya army, this very golden chariot which is seen as a most lofty banner is indeed his. (47)
Even further from here, he is seen indeed surrounded by great and most fierce bull-like Daityas who are mighty chariot-warriors.
"I do not see a path by which I may lead the chariot;
therefore, create a way with your weapon, so that I may drive the chariot. (49)
Thus addressed, that girl of light-handed skill created a path in the midst of the Daitya armies with a shower of arrows in the blink of an eye. (50)
Like a broken dam by the forceful current of a great flood, the vanguard of the army, though raised up by the great heroes among the Daityas, was shattered in an instant. (51)
Some had their chariots broken, while others had lost their horses, elephants, and mounts.
Having encountered that shower of ash, the Daityas fled in all directions. || 52 ||
Others had their arms, eyes, feet, bellies, and heads severed;
likewise, others were cut into pieces as small as sesame seeds by the falling of a multitude of weapons.
The blood-carrying streams of the cowards were like oceans,
abounding in foam and waves, flowing indeed with hot water.
The quarters of the sky, their solar rays shrouded by a great cloud of arrow-nets, became blinded; the Daityas, intent on flight, were not even aware of it.
Those fools perceived that great death had arrived in the form of a child;
there, the heads of the Daityas fell down in great numbers.
Like ripe fruits of the king of grass (the palmyra palm) by a powerful wind:
"Alas, father! son! dear friend! brother! friend! I am destroyed! (57)
Thus there arose a great clamor among the Daityas in the thick of battle;
meanwhile, the mouth of that army was forced open by his impetuous force.
In the battle, the younger brother of the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, the charioteer Viśukra, caused that excellent chariot to enter [the enemy's ranks] in the blink of an eye.
Having seen the face of his own army and the young woman who had arrived,
eager then to go and fight with the king of the Daityas.
Having understood this and reflecting upon it, she surely thought: "This girl, though only eight years of age, is endowed with boundless strength and valor; she fights most wonderfully! (61)
This demoness cannot be conquered by anyone anywhere, even by those who are powerful;
nevertheless, brave men must certainly fight her in battle by all means.
"She alone will undoubtedly destroy all the Daityas, including us;
what more can that goddess Lalitā do in battle? (63)
"One must fight with all one's might; destiny is the ultimate resort in this matter.
Having thus resolved, [he approached] the lord of serpents born of the lineage of Airāvata.
Mounting a white elephant with four tusks, possessing a luster like a mountain of silver,
Viśukra rushed forward with speed; showering arrows like a rain-cloud,
he shone like a dark cloud resting upon Mount Kailāsa.
Having entered the army of the Daityas, he obstructed Bālā as she was traveling in her chariot.
As she approached with speed in battle, seeking the life of the Daitya,
he restrained her with a shower of arrows and then let out a lion’s roar. (67)
At his call, he turned back the fleeing army of the Daityas;
for among those of noble birth, flight from battle is not equal to this [dishonor]. (68)
If you flee from battle out of fear, Dharma and Artha will abandon you; therefore, summoning your prowess and anger, turn back from all sides! 69.
Having been utterly defeated by a woman in battle, you have fled and gone home;
what will you say when questioned by the women at home regarding your retreat from the fight? (70)
"Death itself is better than the humiliation caused by women.
Having heard the words of Viśukra, they then turned back from there.
Having arrived, they surrounded the young Tripurā on all sides;
that girl, stationed upon her chariot, was assailed by the armies of the Daityas.
She shone there like the newly risen sun surrounded by its halo;
then her friend Priyaṃvadā spoke to that charioteer.
O maiden! I consider the burden of the Daitya army to be exceedingly difficult to withstand;
yet there is no one to seize your rear, nor any protector of your wheel. (74)
"If you think the burden of the army ahead is too great, I shall quickly turn the chariot back; this army will then be joined with us again swiftly. (75)
"Having come here, you shall fight these lords of the Daityas as you please.
Hearing her friend's words, she who speaks with gentle voice laughed and said: (76)
"Why are you afraid, my dear? Even a hundredfold army of Daityas is not sufficient for me when I am fighting in battle; they are no match for me. (77)
"Out of sport and curiosity for battle, I am fighting with deliberate slowness.
If you think so, behold for a moment this world of Daityas being utterly destroyed. (78)

"Those devotees are not fit to be abandoned; we are joined to them like a shadow.
Having heard what was spoken by his beloveds, he, overflowing with joy, replied: ||| 12 ||
Listen to my words; this which has been previously contemplated by me shall not be otherwise, for I declare the cause in its entirety.
"By the grace of Goddess Ramā, I remember my former birth;
surely that Tripurā, who dwells in our refuge, spoke thus to me. (14)
For she indeed grants in every way the desired object of those who have taken refuge in her and are devoted to her, even that which is impossible; therefore, our wish shall be fulfilled.
"I am going with you, as I have so desired;
that world shall surely be yours in every way—of this there is no doubt. (16)
Furthermore, even if I have another desire along with my sons and others— to go there— I would indeed be just like that. (17)
I reflect that by the power of her compassion, there shall surely come for me, in due course, even a moment's separation from friends and kinsmen in this world. (18)
Indeed, it is not even possible to endure that in which a single moment expands into a multitude of kalpas;
surely, this much alone is prayed for: that there may never be a moment of such [suffering].
Therefore, you too should pray for this day and night;
she fulfills even the unattainable desires of her devotees. (20)
"I am established in purity; this other [world] is not to be known by me.
O kings, abandon your grief, for here a lofty prosperity has arrived. (21)
Having spoken thus, when the sun had set, he entered the great assembly hall;
then Viśukra and the other brothers, as well as the ministers, arrived.
In the midst of the assembly hall, which was exceedingly radiant, the sons, servants,
and courtiers bowed down to the Asura king and sat down upon their respective seats.
Seeing the king standing there as if grieving, Viśukra,
having offered salutations with palms joined in reverence, addressed him with wonderful words after first wishing him prosperity.
By the illustrious Goddess, through her desire for the fulfillment of the aims of the lord of the Daityas,
the intellect of all the Daityas, which was consistent with policy, was destroyed.
He who was the best among the exceedingly wise, equal to Śukra in discernment, even he— having become devoid of wisdom— spoke what was contrary to his own interest and opposed to reason. (26)
O Agastya, this alone is the task destined for Time to perform here;
it fully awakens the intellect in accordance with the necessity of what is to come to pass.
O Great King, you appear as if grieving while seated here in the assembly;
while we Daityas are still alive, I find this to be improper.
Thus addressed, that lord of the Daityas spoke again in the assembly of the Daityas:
"O Viśukra, what can I say now, in such a reversal of time?"
I am the sovereign over one hundred and five Brahmāṇḍas,
in whose battle even you, headed by Viṣṇu, were turned back in retreat.
He by whose very name the slayer of Vṛtra never even attains sleep, that very I am today being tormented by these throngs of weak women in this futile battle.
"Why do you ask me such a thing, 'Are you grieving?'—you who have the luster of the dead? Death at the proper time is most praiseworthy; for one such as you, there is no need for such torment. (32)
Having heard those words, "O Viśukra," he then spoke these words:
"O Lord of Daityas, you ought not to speak such piteous words. (33)
Who indeed would not feel compassion upon hearing the words "a weak woman"?
This turning away of weapons from women is your innate duty.
"Enough with you, or even with me, or likewise with the princes and others; for in a mere moment, not even the lowliest among the Daityas was commanded by you. (35)
"I shall slay the entire host of Śaktis; here I touch your feet.
You remain in the inner apartments, sporting with hosts of divine women. (36)
"Having conquered her, I shall return and behold your feet once more," he said,
and then he looked toward his side at the commander of the army, whose eyes were squinting.
Then he too, having bowed to him with palms joined in reverence, spoke:
"O Prince, why do you speak thus while I am still alive?"
"Enter together with the prince, along with the king and his attendants;
having gone there with the army and the generals, I shall accomplish that task. (39)
"Otherwise I shall not return; I promise this truth to you.
Having spoken thus and prostrated before them, he departed from the city. (40)
Then the exceedingly powerful commander of the army, named Durmada, arrived accompanied by many akṣauhiṇīs of troops along with his generals.
Accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, mounted on a camel, and wielding a mace, Ahaṅkāra, standing upon a mountain, bowed down and spoke to the commander of the enemy army.
O Commander of the Army! Remain right here, surrounded by your forces;
for your departure is most highly approved only upon the victory over the women.
"I shall bring that mistress of the Asuras back in a mere moment, having bound her by force.
If I do not bring her back within just a moment, then [you must act]. (44)
Having said, "One must strive and one must go," he departed with speed,
repeatedly sounding the musical instruments that form part of a victorious procession.
He went toward the vanguard of Śakti’s army at the rising of the sun,
where there was a great clamor arising from the tumult of the Daitya host.
Having heard this, the mighty goddess Sampatkarī, mounted upon a horse,
went and bowed down to Śrīmātā, as well as to Mantriṇī and Daṇḍinī.
Having informed the Daityas of their mobilization and being granted permission, they departed, exceedingly joyful and accompanied by countless armies of Śaktis.
There, the goddess Sampatkarī, having mounted a great elephant,
ascended the mountain known as Raṇakolāhala, which was as lofty as the Himalayas.
Clad in saffron robes and adorned with jewels,
she was a wave from the ocean of youth and a small island for the flood of loveliness.
Drawing her jeweled bow, which possessed the luster of Indra’s rainbow,
she drew forth arrows resembling the rays of the sun for the purpose of drying up the ocean of the Daityas.
Showering [light], she went forth like the sun situated upon the mountain of sunrise;
likewise, there were innumerable spears mounted upon elephants.
Surrounding him, they advanced while scattering arrows in every direction;
each possessed such power that she could roar while grasping three goads. (53)
Mounted upon the neck of an elephant, she leads the enemy host;
in one place she is alone, while in others she is established as many.
Thus, accompanied by innumerable elephant armies, the sovereign goddess,
as if devouring the host of demons, arrived pervading the earth with her splendor.
Those elephants, resembling mountains with naturally split temples, never retreating in battles, approached the army of the Daityas. || 56 ||
Then there arose the sound of musical instruments from both armies;
the discharge of weapons also began, accompanied by a great roar that steals away life.
The Daityas mounted chariots, elephants, horses, donkeys, camels, and deer; they took refuge upon vultures, crows, herons, owls, hawks, and pheasants.
Others have cats, mongooses, lizards, and ghosts as their mounts;
others still bear fierce spears, swords, discs, and javelins.
Armed with javelins, spears, iron clubs, slings, and maces—
thus joined by such hosts of Daityas, the army of Śakti advanced.
They fought with intense fury, their eyes bloodshot with rage,
hurling at one another words that produced bitter and harsh results.
"You are slain! Stay! Do not show your back through valor!"—speaking such and many other words, the Śaktis [attacked] in battle. (62)
Those Dānavas struck them in the same manner, and they likewise struck the army of Śakti.
Thus did that battle proceed, terrifying and destructive to life.
With their arms, thighs, and heads severed, and their bodies split into halves or quarters—
even such were the Śaktis when struck by the weapons of the Daityas.
Though their limbs were torn apart, they— biting their lips fiercely out of rage—
struck the host of adversaries with weapons, teeth, and fists.
Others, having lost their weapons, forcibly snatched weapons from the hands of the enemy;
and still others fought intensely with broken chariot parts and missiles.
While this terrible battle, resembling the dissolution of the world, was thus proceeding,
rivers with foamy waves flowed, consisting of floods of blood.
The army of the Daityas was destroyed by the Śaktis mounted upon elephants;
pierced deeply, it fled, reduced to only ten Akṣauhiṇīs.
Seeing his own army thus broken on all sides, Durmada,
mounted upon a camel and mace in hand, appeared like Yama, the Destroyer at the end of time.
He dispatched a camel of tawny appearance, ten spans in height,
possessing great speed and immense strength, into the armies of Śakti.
Then, having entered the armies of the Śaktis, the exceedingly swift Uṣtra,
whose tongue was like a mass of flesh dripping from the corners of his mouth, [proceeded]. (71)
Resounding with an echo of the great roar from the churning of the ocean,
he spat out masses of foam and urinated profusely behind him.
Destroying the herd of elephants with his chest, the thrusting of his feet,
the blows of his snout, and even his tusks, he roamed through the army of Śakti.
Though intoxicated, he destroyed the elephants with blows from his mace and the spears with his own weapons;
like the Destroyer of Śakti’s army, he wrought carnage in his rage.
Seeing that destruction of Śakti’s army, Sampadīśvarī incited the tumultuous roar of battle for its destruction.
Then the king of elephants, having approached Karabha, the vehicle of the Daitya,
fought him repeatedly with blows from the tips of his tusks and the frontal globes of his forehead.
He too fought with his tusks, blows to the head, and kicks;
thus a tumultuous battle took place between the young elephant and the elephant.
Then the king of the Atharvans violently struck the young camel, causing it to fall to the ground;
having thrown it down, he trampled it with his foot and deprived the camel of life.
Knowing that the camel was about to die, he, mace in hand, leaped into the air;
whirling his mace, he brought it down upon the heads of the two elephants.
Struck by the mace, the elephant, its head shattered, reeled upon its chest; incapacitated, it fell to the ground on its knees, vomiting blood. (80)
At that moment, although struck in the chest by Sampadadhīśa’s arrow,
Durmada also gave up his life, having been split open by the enemy’s sword.
Seeing the commander of the army slain, the Daitya soldiers fled; not looking back as they went, they sought means of escape for the sake of their lives. 82.

Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Slaying of Durmada," in the *Śrīlalitāmāhātmya*, within the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* of the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent among the *Itihāsas*. || 5494 ||
The sixty-seventh chapter: A description of the slaying of Karaṅka and others in the prowess of Nakulī.
Hearing that Durmada had been slain, Kuranda—the elder brother of Durmada—being of great strength, became enraged and, taking his command, [set out] against Kuṭilākṣa. || 1 ||
Accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs, he advanced swiftly to do battle;
beholding the army of the Daityas returning once more, resembling the sky in appearance.
Mounted upon horses, he advanced with boundless armies;
various lofty steeds shone like waves.
That army, with its various divisions of distinct colors, shone exceedingly;
upon horses resembling masses of foam, there were riders possessing the luster of gold.
Clad in blue garments and bearing swords and shields, they were proud of their youth;
others took refuge upon horses resembling dark clouds at the end of time.
Their luster is like the light of the moon; they wear red ornaments and garments;
they carry bows and arrows; and they are adorned with crests of blue jewels.
Others, resembling emeralds, mounted swift horses with limbs like rubies, adorned with pale red garments and ornaments.
In some places, spears went forth with their handles, ornaments, cloths, and horse-riders all alike;
thus the army resembled the sky at twilight joined with variegated clouds. (8)
Resembling the ocean overflowing its shores, it swiftly devoured the army of Daityas;
meanwhile, there arose the sound of kettledrums, trumpets, cow-horns, tabors, and drums.
It was intensified by the mingled sounds of horses' hooves, spades, and clapping hands,
and made robust by the roars of *huṃ* cries, summoning, scattering, and the slapping of arms.
Filling the space between heaven and earth, he shone forth;
then a terrible battle commenced, which dragged away the lives of living beings. || 11 ||
The mass of dust raised by the tossing of the horses' hooves deafened the quarters of the sky with the great roar of the falling arrows. 12.
Like a mass of great Saṃvartaka clouds, it overspread the sky; for a moment, the sight was obscured, becoming like the darkness of a moonless midnight. (13)
Then, by the showers of blood spurting from the falling of weapons,
the darkness of dust was pacified, and once again there was a great battle.
There was a life-threatening struggle between one another and with the asuras;
the splendor of the Daityas was seized by the exceedingly powerful spears (śaktis).
The army of the Daityas was shattered, violently crushed by the *śakti* missiles;
the great asuras had their feet, hands, ears, bellies, and backs severed. (16)
Casting aside their weapons and repeatedly waving their hands about, crying out, "Alas, we are slain!", they abandoned the battle and fled. (17)
Having observed his own army broken, Kuraṇḍa, overwhelmed with rage,
mounted his horse and, drawing his great bow, discharged arrows.
Having entered Śakti’s army, he destroyed them by the thousands with showers of arrows released from the clouds of his bow, while Śakti’s host [was overwhelmed]. 19.
When Śakti’s army was broken like a high dam by the rush of a great flood of water, she,
mounted upon a horse, charged forward.
She was mounted upon a horse named Aparājita, who shone like molten gold; she was radiant with spotless silken garments and ornaments.
Seeing her holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows, he spoke these words:
"O wicked woman, you have been arrogant for a long time; I shall now remove your pride."
"You shall swiftly reap the fruit of having slain my brother;
only after killing you in battle will I be freed from the guilt of my brother's death. (23)
"First show me that prowess of yours which has been long accumulated.
Thus addressed, she became enraged and struck him with three sharp arrows while mounted upon her horse.
There he pierced him with one arrow and severed the head of his mount;
with a second, he caused his crown to fall to the ground.
With the third [arrow], he violently tore open his chest;
his horses slain, his crown fallen, and struck powerfully in the heart, he was defeated.
Fainted like a great asura whose roots have been severed, he fell down;
then, in a moment, freed from his fainting, he spoke to her at the front of the battle.
"O Goddess, you are indeed praiseworthy in battle and esteemed by me as virtuous.
Having heard this, he spoke again: "Fie upon you, O Daitya! Do you still live? (28)
Indeed, through my effort, you have been reduced to a mere remnant of life;
behold this arrow, the destroyer of life, which removes the pride of enemies. (29)
Having heard the words of the goddess, the Daitya, his form blazing with the fire of anger,
cut the goddess's bow with a straight-knotted arrow.
She too cut with her sword the bow held in the hand of the Daitya;
then the Daitya also split her sword in two with his own sword.
Again, with extreme speed, he struck the horse with his sword;
its head split open by the sword-stroke, the horse indeed fled away.
Then the Goddess also, becoming enraged, bound him firmly with a noose,
dragged him forward, and struck him on the head with a goad of blazing splendor.
With that goad, his head was split open and the Daitya died instantly.
Having heard that Kuraṇḍa had been slain, the commander of the army was filled with rage. (34)
Then, seeing the commanders of the army standing at his side, led by Karaṅka,
the commander-in-chief Kuṭilākṣa spoke with bloodshot eyes.
"O Karaṅka and the other four, you five, accompanied by your own armies, go quickly;
having slain her, bind her swiftly at Vāraṇa. (36)
"Bring it together; surely you possess a power consisting of illusion (māyā).
By that which is called 'the Serpent' (sarpiṇī), all of you shall indeed be unconquerable by gods and asuras. (37)
Thus commanded, Karaṅka and the others bowed to the lord of the generals and,
each accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs, advanced to do battle.
Karaṅka is on the donkey-chariot; Vajradantaka is on the young elephant;
Vajraloman is on the vulture-chariot; and likewise, Kākamukha is on the elephant. (39)
Vajravaktra and the others, who were of terrifying appearance and stationed on the Kharabara mountain,
heard the exceedingly great roar of the Daityas in the fury of battle.
And Queen Sampatī, mounted upon a horse, marshaled her army;
then those two armies of Śakti and the Daitya encountered one another face to face. (41)
Amidst the resounding of various musical instruments and the brilliance of flashing weapons,
they both discharged showers of arrows from afar like masses of clouds.
Then the two armies, locked in combat and slaughtering one another,
were filled with lips bitten in rage and faces contorted by frowns. (43)
Torn by white swords, pierced by tall spears,
perforated by a net of arrows, and crushed by the falling of iron clubs.
With various kinds of weapons, they destroyed one another;
the great army of elephants and horses was exceedingly incensed by the spears.
In just a moment, he completely destroyed the army of the lord of the Daityas;
seeing the host mostly slain, the great Asuras, Karaṅka and the others, [fled]. (46)
Having entered that army of Śakti, they destroyed it by their might;
seeing the army being driven back and struck down by the foremost of the Daityas, [they acted]. (47)
Likewise, Sampatkarī, mounted on a horse, fought against the Daityas;
at that time, the great asuras such as Karaṅka and others were broken by those two in battle.
They fashioned that great illusion (Mahāmāyā) as a female serpent adorned with snakes,
possessing a terrifying form, a fierce roar, and a diverse circle of serpents.
Then, for the destruction of Śakti’s army on the field of battle,
she [the goddess] created circles of serpents emerging from her mouth, eyes, and other parts.
In a mere moment, he destroyed the army of the Śaktis;
seeing that exceedingly fierce slaughter, some of the Śaktis [fled]. (51)
Having fled, they went quickly to report [the matter] to Daṇḍarājñī;
they reached her, who had the face of a boar and was stationed in the presence of Śrīmātṛ. (52)
Having bowed down to the Mantrīṇī, the Daityas also cried out, "Alas, what fear! and said, "O Commander, we have gone forth together with the goddess Sampad and the Asuras."
There a battle took place, terrible, life-destroying, and supreme;
Durmada was slain in the fight, as was Sampadīśa and Kuraṇḍaka.
Even the vast army, led by one mounted on a horse, has been reduced to a mere remnant of fame;
that exceedingly fierce force has been destroyed by us, and thus the Daityas have been utterly conquered.
Now, Mahāmāyā, known as Sarpiṇī, has been dispatched by the five army commanders, Karaṅka and the others, whose foot soldiers have been slain. (56)
Creating countless swarms of serpents repeatedly with her eyes and other senses,
she was struck down, bitten, bound, and reduced to ashes by those snakes.
Indeed, Śakti’s army has become almost entirely like the dead;
for your two goddesses, with a shower of arrows, strike the serpents again and again. (58)
To slay the Daityas, he went forth with a mace made of excellent iron;
the lords of mantras, knowing her to be an infallible serpent, warded her off.
Having gone there with speed, he personally informed the Goddess of those events.
Then, having meditated for a moment, the Mother, her lotus-face yawning, [spoke]. (61)
As she opened her mouth,
a great spear with the luster of gold, born from the goddess's palate, emerged with extreme velocity.
To Nakulī, who was in the form of a garuḍa, the goddess of speech, adorned with jewels,
and standing before her having prostrated, the illustrious Laliteśvarī spoke:
"Go, child, and quickly destroy that female serpent with your own splendor.
Having been thus addressed, she reached the field of battle in an instant.
By the wind from the wings of Suparṇa, all the serpents fled;
then the Śaktis, released from their serpent-bonds, rose up. || 65 ||
She again created serpents to destroy that circle of spears;
seeing that multitude of spears repeatedly overwhelmed by the swarm of serpents, [she acted]. (66)
In an instant, he created from his own body hairs exceedingly powerful mongooses;
those mongooses were of great speed, variegated in color, and fiercely enraged.
With bristling hair and tails, adamantine teeth, and firm limbs, those mongooses were swiftly created; they [pursued] those serpents stationed on every side.
They bit him with their diamond-like fangs and tore him into two or three pieces;
yet even though the snakes were thus mangled and devoured, the mongoose remained unharmed.
The armies of Śakti were completely destroyed, just as those who desire destruction had arisen. Then those mongooses, having annihilated the snakes without exception, [acted]. (70)
They bit the female serpent everywhere, even though she was adorned with serpents;
and when the female serpent had perished, the great asuras, Karaṅka and the others, [continued their assault].
The Nakulas fought with the Goddess many times over with both handheld weapons and missiles;
then their weapons and even their mounts were [destroyed] on all sides. (72)
Having destroyed them all at once, he severed their heads with his sword;
with their heads cut off by the sword, they fell down, deprived of life.
Meanwhile, the army, though commanded, fled in terror in all directions,
while the noble sons of Nakula were being cheered with shouts of victory.
Having withdrawn the Vārāhī-mantra from her limbs and having prostrated before Laliteśvarī,
she, with palms joined in reverence, related the account of the victory.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Slaying of Karaṅka and Others," in the section on the Greatness (*Māhātmyakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrī Lalitācaritra*, within the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of glorious histories. || 5570 ||
The sixty-eighth chapter:
A description of the deliberation on the stratagems for the purpose of defeating the Goddess, in the dialogue between Kuṭilākṣa and Viṣaṅga.
Then, having learned that Karaṅka and the others had been slain,
Kuṭilākṣa sighed deeply and fell into a state of profound anxiety.
"Surely this is a great power that appears invincible to me;
for the arrogant Kuraṇḍa and the powerful [Durmada] have both been slain in battle. (2)
Let it be; that need not be considered, for victory is uncertain.
These men, headed by Karaṅka, are joined with the serpent Amoghā. (3)
How was she—who is heard of as Lalitā by name, the leader of the host of Śaktis, and invincible to gods and Daityas alike—struck down in battle? (4)
She remained there while her retinue destroyed the army;
oh! indeed, what might not happen in this world when destiny is adverse? || 5 ||
This is a marvel: Karaṅka and the others have been slain by a woman;
their strength was diminished, and the powerful commanders of the army were killed when reduced to a fourth part.
"How could it be that not even a single leader has been killed among Śakti's army?
Having promised the king the victory over Śakti, how indeed can I [face him] today? (7)
(687) "I shall say again that it is impossible, just as [it was for] a coward," [said he] while the commander of the army, whose eyes were fixed on the hut, was thus overcome by anxiety.
Viṣaṅga also arrived, dispatched by Viśukra;
seeing Viṣaṅga, the commander of the army, Kuṭikākṣa, rose up.
Having honored him with a seat and other offerings, Viṣaṅga sat down upon his own seat;
then, seeing the commander of the army with a dejected face, he [spoke].
He said to her: "The preeminent Daitya has been deluded by her who, when entreated by the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, desired him—she who grants the desires of her devotees. (11)
O Kuṭilākṣa! Your face appears as if it were despondent;
therefore, tell me quickly what the cause is, for I shall do everything equally.
Having heard everything regarding the destruction of the Daityas and the slaughter of his enemies, as well as the lack of confidence in the Śaktis and the imminent great danger, he spoke.
Having heard this, he laughed at the Daitya, saying, "How deluded!
Though bewildered by the Goddess's illusion, he spoke as if he were wise.
Listen, O General! Having understood everything, I have come here;
for without a strategic means, an opponent who possesses great strength cannot be conquered.
Victory is established in every way for those who are disciplined; it rests upon wisdom.
Victory through power has been determined by me, who possess subtle intelligence, as being generally achieved through the application of intellect.
"O you who have taken refuge in my reasoning, dispel the darkness of grief!
By this very logic, I consider the hosts of Śaktis to be already slain. (17)
Listen, I shall declare to you that which I have resolved for victory;
she must be conquered by means of a stratagem alone, and I shall state that certain course of action. (18)
This very day, at the final portion of the day, they were all armored by the great army of the Daityas and accompanied by Viśukra as well.
Let them go forth against the enemy for battle, accompanied by the princes; indeed, one must go to war according to one's capacity, even if it be with a mere host of commoners.
They fight with complete ferocity, yet she remains playful and alone;
meanwhile, he is surrounded at night by many demons in thick darkness.
Emerging from the side and taking to the rear,
some women there also mounted her chariot.
Having slain the Śaktis, I shall forcibly seize the wicked Lalitā—she who is but the root of the multitude of Śaktis—alive by force. (23)
If he does not surrender his life, I shall strike him severely with my mace;
once she is slain or even captured, [I shall seize] the army of Śakti.
Know that she is already as good as lost; indeed, she is being destroyed by you all—even she who is Queen Lalitā, with her delicate hands and feet. (25)
"It has long been known to me that they are not capable of fighting with me;
thus have I resolved with my exceedingly bold intellect. (26)
"O friend, has anyone heard your opinion, which is free from the distinction of faults?
Having heard these words of Viṣaṅga, the king, whose eyes were crooked, [spoke]. (27)
Deluded by the illusion of Tripura, he considered her conquered;
and rising up delighted, he quickly embraced this or that [form]. (28)
Excellent! O one worthy of praise in the Daitya lineage, I know you to be the most intelligent of all;
indeed, at such a time, a wisdom that brings victory is difficult to find in every respect. (29)
For such wisdom as this belongs neither to Uśanas nor likewise to Aṅgiras;
live long, for you are considered by me to be an accomplisher of the king's business.
Therefore, depart without delay; having informed the king and consulted with the ministers, come by all means to do battle against the princes and Viśukra.
This lord of the day is moving slowly to proceed toward the ocean;
when we engage the army of Śakti in battle, then [we shall act] swiftly.
"Endowed with wisdom and vigor, you shall accomplish that task.
When Kuṭilākṣa had spoken thus, Viṣaṅga then departed for the city.
Having informed King Viśukra of everything there,
the lord of the Daityas, approved by those deluded by Māyā, departed swiftly.
Surrounded by princes, Viśukra, and ministers,
and accompanied by Kuṭilākṣa, he was encompassed by his entire army.
Having learned that the Daitya king was fully prepared for battle, he advanced there to fight where the great army of Śakti was stationed. (36)
Having bowed to the minister Lalitādevī, she informed her of the event— the encounter with the best of the Daitya armies— through the mouth of a spy.
Commanded by Lalitādevī, the minister spoke to Daṇḍinī:
"O child, this great fury of Bhaṇḍāsura is now visible."
"Except for one lord of the Daityas, all have assembled for battle;
we too must go there quickly and completely. (39)
"Prepare the armor for the Kuru army, and especially for the Śaktis.
Thus commanded, Kolamukhī, surrounded by the entire host of Śaktis, [set forth].
Accompanied by her minister, she bowed to the Goddess and went forth into the battle;
that army of Śaktis emerged, teeming with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Like the ocean at the dissolution of the worlds,
he was a flood of sound from the blare of battle-instruments and the roar of elephants, horses, and chariots.
The mingled lion-roar of the Śaktis indeed increased; hearing that terrible, world-shattering, and loud sound, the Daityas [were struck with fear]. (43)
Then they let out a most immense counter-shout;
that sound, mingled with the two armies, resounded as it reached heaven and earth.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Defeat of Viṣaṅga," in the *Śrīlalitācaritra* of the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* within the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of sacred histories. || 5816 ||
Chapter Seventy-One: Description of the Application of Obstructive Yantras by Viśukra for the Destruction of the Śrīcakra.

Then the discus, the trident, the iron club, and the spear—
each time they were hurled, they fell uselessly to the ground, having struck against his body.
Seeing that Daitya who was invincible against all weapons, that Lord of the Gaṇas became like a mass of boulders, resembling a rain of stones or a crumbling crag. || 24 ||
Overcome with anxiety, he struck him with his fist;
then, a most terrible fist-fight ensued between the two of them.
Then, having bound that Daitya with a grip of his arms— joined by a rain of rising fire from the clenching of his fists— he cast him down.
Having struck him down and trampled him with his foot, he tore at his heart with his tusk;
thus torn apart, the Daitya then gave up his life in battle.
Having thus slain that Daitya Ibhaka,
Gaṇeśa, possessed of wonderful prowess, quickly advanced once more toward the Asura Bhaṇḍa for battle.
Then, seeing Gaṇapati approaching, the great asura Bhaṇḍa,
terrified by his prowess, thought of the goddess Lalitā.
"O Mother, let this body, slain by you in battle, perish;
thus fulfill my desire, for I have sought refuge at your lotus feet. (30)
Having understood that, the Great Goddess, seated upon her chariot drawn by the king of discs, called to mind the elephant-faced god (Gaṇeśa) in order to fulfill the desire of her devotee.
Having understood the goddess's recollection, Gajānana arrived;
having prostrated, he said: "O Mother, why have you remembered me while I am engaged in the conduct of battle?"
Having heard his words, the supreme goddess Lalitā said:
"Child, enough with this method of combat; stay now by my side."
"Let these goddesses, eager for battle, fight with the army of the Asuras.
Having been thus commanded, the Lord of the Gaṇas ceased from his wrestling match.
Then, seeing the army of Śakti severely wounded by the sons of Bhaṇḍa,
that young woman approached them in battle, scattering arrows at them. (35)
The sons of the Daitya lords, accompanied by innumerable Daitya armies,
surrounded the girl in the arena of battle as she performed most wondrous deeds.
Tens of millions of Daitya warriors, roaring and intoxicated by the frenzy of battle, showered the young girl standing in her chariot with a rain of various weapons.
Then Daṇḍinī spoke these supreme words to the host of Śaktis:
"Listen, all you Śaktis; I declare the command of Bālāmbā to you. (38)
Against those with whom she fights in battle, she must never suddenly employ her collection of weapons; otherwise, she shall be punished by me. (39)
"Behold her battle; you must not fight her by any means!
Having thus proclaimed this among the armies, she herself, accompanied by the minister's wife, [proceeded]. (40)
She took her place at her side during that display of martial prowess;
indeed, she was filled with joy upon hearing the command of Queen Daṇḍarājñī.
It was a marvel that she, alone, fought against countless Daitya warriors while the foremost of Siddhas,
Ṛṣis, and deities watched from the sky.
They were filled with wonder as she, a single maiden, fought against many;
then she became covered by the multitude of weapons hurled by the Daityas.
Seeing all directions covered on every side by throngs of weapons, like the rising sun obscured by masses of clouds, she became despondent. (44)
Then, in an instant, the young woman, having destroyed that shower of weapons with her own counter-weapons,
struck them all down once more.
Then, with swift strides and marvelous prowess, she simultaneously destroyed the weapons and mounts of those countless beings.
Furthermore, she cut down even the weapons as soon as they were seized;
then, with her sharp arrows, she destroyed the Daityas with extreme speed.
The taking up of the arrow, its aiming, its drawing back, and its release were not perceived by anyone, even with the most keen vision, in any way whatsoever. (48)
But from the middle of her bow, sharp arrows spread forth like locusts falling upon the earth, extending in all directions without any intervening space.
The heads of the Daityas fall in heaps from the king of grass like well-ripened fruits from a *caṭamāra* tree. (50)
Some had their hands, feet, thighs, chests, bellies, and necks severed,
while others were pierced so densely that they appeared like the thousand-eyed Indra.
And others were mangled, their bodies strewn with fragments of Daitya bones;
some, pierced in the chest, remained standing firm though their life-force was stolen.
Bearing weapons, they appear like painted warriors;
some, struck by arrows, are carried along by the force [of their momentum] as their lives depart. (53)
As if intent on flight due to their cowardice in battle,
in this manner she [destroyed] millions of the foremost Daityas in a mere moment.
Their life-breaths departed; those one hundred wounded ones fell.
Not even a single Daitya there, however heroic, was capable of protecting himself.
Where is the battle, and where is it fitting to discharge weapons? The Daityas never know how to wage war while entirely alone anywhere. (56)
They would immediately perceive the battle of millions of Śakti armies;
the Śakti armies stationed in the sky, and the gods and others on all sides. (57)
Seeing that extraordinary and supreme prowess of the girl, they were struck with wonder;
then, seeing the girl thus striking down the army, the Daityas fled.
Terrified, they cast aside their weapons and became intent on flight, crying out, "Alas, we are ruined! This is surely no woman, no child, but a young maiden! (59)
The Destroyer himself has arrived before our very eyes to harm us;
today, in an instant, the army of the Daityas will be utterly annihilated.
Speaking thus and crying out, they fled in every direction;
yet, finding no path for their exit, they were densely covered by streams of weapons.
Shattered by showers of arrows, the Daityas fell in great throngs;
some, their heads deeply pierced, collapsed into heaps of corpses.
Terrified, they settled down and protected themselves from the fear of death;
thus, at that time, the army of the Daityas was for the most part destroyed and fled. (63)
Then, having heard what remained [to be said], the sons of Bhaṇḍa arrived;
they were mounted on chariots drawn by lions, bearing great bows, and were exceedingly fierce. (64)
In their fury, with a single bound, they surrounded the young woman on all sides—
dark as great clouds, roaring like the king of beasts.
Raining down showers of arrows like the young sun in the sky,
she was assailed by those many youths, whose prowess equaled that of Viṣṇu.
Having encountered them in battle, she fought them with ease;
and the chief ministers, Daṇḍinī and the others, beheld the prowess of the girl.
Filled with wonder, they reported the great battle to the illustrious Parādevī:
"O Goddess, surely that maiden is not capable of being overcome. (68)
Today he will undoubtedly destroy Bhaṇḍa, as well as his two brothers and even his sons who have come with the army, leaving nothing remaining, as if in mere sport. (69)
Having thus fought for a moment with the sons of Bhaṇḍa, who were exerting themselves feebly,
he simultaneously destroyed their mounts, banners, and umbrellas with his arrows.
Having warded off that shower of arrows with counter-showers,
he gradually severed their bows with well-feathered shafts.
Then, enraged, they seized weapons such as swords and maces in order to slay her; but just as they were about to do so, she quickly [fled] toward you. (72)
She cut off each piece as it was taken up; that was like a marvel.
Thus the Daityas were rendered weaponless by her prowess. (73)
They considered it most extraordinary and fell into even greater anxiety,
having indeed witnessed the boy thus devoured by Mahākāla in battle.
Viṣaṅga and Viśukra, surrounded by a great army, quickly approached indeed to protect those princes. || 75 ||
"Do not fear; we have come," said that auspicious goddess as they spoke, while she beheld them discharging showers of weapons like dark clouds at the end of time.
Seeing that shower thick with weapons, the boy, with great joy,
effortlessly warded off that army of Daityas.
Then, with the Vāyavya weapon, she reduced the great wind to nothing but a name, like a jar [shattered]; at that, the two of them became exceedingly enraged.
Seeing both of them approaching with extreme speed, mace and sword in hand, he swiftly destroyed their mounts and elephants with arrows in that battle.
Then, struck forcefully on the region of their chests by each other individually,
they fell to the ground in a swoon, like mountains struck by thunderbolts.
In the meantime, the sons of Bhaṇḍa turned back for the sake of their weapons;
seeing them returned, he deprived them of their chariots in an instant.
Having quickly struck down those who were moving on foot with sharp arrows in their shanks, the heirs of Bhaṇḍa have attacked; how can this be for you heroes? (82)
"Tell us, is it proper for those who flee to show their backs in battle?
Having heard these words, whose bitter fruit was yet to come, those excessively proud men [replied]. (83)
With eyes blazing with wrath, they would say as they turned back to face him in battle:
"Fie upon you! Having seen this innocent girl, you have become compassionate by your very nature! (84)
Since Jīva has somehow encountered us, who are like Death itself, behold this: we shall instantly render you devoid of pride; therefore, steady yourself! 85.
Having spoken thus, he raised his fist and, as they ran toward him,
he severed each one's head with sharp, crescent-headed arrows.
Then their heads fell like ripe tāla fruits;
a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose at the front of the Daitya army.
The Lord of the Gods showered fragrant flowers upon Bālā, and a great cry of "Victory! arose on all sides among Śakti’s armies.

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Bhaṇḍa’s Sons," in the *Śrīlalitācaritra* of the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* within the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of sacred histories. || 6066 ||
Chapter Seventy-four:
A Description of the Meeting of Both Armies.
When Bhaṇḍa’s sons had thus been slain, the minister Daṇḍanāyikā, observing that the young woman was once again eager for battle, [spoke].
Having seen, bowed to, and informed the illustrious queen, O Goddess, they said:
"Permitted by you, we shall go forth immediately to engage in battle."
Let the Daityas then come forth for battle, well-armored;
you have rendered them invincible, and this is not within our power at all.
Having spoken thus, he took her with him and went into the presence of the illustrious Mother;
having ascended the chariot known as the Cakrarāja and having bowed to the Supreme Mother (Parāmbikā), [he departed].
Having heard of the great and wonderful valor in battle displayed by the girl, as well as her victory, the venerable Mother Lalitā was then pleased. (5)
Embracing the girl with great affection, he settled her by his side;
seeing the sons of Bhaṇḍa slain, they cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas! (6).
Fleeing in all directions with parched mouths and lusterless, they departed upon hearing of the destruction of their son; then the demon Bhaṇḍa was exceedingly distressed.
Reflecting again with a virtuous mind and summoning fortitude with haste:
"Alas! A vast delusion and a lapse of memory have arisen within me. (8)
"Why do I grieve in vain? My desire has been fulfilled by the Goddess; exactly as I prayed, so indeed has it been done."
"Surely they will grieve for me; therefore, let them go to their death before my very eyes, slain in battle by that goddess."
"I shall attain that state of the world together with my retinue"—
this was my former resolve, and the Supreme Mother was entreated accordingly.
Then she, the milker who fulfills the desires of those seeking her grace, performed [her service] there; meanwhile, Great Delusion thought, "Why has he come to me in vain? (12)
Therefore, enough of my delusion, O Goddess! I have come to you for refuge;
O Maheśvarī, quickly fulfill that remaining desire of mine.
Then, having withdrawn the remainder of my army along with my two brothers,
quickly bring me, together with the host of women, purified by the fire of weapons in battle.
Having performed [this], you ought to bring me into the proximity of your own lotus feet.
When shall I behold Him who bears the moon upon His crest and is beautifully adorned with three eyes? (15)
Beholding the face of the illustrious Mother, with its corners of the eyes reddened by anger and a frown knitting the brows, he was consumed by the fire of her arrow.
"Seeking that form, beautiful as ten million gods of love, he said: 'I go to the sorrowless, immortal state, which is very difficult for yogins to attain. (17)
Meditating upon the goddess Śrī Lalitā, he became free from conceptual thought for a moment;
at that very instant, the two brothers of the king of the Daityas arrived there.
They saw him standing utterly motionless like a pillar;
they thought him to be overcome by the weight of grief for his son and deeply fainted.
There, they both spoke words of reconciliation suited to the occasion;
through those words of theirs, intent on peace, his mind withdrew from the object of its meditation.
Opening his eyes, he saw his two brothers standing before him;
he stood facing his brothers for the purpose of concealing his true form.
Then, laughing at those two, he grieved intensely in his mind for his sons, saying:
"Alas, my sons! Having abandoned me, your father, in this ocean of sorrow..."
Where have those who abandoned their affection gone, leaving you sinking in extreme misery?
Your mothers, so tender and distressed by their deep maternal love, are in such a state! (23)
Seeing those two brothers then lamenting thus, "Having heard [this], how could they not be as if their hearts were rent asunder? and so forth; 24.
Bewildered by the illusory power (māyā) of the illustrious Goddess, the two spoke these words to the lord of the Daityas:
"Enough, O lord of the Daityas! With this grief that robs one of courage and valor. (25)
Beholding you grieving, O Lord of countless worlds,
fever consumes our bodies like fire consumes dry cow-dung. (26)
O King, maintaining your fortitude for a moment, remain steadfast;
having gone there in a single stride, we shall slay her with sharpened arrows.
"We shall quickly bind and lead away this woman known as Lalitā, who is like a son-destroying Mārī come among the Daityas—whether she be living or even dead. (28)
Having spoken thus, those two of exceeding strength and prowess took up their bows with arrows and, mounting their chariots, advanced for the sake of battle.
Surrounded by an army of two hundred akṣauhiṇīs and well-armored,

On the right side of the excellent chariot, the king of wheels, the powerful Viṣaṅga arrived with great speed,
accompanied by an army of one hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
And Viśukra also fell swiftly with his left side on the morning of the third day of battle, at the rising of the sun.
When they suddenly fell upon both flanks of Śakti’s army, a great clamor arose among the troops on both sides.
Then, hearing the sound of battle, the minister and the commander-in-chief became extremely apprehensive and spoke to the venerable Parāmbikā.
O Goddess, the terrifying sound arising from the encounter of the Daityas' army with Śakti is heard; the Daityas are fighting with deceit. 35.
"O Maheśvarī, we are fighting unexpectedly, fully armed and having made no prior agreement; therefore, grant us your permission quickly. (36)

Then, having been granted permission and having bowed down, the two ministers— the female counselor and the commander of the army— set out quickly for battle, each surrounded by her own host of Śaktis.
Standing on the right side of the Goddess, Daṇḍinī, of fierce prowess,
emerged from the southern gate of the chariot of the illustrious Cakrarāja.

Where Bhairava himself stood as the charioteer of the yoked chariot,
on its two sides moved those mounted upon chariots drawn by lions and tigers.
Likewise, Svapneśvarī, Kālasaṅkarṣā, and Yudhasambhramā, together with the Baṭukas, the hosts of Kālikās, and the Varāhamukha-Śaktis. || 41 ||
Surrounded by innumerable [attendants], that minister went forth from the northern gate of the chariot-circle to wage war. Thus [it was] from the northern gate of the chariot-circle. 42.
Having emerged upon the exceedingly lofty chariot-king Geyacakra, which was endowed with seven sections and moved by the horses of the Vedas and the directions; 43.
Laughing, Śyāmalā became the other charioteer there;

With Saṅgīta and Sāhitya on her left side, both preceded by Śyāmala,

From all sides, millions upon millions of dark-complexioned beings emerged swiftly from the singing-wheel of the chariot of the Self, having arisen from the limbs of the ministers. (46)
All sixteen-year-old women, endowed with the beauty of youth, set out mounted on chariots and laden with the equipment for battle.
Clad in garments of red silk and adorned with ornaments of the nine gems, they delude the entire world with their sidelong glances and gentle smiles. (48)
Their eyes were rolling with intoxication from drinking Kāpiśāyana wine;

Devoted to jests and play, and intent upon the sport of excessive laughter,
that army of the lords of mantras then shone forth exceedingly.
Like a row of *tāpiccha* trees with blossoming, beautiful clusters of blossoms, there then occurred the encounter between the army of Śakti and the army of the Daityas. 51.
Then, on the earth, there was a meeting like that of two overflowing oceans,
accompanied by the sounds of roaring, battle-cries, "huṃ" shouts, and the crashing of blows.
The deep and resonant sound of chariots, elephants,
and the neighing of horses deafened the quarters of the sky there between the two armies.
By the downpours of arrows released from the great clouds of the Śakti-saṅgha,

Having entered that army of the Daityas,

Some were densely pierced by arrows, some were transfixed by iron clubs,
and others had all their limbs severed by swords and were deprived of life.

thus was the army being destroyed by the army of Śakti.

Then, like a cloud pouring down showers of arrows,

Now, the sons of Viśukra, whose prowess was equal to that of their father,

Then, becoming enraged, the asura cut [it] off in half a blink of an eye and struck the chariot and its vehicle with a sharp-edged sword.

Seeing him fighting firmly with his mace, [the Lord], having leaped up, struck that Asura on the head with His own mace, which had severed his banner, chariot, and horses. 69.
With his head shattered, the enemy of the gods fell down, deprived of life;

Having completely conquered him with various weapons and missiles, he swiftly hurled a trident at his chest; with his heart shattered by it, he immediately lost his life.

Taking up his mace, he rushed with speed toward her to slay her;

With his head shattered by arrows, he fell to the ground unconscious;

Leaping swiftly from the chariot, he seized him with both arms;
meanwhile, the other woke up, realizing it was indeed his own captivity.
She struck the Goddess with her fist, and she too fell into a slight swoon;

Tens of millions of armies and spears also surged forth;

With his eyes reddened by intense rage,
Bilśpya blazed forth and scattered that army of Śaktis with showers of arrows.

Like a rain-cloud, Nīla showered the peak of the mountain intensely with streams of sharp arrows; Viśukra was thus utterly mangled.

Deeply pierced by the minister’s wife, his form blazing with rage,

Chapter Seventy-Five: A Description of the Slaying of Viṣaṅga.
When Vārāhī was joined by Viṣaṅga in the battle, then a terrifying combat took place between the spear of the Daitya and the trident of Ambā. || 1 ||

Seeing the Daitya army for the most part destroyed by multitudes of spears, those whose bodies were cut into pieces like sesame seeds gave up their lives on the field of battle. || 3 ||
Enraged, the sons of Viṣaṅga— resembling mountains, possessing uplifted and formidable prowess, and exceedingly heroic— rushed toward the army of Śakti.
Karālavaktra, Viśikha, Vibhāṇḍa, Vikaṭekṣaṇa, Indraśatru, Surārāti, Mahākukṣi, and Madoddhata. || 5 ||

and beholding that army of spears being slaughtered by them, [he saw it] indeed.

Then the enraged Jambhanī struck off his head with a sword;

The immobilizing arrow, mounted upon a deer, struck Viśikha with three shafts; as they lodged in his head, Viśikha shone forth exceedingly.
Like the lord of the Daityas with three peaks, he shed much blood;
he too, enraged, [struck] with great speed using a sharp-edged barbed arrow.
Again, having scattered sharp arrows, he severed the bowstring;
meanwhile, she became enraged and paralyzed him with a vulture-feathered, flaming shaft.
His mount fled toward the city of Death, having been cut down;
then, in that very instant, with three sharp arrows, [the Lord struck] him.
In that battle, he simultaneously severed [the demon's] quiver, crown, and bow.
With his bow broken, he, filled with great rage, took up an exceedingly radiant trident.
At that moment, she of swift prowess hurled herself at Stambhinī;

There, Andhinya, proud of his strength, fought with Bibhāṇḍa,
engaging him incessantly with various weapons and missiles in a series of counter-attacks.
Andhinī was mounted upon a buffalo, and Vibhāṇḍaka had a donkey for his vehicle;
after fighting with him there for a long time, [he was struck] by that arrow drawn back to the ear.
He struck the Daitya on the chest; thus pierced, Vibhāṇḍaka fell down deeply unconscious, like the king of mountains with its wings severed.
Then his mount, a donkey resembling a mountain and exceedingly grey,
let out a terrifying bray and raised its tail.
The powerful one, his body-hairs bristling with rage, stationed himself among Śakti’s troops;
he struck some with kicks from his hind legs, others with his teeth, and others by shaking them.
Others, by the force of their own movement, struck down the spears;
then Andhīnī saw Khara thus destroying the spears.
Filled with great rage, she struck him with an arrow drawn back to her ear;
pierced by that sharp shaft, he fell to the ground in a swoon.
Then, freed from his swoon and exceedingly enraged,
the powerful Vibhāṇḍa struck her vehicle with a mace with great force.
The buffalo, struck violently with the mace like a blind ox,
fled in a blaze of fury and gored him with its two horns.
Vibhāṇḍaka, having been hurled by the buffalo and reaching the sky with great speed, fell to the ground a yojana away, utterly unconscious. (27)
Just then, his mount, a donkey with a crest, approached him,
emitting very swiftly the sound "hee-haw" along with a loud, rasping roar.
Having returned and once again turned toward Mahiṣa with great speed,
he struck him most forcefully with a blow from his hind leg.
Then that enraged buffalo bit him again on the neck;
striking him violently against the ground, he tore open his belly with his two horns.
With his entrails protruding and his eyes bulging out, the donkey met its death;
meanwhile, as it lay unconscious, Vibhāṇḍaka approached and struck it with his foot.
Then, with an arrow, Andhīnī struck off the head of the Daitya Mahiṣa;
his head severed, he died.
Mohinī fought the fierce-eyed Daitya with various weapons;
Mohinī was mounted upon Garuḍa, while the fierce-eyed one stood upon a vulture.
A terrifying battle took place between the eagle and the vulture in the courtyard of the sky,
as exceedingly wonderful as that between two winged mountains.
Then, struck by the two wings of Suparṇa, Gṛdhraśekhara,
his body torn by claws and beak, fell to the earth and died.
When his mount was slain, Vikaṭākṣa became enraged; after fighting with her for a long time, his throat severed by the Mohinī-cakra, he met his death. (36)
Indraśatru, stationed upon a serpent and joined by Bhairava,
fought with extreme audacity on his most terrifying mount.

Bhairava, resembling a dark rain-cloud, is constantly attended by eight groups of Bhairavas who possess forms identical to his own and are joined by hosts of attendants numbering ten million. || 38 ||
All were endowed with tridents and staffs, possessed three eyes, and had the moon as their crest-jewel;
they resembled dark clouds, were adorned with serpents, and wore skins as their garments.
Having encamped the terrifying army of Indra’s enemy, which consisted of ten akṣauhiṇīs,
they destroyed it entirely by their prowess in the blink of an eye.
Some were impaled upon spikes, some were split apart by clubs;
some had their limbs torn by claws, and others were struck by fists. (41)
Then those hosts of Bhairavas placed garlands of entrails upon the Daityas;
having thus seen his own army destroyed, Indra’s enemy (Mahiṣa) was filled with rage.
With his mace, he crushed the host of Bhairavas on all sides;
thus, seeing the Gaṇas being crushed by the Daitya in the battle—
Manthāna and the others, known by their afternoon names, along with Asitāṅga and the other Bhairavas,
fought against Indraśatru, who resembled a mountain and was mounted upon a serpent.
The Daitya, alone on the field of battle, fought all of them;
his adamantine body was shattered by the falling blows of the spear-staff. (45)
Just as a boulder is entirely unharmed when struck by fruits, so too did he see that Daitya Bhairava, who was free from pain and terrifying to the Bhairavas themselves. || 46 ||
The lord of the Bhairavas fought with him in battle;
after fighting for a long time, he [the Bhairava] rose into the sky in order to strike him with his mace as he leaped up.
Having pierced him in the heart with a spear, he cast the lifeless one onto the ground;
even the enemy of the gods, having fought, was struck by the one named Kālakarṣṇikā.
Mounted upon a buffalo, the powerful Kākasastha remained for a long time,
having utterly destroyed the great hosts of Daityas with his multitude of spears.
Then, his head split by the blow of that goad, he died;
meanwhile, the Daitya Mahākukṣi, who took refuge in a wolf, fought with Svapneśī.
As he, the mighty Mahākukṣi, fought for a long time, the army mounted on chariots was destroyed by his multitudes of spears.
Having split open the belly with his sword, he destroyed that preeminent demon;
for even one intoxicated by pride is subdued when united with Baṭukabhairava.
Likewise, there were ten crores of *baṭukas* identical in form to himself,
equipped with great skull-staffs and adorned with ornaments of serpents.

It was surrounded on all sides by five-year-old elephants, intoxicated, clad in the quarters as their garments, with reddish-brown eyes, resembling masses of darkness, and bearing the moon upon their crests.
Accompanied by ten akṣauhiṇīs, that exceedingly powerful one fought;
meanwhile, the hosts of the Baṭukas, filled with rage, took their positions against the army of the Asuras.
Having struck them down with clubs, they swiftly brought us to destruction;
then [they encountered] the enraged Lord of the Daityas, who was descending as a wielder of the mace.
Baṭukeśa playfully struck Uśīra on the head with his staff;
from that blow of the staff, his head split open and he vomited frothy blood.
Having fallen down, the crest-jewel of the Asuras quickly became motionless and died;
thus Viṣaṅga was exceedingly distressed when his sons were lost.
Then Vṛtra, filled with wrath and accompanied by twenty akṣauhiṇīs,
fell down with a single bound, possessing the speed of the wind at the time of universal dissolution.
Then, above the Kiricakra, the sound of resounding musical instruments arose;
indeed, discharging streams of weapons, it made the quarters of the sky shrouded in darkness.
Like swarms of moths in a great mass of blazing fire,
they were destroyed in a mere instant by Jambhinī and the other leaders.
Like moths before the flames of weapons and fire, some abandoned their lives, their hearts shattered by tridents as Viṣaṅga’s army struck them down. 62.
Some had their limbs scattered by clubs, others were pinned by iron bars;
some were covered with arrows, while others were torn apart by fists. (63)
Others had their feet, arms, thighs, and necks severed by swords;
some had their bodies hacked into pieces by the falling of a multitude of weapons. (64)
When his own army had thus been destroyed, Viṣaṅga, overcome with rage,
struck down Śakti’s army with his mace and pierced it entirely through.
Having struck the buffalo that drew the chariot of Daṇḍarājñī and the two lions with his very club, he ascended the sovereign chariot.
Seeing Viṣaṅga swiftly mounting his chariot and looking about in all directions, a great cry of "Alas! arose among Śakti’s armies.
Having violently crushed even the spears fixed upon the chariot,
the powerful one swiftly entered the space between the fourth joint.
Seeing that Daitya approaching nearby, Daṇḍarāja also descended from his horse and fought with a mace, like a mountain.
There, a great battle took place between Daṇḍinī and the king of the Daityas,
using various weapons and missiles that caused terror to all the worlds.
Knowing that Daṇḍinī was invincible by means of missiles and weapons,
the foremost of the Daityas manifested a great illusion that struck fear into all the worlds.
There was darkness, a rain of dust, a rain of stones, and a great roar;
there was a rain of fire, and a rain of blood, impure matter, and the like.
Then, [he beheld] a most terrifying rain of shaven heads and the great army of the Daityas,
as well as himself with a thousand feet, arms, and mouths, appearing in a hundred forms.
Terrified by such an illusion, all those Śaktis were struck with fear;
and seeing them afraid, the Śakti Daṇḍinī [assailed them] with showers of arrows.
Then the king of the Daityas, having destroyed those illusory [creatures], again created a great illusion; all the Śaktis beheld it.
Then, as the chariot drawn by wheel-born horses was swiftly approaching,
he himself quickly slew the steeds and shattered the chariot into many pieces.
With speed, he seized Queen Lalitā by her mass of hair;
by his power of illusion, the Śaktis cried out loudly, "Alas! Alas! (77).
Then the illustrious Bhairava, the leader of the chariot, spoke to the Goddess:
"O Goddess, enough of this playful instilling of fear in the Daityas."
Behold, O Śivā, the powers (Śaktis) overcome by fear and grieving on all sides;
quickly destroy this Daitya, who is devoid of illusion, with your weapon that dispels illusion. 79.
"The twilight is approaching; during that time, illusion is difficult to overcome.
Having heard the words of Rathanetr and considering them appropriate, Daṇḍinī [acted accordingly].
Having discharged the weapon of illusion (nirmāyāstra), he destroyed his [the opponent's] illusion;
like mist by the wind, that illusion was destroyed on all sides.
Then Gadādhara was seen again approaching from the front;
as soon as she saw him, Daṇḍinī became enraged and [struck] his head with her sword.
In half a blink of an eye, he cut him down with his thunderbolt, just as [Indra] did to the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
When that Viṣaṅga of terrible prowess had thus been slain, (83)
The drums of the gods resounded, a rain of flowers fell, the quarters became free from darkness, and the sun shone with brilliant light. (84)

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of Viṣaṅga," in the Lalitāmāhātmya of the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa within the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories. || 75 ||
Chapter Seventy-Six:
A Description of the State of Contentment through the Attainment of One’s Own Desired Goal by Means of Bhaṇḍadrāra.
Thus, when Viṣaṅga was slain, a great cry of victory arose;
all the Śaktis were delighted and praised Daṇḍanāyikā. ||1||
Hearing that his two brothers, along with their retinues, had been struck down in battle,
the great asura fell into a state of agitation from grief and was somewhat overcome by delusion.
Then, having reflected and cast off his grief, as if laughing at himself, he thought:
"Aha! What am I saying here, grieving out of a sense of being liberated?"
That which was long desired by the Mother of the World has been fulfilled for me;
thus she shall quickly fulfill the remainder—of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, I shall go with the remaining attendants into the range of vision of my mother;
enough of this delay for me, for [this place] is crowded with obstacles to one's welfare.
Aha! In this world, she alone grants everything that is requested in every way and by all means;
for the Supreme Mother, who is the embodiment of existence, is indeed the cow of plenty.
Thus, struck by fate, a person abandons her who dwells within his own heart, who bestows fruits exceeding all desires, and who generates supreme bliss.
