By the terrible form of desire for objects that are essentially suffering and of little value,
one is led incessantly and in vain to the state of being a condiment for Death's meal. (8)
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, since by beholding the lotus feet of the illustrious Goddess, I have cast off this wretched body and its delusion.
"I shall attain the supreme state, free from sorrow and beyond doubt"—having thus reflected, the lord of the Daityas [acted] for the protection of his own inner self. (10)
Having fully mustered the army of the asuras like one exceedingly enraged, he,
equipped with armor, joined that force with vigor for the sake of battle.
Having mounted a highly elevated chariot drawn by a thousand lions,
he was shaded by a white pearl parasol and fanned with chowries.
He was joined by fifty commanders of the army, arrogant in their strength,
accompanied by the loud resonance of sounding musical instruments and the swelling noise of their slapping arms.
Filling the world with the deep sounds of chariot-rims, with frequent neighing,
and with the roars of the lions that were the chariot-steeds.
He set forth for the sake of a victorious expedition, as if shaking the very earth;
then Śakti’s army encountered the great ocean that was Bhaṇḍa’s host.
There, the great queen of mantras, Bhīma, who is shoreless, unassailable, and deep-sounding,
encountered Bhaṇḍa for battle.
Having observed the illustrious Mahārājñī and bowed to her, he addressed her who was surrounded [by her retinue]:
"O Goddess, Bhaṇḍa himself has arrived, fully intent on fighting. (17)
If you so deem it fit, let there be for you a victorious expedition here, accompanied by the entire army as well as all the commanders of that army. (18)
Having been thus informed by the minister's wife, he also considered it appropriate;
then, within half a blink of an eye, Śaktisenā was fully prepared for battle.
Mounted upon horses with cavalry forces, she presides over the front of the army;
behind that, she is the mistress of the elephant divisions and the sovereign of prosperity.
Then the young women, mounted on chariots and surrounded by groups of maidens, followed;
after them set forth the goat, whose great chariot was the wheel-king (cakrarāja).
Indeed, joined with the joints of his name and enveloped by the powers beginning with *aṇimā*,
he possessed a great, raised white umbrella and the uplifted banner of the lotus-emblem.
Mahātripurasundarī drives that supreme chariot, which is strewn with the nine gems, whose self is the senses, and which is yoked with horses.
Cakreśvarī, holding a sword and a shield, shone resplendent on the left and right sides of the body of the Lord of the Hundred Wheels, whose nature is discernment.
The two exceedingly lofty chariots, Kirigeya and Cakra, shone resplendent,
occupied by the armored Daṇḍinī and Mantriṇī.
Accompanied by their respective armies and equipped with the necessaries for battle,
Tiraskṛti took her seat upon the back of the Cakrarāja chariot. (26)
Resembling a mass of darkness, she was mounted upon an exceedingly tall four-limbed elephant;
she brandished a most formidable sword that was being drawn and shaken.
Thus, the illustrious Goddess Lalitā set forth with her army, her mandala formed by the flood of powers that take on forms identical to her own.
Having donned their armor for battle and being praised by the lords of the gods,
[the armies] of both hosts— consisting of horses, chariots, elephants, and infantry— [stood ready].

The earth, its surface densely packed with dust raised by the forceful impact of the soldiers' feet, produced a thick darkness that was like the blindness of those afflicted by cataracts. Or rather, it was as if the earth itself were being crushed by the army.
Having attained extreme emaciation due to affliction, she approached her protector out of fear;
likewise, she was driven upward by the force of the great mass of passion (rajas). || 33 ||
"Due to the absence of ground, the army appears as if moving by its own momentum";
thus did the hosts of celestial beings then fall into such reasoning. (34)
Then a great battle took place between the two armies of Śakti and the Daitya,
while the war-drums resounded and they were engaged in the clapping of hands and roaring. (35)
With arrows, spears, double-edged swords, tridents, scimitars, sharp-edged swords, barbed missiles, and tomara-javelins;
with maces, discuses, bhindipāla-throwers, iron clubs, goads, and staffs. || 66 ||
A pair of arrows was discharged with such continuous pervasiveness that we are utterly destroyed; our grief from the loss of our sons and others is complete. (37)
What would be the use of life for those who have been utterly defeated by their enemies?
By exerting my prowess and conquering them in battle, I shall obtain these boons.
"Otherwise, even if slain in battle, we shall dwell in the Nandana grove.
Having thus resolved, those Daityas fought with even greater strength. (39)
"Even though this is the limit of the Daityas' power,
by slaying these [demons] in every way, we shall surely attain supreme victory this very day."
Thinking thus, those most heroic ones fought with great speed;
while the sons of Diti were thus engaged in combat with their spears, then—
Struck by one another’s weapons, they fell down, deprived of life; their limbs were covered by nets of arrows, and their vital breaths had departed. || 42 ||
Through the success of their vow of battle, they attained the state of being the thousand-eyed Indra;
for some, by the stroke of a sword, the head flew off with a sharp *caṭiti* sound.
Like the head of Rāhu in the sky with its mouth wide open to swallow the sun,
they were crushed by blows from mallets and split asunder in the midst of the discus. (44)
Some there were impaled on long spears in great numbers; their heads, severed by arrows, sped with speed through the sky. (45)
Then the battlefield, strewn with limbs and resembling a mass of fledglings with outspread wings or a flock of birds in flight, shone brilliantly.
At the outset, the limbs of the image appeared as if painted upon a cloth;
however, there flowed blood there due to the negligence of the painter. (47)
For a slip, like red lac, sometimes reaches a state of drying;
it speaks as if suddenly wiped away by a painter. (48)
Pierced by arrows and deprived of life, some remained here and there like figures drawn in their entirety within a painting. Indeed, they appeared as such. (49)
Thus, in a mere moment, the great army of the Bhaṇḍa Daityas perished instantly, like moths in the fire of Śakti’s troops. 50.
Then the commanders of his army, their eyes reddened with rage,
tormented Śakti’s army with showers of excellent weapons and great missiles.
Seeing the army crushed by the generals and utterly overwhelmed, Mantriṇī, Daṇḍinī, Aśvārūḍhā, and Sampadadhīśvarī [advanced]. 52.
Endowed with the power of their retinues and inflamed by fury, they fought;
having fought for a very long time with the exceedingly powerful Daityas, the lords of the Sina region. (53)
For they violently destroyed all those generals:
Vakrākṣa, Vāmana, Tāla, Dīrghanasa (Ghoṇa?), and Subāhuka.
In the battle, Sampatkarī destroyed Vidyujjihva, who was mounted on a horse,
as well as Tālajaṅgha and the war-exultant Kuṭilākṣa.
She deprived the cruel Niśaṭha and Śambara of their lives in battle;
Jambhanī struck the cruel-faced one, and Stambhinī struck Sucikāmukha.
Andhinī [assailed] Kaṇṭhakara, Mohinī [assailed] Mṛgavaktra, Bhairavī [assailed] Kālakeya, and Kālakarṣiṇī [assailed] Vyāghrāsya. || 57 ||
Svapneśī has a shaven head; Vaṭuka is characterized by speaking nonsense; Umluka has the face of a camel; Mahākukṣi has the howl of a jackal. || 58 ||
Daṇḍinī destroyed in battle Śoṇitākṣa, Tālaketu, Tālaśrava, Mahāhanu, Gṛdhravāha, and Kākamukha.
Śukaśyāmā, Śārikā, Saṅgītā, Laghupūrvikā, Sāhityaśayāmalā, Nikumbha, and Kumbhamastaka—[these are the attendants]. 60.
They destroyed Cakrākṣa, Dīrghadaṃṣṭra, and Ulbaṇaka; as well as Kaṭaṅkaṭa, Karañjākṣa, Muṇḍa, Caṇḍa, and Kṛkānana.
One with a lax belly, two-horned, a dog-like face, ears like winnowing baskets, a crooked belly, a left-facing mouth, black, hollow-eyed, and foul-smelling—[these are the defects]. (62)
The minister, having forcibly attacked them, destroyed the Dānavas;
thus, when the entire army along with its generals had been slain, [the situation was as follows].
Seated upon his chariot, Bhaṇḍa, with a joyful heart, spoke to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, drive my chariot quickly toward the army of Śakti."
"Behold today my wondrous and hair-raising prowess!
Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, he quickly drove the chariot.
Then, full of doubt, he bowed and questioned the lord of the Daityas:
"O Lord of Daityas! Commanded by you, I desire to ask something. (66)
"Give that to me, who am bowing before you; I am entirely in doubt.
Thus questioned and commanded by the Daitya, the charioteer spoke: (67)
O Lord of the Daityas, I consider this army of Śaktis to be invincible,
by whom Viśukra and others were slain in battle as if in mere playful sport.
But now I behold you, having lost your brothers, sons, and others,
yet with a heart joyful within and untouched by even a trace of grief, like one who has renounced the world.
Previously, in battle, you were observed to have an exceedingly great devotion toward the Goddess along with your daughter; tell me that exactly as it happened.
Thus, even in such a defeat and in this exceedingly terrifying state of suffering,
I do not perceive in you even the slightest trace of grief or fear. (71)
To that Daitya, his long-time servant, who was thus questioning him further, Bhaṇḍa spoke with a slight smile, beginning: "Listen, O Daitya! (72)
This goddess Lalitā is the supreme Śivā, higher than the highest;
slain by her in battle, I shall obtain the most excellent fruit. (73)
That world is free from sorrow, fearless, and entirely blissful;
whereas this world is indeed full of sorrow, accompanied by fear, and consisting of nothing but suffering. || 74 ||
Deluded by illusion, a living being vainly considers that [world] to be most excellent;
even there, indeed, exists the world of the asuras, which is rajasic and exceedingly terrifying. (75)
He who considers this boon is known as one whose cattle have been utterly destroyed;
I am the messenger Śrīpadmasaṃsthāna, crowned with a crest-jewel.
Having reached this wretched state by the power of the ripening of my own karma, nevertheless, through the grace of the Goddess, memory does not indeed abandon me. (77)
This supreme goddess is the sovereign of all and the mother of Brahmā and the other gods;
by her my brothers and even my sons were slain in battle. (78)
"Purified by weapons and fire, they have attained the highest world;
you too, along with your brothers, shall quickly reach that world together with me. (79)
"You shall be reunited with your sons, and thereafter you will go to the state of the immortal.
Having heard these words of Bhaṇḍa, he, along with his charioteer, was struck with wonder. (80)
Having praised that king of the Daityas, he cast off the grief residing in his heart;
seeing Śrī Lalitā before him, he prostrated with great devotion.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Revelation of the Secret of Devotion to the Holy Goddess through Bhaṇḍa, the King of the Daityas," in the *Lalitāmāhātmya* of the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* within the *Śrītripurārahasya*. || 6331 ||
The seventy-seventh chapter:
A description of the slaying of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura.
Then, having encountered Daṇḍinī and Mantriṇī, who were mounted upon excellent horses and presided over the success in battle, [he witnessed] their manifest skill in combat.
Having displayed them and fully gratified them, he spoke in due order during the battle: "O goddesses, I have been pleased by your skill and prowess in combat. (2)
At this moment, my mind is eager to fight with the mistress; therefore, all of you shall be witnesses to my deeds in battle.
This arm of mine is ashamed to be with the groups of maidservants in battle;
having completely conquered her position in the fight, may I bring you victory.
"Let it be so for me who entreats you"— hearing these words of his at that time,
the goddesses considered him invincible by their own prowess.
And it was fitting that the defeat of the lord of the Daityas by the Great Queen should occur;
they gave way for the wrestling match between the Great Queen and the Asura.
Then, having mounted the chariot known as the Śrīcakra-rāja in the battle,
the demon Bhaṇḍa then commenced an exceedingly wonderful combat.
There, the great army of Śakti became a spectator of the battle, along with hosts of gods traveling in celestial chariots, as well as Siddhas and groups of ṛṣis. (8)
At that time, the entire sky was filled with those who had come to witness the spectacle;
Bhaṇḍa, having approached and seen Lalitā before him, was exceedingly delighted.
She immediately bowed her mind to you and quickly followed after him;
he pierced her with five arrows, and that was like a marvel.
There, two heaps of beautiful flowers fell at his feet;
the third became a garland of blossoming lotuses around his neck.
After that, there was a rain of flowers falling upon his head;
finally, a jewel-encrusted ornament remained fixed upon his crown as a headpiece.
Thus, seeing the worship performed by her, the Goddess was exceedingly delighted;
and the gods and others, having seen that, were altogether filled with apprehension.
Having heard from Nārada that the Daitya Bhaṇḍa was foremost among devotees,
the Lord of Gods was filled with great wonder at that.
Then a great battle took place between Lalitā and the demon Bhaṇḍa,
filling the vast expanse of the sky with a multitude of various weapons and missiles.
The Daitya Bhaṇḍa, an expert in supreme missiles, also fought, striving to gratify the Supreme Goddess with his own prowess.
Having mentally prostrated before the Goddess who had come before him face-to-face,
he proceeded to revile her with words that were secretly malicious. (17)
"O Lalitā, listen to my words: you appear to me like an actress; you are constantly devoted to false conduct and have taken refuge with a man who is a slave to women. (18)
Though you bear the form of a woman, you are devoid of the nature of a woman;
I consider you neither a woman nor even a man at any time. (19)
Your conduct is loathed by the world, and you are devoid of shame, apprehension, and the like;
you do not appear to me to be born of a noble family, but rather as one from a base lineage.
It appears to me that you have been touched in every way by undiscerning men who stand upon paths censured by the world. (21)
"Alas! Such indeed was my past karma, that I now behold you standing before me—even though you are one who truly does not deserve to be seen by me. (22)
Listen, I shall speak with truth; let it be exactly as it is. Somehow or other, you have now come within the range of my vision. (23)
Abandoning deceitful conduct and illusion, become firmly established in me;
I have been attained by you this very moment—do not turn your back on me.
Nor indeed can you possibly attain invisibility by deceiving me while I stand right before you; therefore, remain perfectly steady.
Having understood my firm and resolute intention,
and having seen my prowess, accomplish your own vow. (26)
Having heard those secret words, the gracious Mother Lalitā said:
"Listen, O Lord of Daityas; that which was spoken by you is exactly so. (27)
I shall accomplish your desire and cause me and my attendants to depart;
for once I have come within the range of your vision, I shall never again appear anywhere. (28)
"May that desire for battle and the rest be entirely stabilized!
Having said this, he rained a shower of arrows upon the lord of the Daityas. (29)
Then that Daitya also rained down with great speed every year,
preceded by a display of his mastery in the application of weapons.
A great battle took place between the two of them, tumultuous and hair-raising;
having thus fought for a very long time, the Daitya discharged his missiles.
The Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Saumya, Kauvera, Pārvata, as well as the Pārjanya, Aindra, Vāyavya, Brāhma, and Kaumāra [weapons]. || 32 ||
In this manner, the supreme goddess Lalitā quickly destroyed those weapons with her counter-weapons,
just as the sun destroys the frost.
Likewise, he destroyed those newly created [weapons] in an instant with counter-weapons;
then the demon Bhaṇḍa created Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
[He slew] Somaka, Hiraṇyākṣa, and likewise Hiraṇyakaśipu;
Bali, the one named Arjuna, Haihaya, and likewise Rāvaṇa. (35)
Kumbhakarṇa, Mura, Grāha, Kaṃsa, Dvivida,
and all such enemies of Viṣṇu who were destroyers of the worlds.
Created by the Daitya Bhaṇḍa, they possessed his own nature and prowess;
intent on the destruction of the worlds, they were devoted to a state of darkness.
Then Laliteśī, for their destruction, produced from her fingernails ten separate incarnations of Nārāyaṇa.
They were destroyed in an instant by those forms of Viṣṇu created by him;
then [he created] Death once more against Andhaka, as well as Kāma and Tripura.
In this manner, the crest-jewel of the asuras created the enemies of Mahādeva;
seeing them, the illustrious Goddess Parā emitted them from her third eye.
Because they [worshipped] Mahādeva, the God of gods, they met their destruction;
then [he beheld] the vast, innumerable, and terrifying army of the Daityas.
Manifesting himself in an instant with his powers, he [confronted] those who had previously been slain by him:
Viṣaṅga, Viśukra, and his sons, who possessed four arms and faces.
Like the Unborn (Aja) creating that which was lost, Karaṅka, Kuṭilākṣa, and the others [reappeared];
then, though greatly distressed, they fought with the armies of the Śaktis.
Seeing that wonderful power of Bhaṇḍa, they were all struck with amazement;
then the gods and the Śaktis became afraid, wondering, "What will happen now? (44)
Then a great battle broke out once more, just as it had begun;
for every Daitya slain there, he created another again and again. (45)
Seeing that, the Śaktis and even the deities were utterly terrified;
then the gods, headed by Brahmā, praised the goddess Śrī Lalitā.
And the minister, having approached the Great Goddess and bowed down,
with palms joined in reverence, made a request in sweet words.
O Goddess, I consider the power of the Daitya to be most terrifying;
behold the entire host of Śaktis, their faces parched and utterly distressed. (48)
As they fought without rest, two watches passed;
for every spear that was destroyed, she would create another again in an instant. (49)
His four sons, each with four arms and four faces, were struck down in battle;
now they are fighting again with the maiden for the seventh time.
Likewise, Viṣaṅga was slain in ten ways and Viśukra in nine;
yet, having been killed, he was created once again by the demon Bhaṇḍa and fought.
Even Karaṅka, Kuṭilākṣa, and the others have been slain many times in this manner;
yet, once created, they fight again. Indeed, this is not something we can achieve.
Behold the Śaktis on all sides, terrified, exhausted, and deprived of their luster;
protect this entire world, for it is not right for you to remain indifferent. (53)
Thus entreated, the Goddess smiled and said to her:
"Do not fear; behold, in this very moment I shall destroy the lord of the asuras. (54)
Having spoken thus, he quickly fixed a single arrow upon his bow,
invoking there the Pāśupata weapon that strikes terror into the worlds.
Within half a moment, he released that weapon upon the army of the asuras;
it reduced the host of the Daityas, which was as vast as the ocean, to ashes.
Then, as he again fixed an exceedingly brilliant arrow upon his bow,
the quarters of the sky instantly became enveloped in garlands of flames on all sides.
The earth trembled, the oceans were split asunder, and fear entered [all beings];
the entire web of the world, both moving and unmoving, shook, and meteors fell by the thousands.
Mṛga and the others moved to the right of Bhaṇḍāsura;
meanwhile, they saw their own army, which resembled the ocean, being destroyed.
With his inner mind made steady, he meditated upon the lotus feet of Śrī Lalitā until Bhaṇḍa, the great asura, attained the state of being identical with the object of meditation alone.
Then the illustrious Goddess Lalitā, having joined an arrow with the weapon of Kāmeśa, released it at Bhaṇḍa; that arrow was exceedingly terrifying.

Emitting flames like the fire of universal dissolution and possessing great radiance in every direction, he seemed to consume the entire web of the world, with its moving and unmoving beings, in the blink of an eye.
Stealing away the eyes of all like a forest fire consumes straw,
he [reduced] Bhaṇḍāsura along with his chariot to a desolate city. (63)

There, he reduced to mere ashes the world of living beings, including women, the elderly, and children, as well as the entire circle of creatures in their six states of existence; it was truly like a marvel.
There, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others [beheld] Bhaṇḍa, or his army,
or the city of the one who had been struck down, or even a Daitya child somewhere.
Not seeing him, they were filled with wonder and uttered cries of victory;
hosts of Śaktis struck them, and thousands of musical instruments resounded.
The celestial instruments resounded, the leaders of the Gandharvas sang,
and the divine courtesans, led by Urvaśī, performed the Lāsya dance with great joy.
The ṛṣis recited hymns, the Siddhas muttered the supreme Śiva-mantra, the hosts of munis meditated upon His form, and other people prostrated themselves.
Clouds of gentle form, thundering very softly, rained down clusters of blossoms that were fully bloomed and exceedingly fragrant. (69)
And the winds, laden with fragrance and touching all with joy, blew, carrying drops of scented water mixed with yakṣakardama.
Divanatha became radiant with splendor, and Sagarasvamin was led away;
the waters in the rivers and other streams became as tranquil as the minds of the virtuous.
When the demon Bhaṇḍa was slain, the world was created anew, shining as if at the end of a dissolution; it was then free from turmoil and undisturbed by confusion. (72)
Thus, seeing the Daitya named Bhaṇḍa, that thorn of the world, slain, all the gods, great seers, and Siddhas approached the Goddess.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Slaying of the Asura Bhaṇḍa," in the *Śrīlalitācaritra*, within the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* of the *Tripurārahasya*, the most excellent of sacred histories. || 6404 ||
The seventy-eighth chapter:
A description of her consecration upon the Śrīcakra on the peak of Mount Meru, preceded by the hymn of praise to Śrī Lalitā.
Having approached that supreme Lalitā, all those led by the gods,
their hearts overflowing with joy, praised her with various hymns.
The Praise of Śrī Lalitā:
Victory, victory, O Mother Lalitā! What desired fruit would Your lotus feet not bestow upon those who worship them in this world?
Furthermore, he very swiftly bestows upon those who have sought refuge the foremost of celestial trees, which grant all desires and even their own inherent natures.
We here, afflicted by calamity, our wings scorched by the fierce and tangled flames of the fire of the demon Bhaṇḍa’s prowess,
were submerged together in a boundless ocean of fear; yet surely we have been swiftly uplifted by that very same power.
The paths of the sky. || 3 ||

This lotus-foot of Yours, which removes the intense anguish of the hearts of those who bow before it, which restrains the powerful delusions that are the bees of misfortune for those who take refuge in it, and which is the life-string for all living beings striving toward stability— this world-governor of Yours flourishes.
Your mother is the very grace that illuminates all the worlds; why then should you undergo such exertion here in battle with the Daityas?
May she reside eternally in our stainless minds, which possess the nature of fully blossomed lotuses and are perfumed by sublime impressions.
Indeed, this is well known: for embodied beings, you alone are the refuge and the pure cause of all desired blessings;
for those long mired in ignorance, your swan-like feet are the sole cause of discernment, acting as the vehicle for Brahman.
Having thus praised her by prostrating themselves like a staff, the foremost among the gods,
headed by Brahmā, repeatedly extolled Ambikā with various hymns of praise.
O Pot-born One! At that moment, Brahmā and the other lords who are the causes of the universe, accompanied by their primary power Bhāratī and others, arrived from millions of cosmic eggs.

With their hands joined in reverence as ornaments, bowing down and filled with intense devotion, they spoke to the one worthy of praise, whose speech was charming, while raising their lotus-like hands.
O Queen of the Gods! Because of the slaying of the Daitya Bhaṇḍa today, these one hundred and five cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) have been well protected; for he was indeed their sovereign. (10)
When the eggs were thus spoken of, some among them, such as Śakra and others, were bound, while others fled;
he alone exercised sovereignty over all the worlds on behalf of the Daityas.
The Vedas of the Daityas and the sacrifices of the Daityas were propagated everywhere;
O Śaṅkarī, neither the sacrifice to the gods nor even the sacrifice to Brahman existed anywhere.
O Maheśvarī, when the Daitya was slain by you in battle today, the administration of the kingdom that had been carried on by Bhaṇḍa, O Brāhmaṇas, has come to an end.

The hosts of Daityas fled and the world-protectors (lokapālas) were established once more; all was restored to its former state, free from agitation, as each resumed their respective duties and offices.
While the gods were speaking thus, the Creator of the Universe arrived there;
having prostrated before the Goddess and the leaders of the gods, he stood with his palms joined in reverence. || 15 ||
"O Grandfather, I have been commanded by you regarding the construction of the city of Śrī for the Goddess upon the summit of Meru; that has been executed by me accordingly. (16)
"You ought to see that quickly, O Lord, together with the goddesses and the gods.
Thus requested by Tvaṣṭṛ, the Unborn One (Aja) informed the goddess of what had occurred.
Requested by the lords of the gods, the supreme goddess Lalitā,
accompanied by her army of Śaktis and the hosts of deities, went there swiftly.
They beheld that most beautiful city, fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ,
which appeared like a reflection cast from the city of Mahāśrīpurarāja.
All these gods and the hosts of Śaktis were filled with wonder.
Then, while residing there, the gods [beheld] the venerable Mother Lalitāmbikā.
Then, with their heads bowed down in every way, those led by Buddhiśa, having obtained his consent, made an exceedingly earnest request.
They prepared the most excellent materials for the royal consecration;
having arranged all the necessary provisions, they waited for an auspicious moment and hour.
Accompanied by hosts of sages, Brahmā performed the consecration rite according to the path seen in the scriptures, following the procedure of the highest kalpa.
The hosts of gods, the Vṛndārakas, the Mārutas, the Vasus, Agni, the Gandharvas, the messengers of the gods, the guardians of the quarters, the Yakṣas, and the Guhyakas. || 24 ||
Yātudhānas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Kinnaras, and even Uragas; Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Munis, Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, and Asuras. || 25 ||
Tens of millions of Brahmās, Rudras, and Haris reside within the cosmic egg,
as do Sadāśiva and Īśvara, as well as Śrīkaṇṭha and Ananta.
Gathered there for the consecration of Lalitā Mahārājñī, they attended upon Queen Mother Lalitā on all sides.
Tens of millions of Brahmāṇīs, Kamalās, and Gaurīs, filled with devotion,
reverently worshipped him with various distinct offerings.
Thus, having performed the rites for auspiciousness and taking recourse to the practice of auspicious conduct,
while auspicious musical instruments resounded and those skilled in melody played sweet strains, (she departed).
While the Gandharvas danced on all sides and the celestial courtesans performed, accompanied by the movements of descending and ascending scales, rhythmic pauses, and the breath of musical notes.
While throngs of sages were muttering prayers, while seers were reciting aloud, while various beings were praising loudly, and while living creatures were watching with great effort; (31)
The officiant caused the Goddess to ascend the auspicious great lion-throne;
then, with waters purified by mantras, [he sprinkled her] upon the throne variegated with the nine gems.
Surrounded by the joyful Vasiṣṭha and others, the Creator of the World consecrated him with jars filled with water originating from rivers and the ocean.
Having consecrated the Great Goddess, resplendent with priceless ornaments, clad in various divine garments, and beautifully adorned with the Śrīcakra; || 34 ||
The immortals worshipped Lalitāmbikā, who graced a couch fashioned in the form of the five Brahmās,
with various excellent offerings.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, each absorbed in their respective devotions,
praised him with various hymns and prostrated themselves on the ground like a staff.
Thus, at that time, the goddess Śrī Lalitā was consecrated upon the lion-throne there in the preeminent city of Śrīpura, which was like the great city of Mahāśrīpura.
O Sage born from a jar! Thus, on the exceedingly lofty peak of Mount Meru, he assigned separate abodes for those headed by Mantriṇī. (38)
They resided together in Śrīpura, intent on carrying out the commands issued from the mouth of Brahmā;
[the city] was constructed from the very essence of the skill and artistry of the divine architect.
The city was the ornament of the illustrious Mahādevī; having been entreated by the foremost of the gods, she accepted the royal umbrella and sandals out of compassion. (40)
"Even thus, she remains as a mass of consciousness and bliss, assuming a body for her divine play.
Having heard this most purifying narrative from Hayagrīva, [he was filled with wonder]. (41)
Agastya, his mind satisfied yet filled with great apprehension, asked: "O Hayagrīva, ocean of compassion! That which was spoken by you on this Mount Meru—" (42)
That city of the illustrious Mahādevī appears as a wonder to me;
indeed, there is no place within the universe that is unknown to me. (43)
Even there, on Mount Meru, there would be no place unknown to me;
for Meru is conceived as the wall of the variegated picture of the world. (44)
There are indeed seven worlds above and seven nether regions below;
on the summit of Mount Meru, there are the abodes of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
"In that regard, there is not even a space of two finger-breadths unknown to me.
Therefore, tell me how Śrīpura was described there."
Thus questioned by the Pot-born, the mouthless one (Āsya) spoke with joy:
"Listen, O Pot-born! I shall tell you this most excellent secret. (47)
Indeed, that abode cannot be seen by anyone in any way;
however, those who worship the venerable Śakti Tripurā according to the prescribed rite [may see it]. 48.
That which is attainable by them is visible even to others, though never to anyone else;
having heard of that majesty, devotion has arisen in my heart. (49)
Once supreme devotion has been attained, nothing remains unattained;
just as when the ocean, the mine of jewels, is reached, one cannot be devoid of jewels. (50)
That faithful wife of yours, Lopāmudrā, was your supreme beloved;
having undertaken her initiation and having worshipped the Supreme according to the prescribed rites, [you attained success].
"Once you have attained perfection, you shall behold that city, and never otherwise. O Pot-born one! This most wonderful account of Lalitā has been told to you. (52)
For men who hear of this dissolution, it destroys all sins—even for those people in the Kali age whose hearts are defiled and whose intellects are dull-witted. (53)
Apart from the majesty of Tripureśānī, there is no other supreme refuge;
it is attained through Vedic rites performed repeatedly with freedom from desire. (54)
From that [point], faith regarding other deities arises during the stages of worship;
subsequently, through its full maturation, it arises toward Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the Śaktis at the very end.
Through the worship of the form of Tripurā, there arises eternal faith;
by this very adoration, one comes to know [the Goddess] as one's own self-form.
One whose supreme sovereignty has been fully manifested does not undergo rebirth, having realized the Great Sovereign of all worlds, who consists of non-dual consciousness and bliss.
Thus, this first step toward attaining the state of one's own Self is the hearing of the exalted majesty and power of the venerable Supreme Śakti. (58)
Therefore, one who desires the highest good should listen to this at the very outset in every way;
for it pacifies all sins and brings about the fruit of all desired objects. (59)
"Having swiftly generated devotion, he shall liberate [the devotee] from supreme fear.
Having spoken thus, the horse-faced one (Aśvānana), who is greatly honored by the pitcher-born sage (Agastya), [departed]. (50)
Having taken his leave, the Lord departed toward his own desired direction.
Thus, O Rāma, this auspicious story of Lalitā has been told to you.

Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Coronation of Śrī Lalitā in Śrīpura," within the *Śrī Lalitā-māhātmya*, in the dialogue between Dattātreya and Paraśurāma, in the *Māhātmya-khaṇḍa* of the glorious *Tripurā-rahasya*, the best of histories. || 6465 ||
Chapter Seventy-Seven:
Description of the Nature of the Āgamas, in the dialogue between Śrī Datta and Bhārgava.
Thus, having heard the majesty of the illustrious Goddess Lalitā, which is supreme in every respect,
the son of Jamadagni was drenched in the nectar of joy.
Immersed in the ocean of devotion, thick with the rising of horripilation, and drenched by the incessantly flowing water of tears from eyes overflowing with joy. || 2 ||
Appearing as if unconscious for a moment, like one intoxicated by wine,
he spoke again with a faltering voice, having once more joined his palms in reverence.
O Blessed One, I have now been utterly purified by you through the sprinkling of the streams of water from the sacred bathing places of the stories of others.
Truly, you have been lifted out of the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra by your compassion;
salutations to you, O illustrious Guru, O Lord, the sun for the darkness of suffering! (5)
I pay homage to that peaceful sage Saṃvarta, who is fearless from any quarter,
who pointed out the path to me as I was wandering like one blind.
Until today, I have spent my time in this world in vain;
like a frog in an empty well, I have never known my own true purpose.
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, by taking refuge at the feet of Bhava; for I have indeed become one who seeks to attain the glory of liberation in every respect. (8)
O Blessed One, a great doubt resides here within my heart;
I ask you about that, for it behooves you to explain it to me.
I know that your favor toward me is absolute, O ocean of compassion;
for you, who are so merciful, there is nothing that should remain unsaid to me, your disciple.
How is it that the sage born from a jar (Agastya), who was proficient in all the scriptures, did not worship that Supreme Power, the Great Sovereign of all the worlds? 11.
By which [power] the excellent city of the illustrious Goddess on Mount Meru became invisible; for how could there not be a vision of it for those devoted to knowledge? 12.
"Tell me further how that city was seen by him.
Thus questioned, the sage Dattātreya spoke to the son of Jamadagni.
Listen, Rāma, for I shall proclaim this most excellent secret;
for in this matter, mere scripture alone is not accepted as the means.
For living beings whose selves have been perfumed by impressions previously cultivated, a hundred impressions are individually accumulated in the mind. (15)
Upon attaining awakening, association with the virtuous spreads forth as its enlightener;
for as long as one attains the company of a certain thing, so long will that state persist, and not otherwise.
Having approached Hayagrīva and heard the majesty of Tripurā, he conceived devotion for Tripurā and received initiation from his wife. (17)
As long as one does not obtain initiation, even though one may be a worshiper of Tripura, one is not capable of ascending the steps of the palace of liberation. 18.
Just as the twice-born lack eligibility for all rites without the initiation of the upanayana,
so too here, O descendant of Bhṛgu, there is no eligibility without initiation (dīkṣā).

Without having received initiation from a true guru and without knowing the guru’s traditional method, an action performed according to one's own intellect—even if it is accompanied by the prescribed ritual rules—[is ineffective]. (20)
Nevertheless, it utterly destroys the practitioner quickly in every way;
just as unrefined elixir (rasāyana) kills the one who consumes it.
He who, by his own intellect and without a guru, should acquire a mantra and the ritual procedure for its application, indeed incurs the offense of hostility toward the deity. (22)
Neither this world nor the next exists for those who bear malice toward the deities;
how can an ignorant man destroy the fault committed through his malice? 23.
This is a worldly maxim: kings indeed subject a man who violates a command to various kinds of severe punishments. (24)
They do not overlook a man who in every way violates their commands;
indeed, by the doctrines of the Vedas alone, there can be no eligibility for this [task].
The Vedic procedure for the twice-born is intended for the purpose of qualifying them for meditation;
indeed, no human goal whatsoever exists apart from the injunctions of the Veda. (26)
If [this were so] for men who know the Vedas, who pursue false fruits, who have become as small as an atom, and who pride themselves on their own human purpose; (27)
If it were argued that human effort is supreme, how could it apply to inanimate objects like pillars?
For those who follow the Vedas consider themselves immovable, yet their fruit arises from smoke.
Where indeed has it been seen that what is unstable can be considered a stable fruit? For those who perceive pleasure in fruits that are limited and consist of suffering. (29)
Indeed, ignorant of the true nature of the fruit, they praise the fruit in what is not the fruit;
thus the Creator, for the sake of the world's activity, set in motion the Veda consisting of the gunas.
For the sake of increasing the course of the world and for the complete satisfaction of the gods,
it is like poison to one desiring death, yet like the disease of desire to those possessed by passion.
Furthermore, that portion which is hidden in the Veda, they do not know it;
because the Creator himself has concealed it, they are deluded regarding those secret states.
Vyāsa, who is Nārāyaṇa himself, leads him in a completely different way, out of compassion for living beings, by means of that which is suitable for the proper development of the mind. (33)
One should further augment that which is the sole means for attaining the ultimate truth;
therefore, eligibility for this is prescribed for those who have renounced desires.

Even for a renunciant (saṃnyāsī), the worship of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is desired. However, one who has been struck down by the delusion known as ignorance, or who abandons the practice of knowledge (vidyopāsti), [should not do so]. (35)
He shall enter the Andhatāmisra hell, and for him there is no further rebirth;
however, by a renunciant, everything that exists as a bond to the self must be abandoned.
O Rāma, this worship of Śrīvidyā, which is of the nature of liberation, is certainly not fit to be abandoned, just as the status of a Brahmin is not to be abandoned by an ascetic. (37)
Indeed, the abandonment of one who has committed a great offense is fraught with danger for the worshiper;
[he falls into] Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka, and Avīci. 38.
For those people, intent on further offenses, fall back again upon the most terrifying powers commanded by the Queen of Punishment.
Saṅkarṣiṇī, Karṣiṇī, and likewise Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī [protect] people who are afflicted by the path of worship and those intent on transgressions.
The supreme mothers join [the practitioner] to the aforementioned places of suffering;
the mortal intent upon worship attains the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Whatever supreme goal may belong even to a Tantric practitioner who performs ritual actions, that is not attainable in any way by a follower of the Vedic path. 42.
For Vedic ritual action is in every respect outward-turned;
it is human effort devoid of the Lord, and therefore it is appropriate for the fruit of being a bound soul (paśu).
The Tantric ritual dedicated to Īśvara, when combined with knowledge and worship,
and strengthened by faith and devotion, swiftly liberates one through perfect accomplishment. (44)
Having attained purity of mind through the practice of the prescribed rites, Śiva-hood is indeed attained right here in this world by the awakened ones through knowledge and human effort. 45.
Even the ignorant are liberated by performing ritual action in the proper sequence;
however, there is no entitlement to ritual action or the means of knowledge without initiation.
But those who have undergone initiation, having reached the highest of worlds at the end of the body,
are fully awakened by Sadāśiva and become identical with Śiva.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, those who are merely performers of ritual actions remain unawakened;
therefore, the state of true well-being is not attained through dry Vedic scriptures and the like.
O Bhārgava! Without service to the illustrious Tripurā, how could there be any virtuous activity? There is neither the means, nor the fruit, nor even any purposeful engagement.
Without the grace of the illustrious Tripureśānī, that fruit which is obtained even by worshipping Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others will not come to pass. (59)
And it is certain that even that [worship] occurs through her grace;
the worship of all the gods is the worship of the Supreme Śakti. (51)
Without Śakti, the acceptance of worship is not possible anywhere;
therefore, worship of Śakti is prescribed by people everywhere. (52)
Having first deliberated upon the power to bestow fruits, the wise worship the Lord individually; in that manner, they obtain the fruit. (53)
O Bhārgava, even in this world, one who is powerless would not be honored anywhere;
for apart from Śiva, power does not exist at all because it requires a substratum. (54)
If this is so, then Śiva, being devoid of his own power of existence, would likewise be like a sun deprived of its power of light; where and when could such a thing possibly exist?
In whatever way [it may be], how could Śiva exist without the power of consciousness (citi-śakti)?
Or how could even a blade of grass be devoid of the power of consciousness? (56)
For when consciousness exists, everything exists; otherwise, nothing at all exists.
Know this, O descendant of Bhṛgu: that which exists is consciousness. (57)
For this is indeed Śākta consciousness; nothing exists apart from me.
Thus, by means of such intellect, even something as small as a blade of grass is of the nature of Tripura.
In this world, wise men indeed dispute over mere designations;
therefore, abandon all doubt in this matter, for it is the same everywhere.
Indeed, that which proceeds from the verbal expression has reached the state of being an object of specific distinctions;
however, its true nature is devoid of distinctions, consisting of the single, indivisible consciousness.
One may become a knower of distinctions only so long as one is not devoted to that [Ultimate Reality];
for the Vedas abound in distinctions and conceal that which is without distinction.
Therefore, even though Agastya was well-versed in the Vedas, he did not perceive that city;
for that city must indeed be the supreme meaning of the Vedas itself. (52)
Therefore, for the successful accomplishment of the Traipura [rite], the Veda is declared to be the means of attainment;
and Vyāsa spoke of the Purāṇa as the very expansion of the meaning of the Veda. (63)
For the Veda is the portion consisting of scripture (āgama), and likewise, scripture is a collection of sounds;
therefore, everything has proceeded from that form, by taking refuge in it.
By virtue of the eligibility of the three social classes, the Veda proceeds forth;
the Supreme Lord, out of compassion and with the desire to uplift all beings. (65)
Manifesting the unsurpassed consciousness known as the Veda and Āgama, it is certain that the Āgama of the Supreme Lord is reflective awareness (vimarśa). 66.
That which arose sequentially from the mouths of the foremost of the Brahmas is indeed the boundless ocean of scripture, present throughout all the worlds.
However, observing that those of dull intellect were becoming distressed over time, the sages, through their vast wisdom, churned that ocean of scriptures. (68)
The unsurpassed nectar of the Ātmatantra, which consists of a compendium of the essential points, has been clearly elucidated separately according to the distinctions of various regions. (69)

In that regard, for the twice-born whose selves have been refined by the rites prescribed in the Vedas, there is indeed eligibility for the Tantric path only through the gateway of the Vedic (śrauta) rites. (70)
However, for Śūdras and others, there may be eligibility for Tantra due to their state of isolation (kaivalya);
for the Veda itself is Tantra, and Tantra is proclaimed to be the Veda. (71)
No difference exists between these two even in the slightest degree anywhere;
for indeed, the Tantric portion is seen within the portions of the Veda. (72)
In that [Veda], the ritual procedures for mantras, yantras, and worship are clearly established;
such is the portion of the Veda, because it is situated at its very head.
Then, joined with the conventions of the Tantras, there is the most excellent Tantra;
even within the Tantras, there are portions of the Vedas, distinguished as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa. (74)
Therefore, the Tantra is seen to be the most excellent among the ritual procedures for action;
likewise, a portion of the Tantra is observed in the Purāṇas and other such texts. (75)
Likewise, the portion characterized by creation and so forth is seen in the Tantras;
know this, O Bhārgava, to be indeed the Purāṇic portion! (76)
Therefore, from that [source] known as the illustrious Tripurā arises the innate realization;
from that, contemplate the ocean of Āgamas, as well as the Vedas and the Tantras.
For that which is destiny is its power, by which everything is established;
therefore, Agastya, even though he was a follower of the Vedas, was devoid of initiation into the Tantra.
Constrained by destiny, he did not see that city there on Mount Meru;
then, having heard of the supreme majesty of Mahādevī, which excels all else— (79)
Endowed with devotion, having received the Tantric initiation according to the sequence,
he worshipped Tripurā there together with his wife within the Śrīnātha-maṇḍala. (80)
Having reached that place and being united with his beloved, he was filled with supreme bliss; thus he beheld that most excellent abode occupied by him.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of Āgama," in the Māhātmyakhaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurārahasya, the best of histories.
Chapter Eighty:
A Description of the Primary Duties of a Lay Devotee (Upāsaka)
Having thus heard the narrative related by Dattātreya, Rāma,
with a serene mind, bowed down with palms joined in reverence and spoke once more.
O Blessed Lord, Protector, that which was spoken has been heard by me like nectar;
I am now freed from doubt, yet I wish to ask something further. (2)
Having thus obtained initiation and being intent upon the worship of Tripurā, by what specific ritual action should one perform the daily rites? (3)
O Guru, please explain to me out of compassion for your servant how even a king, though possessing nothing, might quickly attain great fruit.
Thus questioned, the Guru Datta, delighted by that devotion, said:
"Listen, O Rāma, to this great secret which brings pleasure to Tripurā."
Just as Śiva is [pleased] by consecration, as the Maker of Day (the Sun) by prostrations, as Gaṇeśāna by food offerings, and Hari indeed by ornaments; || 6 ||
Through worship with specific offerings and according to the prescribed rite, the Great Goddess Parāśakti is likewise pleased; hear now that which is supreme therein. (7)
Having constructed a lofty and variegated palace by means of his own power,
he should place there either the King of Śrīcakras or an image endowed with auspicious marks.
Having installed [the deity] there according to the prescribed rite, either by oneself or through another,
one should worship it daily, or at five times, or at four, three, two, or one time per day.
At dawn, at morning, at midday, at nightfall, and at midnight;
or daily at two, three, or one time, and at five times during the sacred festival days (parvan).
A festival must also be celebrated in every way on the great parvan days,
with a chariot, vehicles, or carriages, carrying the festival image outside.
Whoever performs this circumambulation in the world according to the scriptural injunctions, accompanied by dances and auspicious songs, shall dwell within the city of Śrīpura.

Within the intervals between the blue ramparts, having provided all enjoyments, one who is incapable [of performing other rites] should install the Lord of the Circle (cakranāyaka) in that which has been prepared by another. || 13 ||
There is nothing as dear to Tripurā as the installation of the Cakra;
for him there is no return [to saṃsāra], and he gradually attains union (sāyujya). 14.
It is declared that the fruit is infinite simply from the installation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
wherever a stationary yantra exists, one should dwell in its vicinity.
The lay devotee (upāsaka) always dwells upon a rampart made of gold;
indeed, the lay devotee should know that field to be superior in every respect. (16)
If one is unable even for that, out of consideration for one's limited resources, one should worship the stationary *cakra* or the image with devotion on auspicious festival days. (17)
O Rāma! There is no doubt that the worship of a stable yantra and so forth brings a fruit a hundred thousand times greater than the worship of a mobile yantra and so forth. || 18 ||
One should worship the Mother within the yantra according to the prescribed rite, meditating upon her in each respective place for the attainment of great fruit. (19)
Just as the rays of the sun are established everywhere, so too his arms,
which are of the nature of the sun, bring delight to all the worlds.
Likewise, the deities known as the retinue of Tripurā, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), are the destroyers of cold, darkness, disease, and other afflictions for living beings. (21)
Appointed by her very self for the sake of granting the desires of the world, they are indeed all portions of her; therefore, they are to be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Just as the sun, situated in the sky, consists of a mass of rays, even so Tripurā is considered the unified essence of the powers of manifestation. 23.
Seated within the Bindu-cakra is the Great Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods;
one who is unable [to perform the full ritual] should worship her with devotion according to what is available and in the proper sequence. 24.

The Supreme Goddess in her stationary form (sthāvara) should be worshipped with offerings consisting of the alms-gathering (parivāra-piṇḍa), or with common material riches, or in whatever manner possible. || 25 ||
But he who, having obtained a stationary [image] such as a discus and the like, does not worship it,
one should know him to be a slayer of his own self, censured by all the world. (26)
If one is unable [to perform the full ritual], one may do so with perfumes, flowers, fruits, unbroken grains (akṣata), and water;
likewise, by means of an offering fee (dakṣiṇā), betel, a lamp, prostrations, and circumambulations. || 27 ||
One should worship her there with all [the names], or with one, two, and so forth, according to one's capacity;
or he who worships in the wheel and other locations with a thousand or more names.
"By worshipping [it] even once, a man or a woman is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. (29)
Now listen as I tell you the procedure for the worship of a hundred thousand [offerings] and so forth;
one may begin it on special festival days or even on a Friday. (30)
Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) and worshipped Gaṇeśa, he should indeed have the Brahmins recite auspicious prayers;
then, having worshipped Maheśvarī according to the prescribed rite up to the concluding circumambulation (āvṛti).
One should worship the goddess Sāvṛtti with the five types of offerings;
therein, one should perform the worship in place of the offering of flowers.

Then, one should duly conclude the worship with incense and other offerings by means of the names beginning with "Sahasra" (the Thousand Names); and in this manner, one should perform the worship every day.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess daily in sequence according to the prescribed number of repetitions, using flowers of a single species wherever one performs the worship. (34)
Either by oneself, or through one's sons, wife, and so forth, or even through a Brāhmaṇa,
at the conclusion [of the rite], [the image] should be placed within a Sarvatobhadra diagram endowed with nine yonis.
Having properly established a water-pot made of gold or other materials, adorned with threads and cloths, in the center upon a mound of rice; 36.
Having placed [the vessel] adorned and fumigated while reciting the mantra,
one should fill it with water scented with eight fragrances and containing the five jewels.
Having placed that [object] therein in the same manner, and having gradually covered it with five sprouts, one should place a fruit containing rice and a full vessel upon its opening. || 38 ||
There, having projected the primordial form of the Goddess, adorned with all her limbs, and having invoked her into it, one should perform the worship. (39)
Therein, first one should worship the deities of the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] in their proper order,
as well as the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in the ten directions and at the four chains.
One should worship Dharma and the others in the white central chamber, and Adharma and the others in the red eastern chamber; one should perform the worship proceeding clockwise from the east.
Having thus worshipped the pair beginning with Asitāṅga and the three qualities (guṇas) in the girdles, preceded by the worship of the pedestal, [one should worship] in the jar.
Having invoked Tripurā according to the prescribed rites, one should worship her with ritual offerings; these flowers and other items should be made of gold or silver.
One should make [the offering] no less than one māṣa or even one karṣa, making it excellent;
or having made half of that, or even a quarter, nine times over.
One should worship [the deities] during the ritual services with names beginning with "Vaśinī," and at night, one should worship Tripurā in the center as the mistress of the wheel (cakranāyikā).
To the west of the water-pot, upon the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
one should perform worship either personally or through a preceptor who knows the ritual sequence.
Having worshipped, according to the scriptures, the maiden and likewise the young boy (baṭuka), as well as the preceptor, the married woman, and the Brahmins and others in due order; 47.
Having completed the worship that is devoid of the ritual dismissal (udvāsa), and remaining entirely concealed,
one should keep a vigil at night with stories, songs, and dances.
Then, having accomplished his purpose on the following day, he should worship the Lord of the Wheel (Cakranāyaka);
thereafter, having duly propitiated the fire according to the scriptures, he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) that is an ancillary part of the worship.
One should offer oblations there with those respective flowers one thousand times according to the prescribed rule;
having completed the worship and lifted up the pitcher covered with cloth, [one should proceed].
One should present [the offering] together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a married woman;
likewise, one should provide sixteen Brahmins and eight married women.
Free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should feed the young boys and maidens with various kinds of food and edibles, and satisfy them with sacrificial fees and other gifts.
Thus, by mere worship, one is liberated from all sins;
the gracious Mistress of Tripura becomes the bestower of desired objects. (53)
Endowed with all prosperity and likewise possessed of sons who continue his lineage,
he uplifts all his ancestors and attains liberation in the infinite [state]. (54)
One obtains a kingdom with lotuses, great prosperity with karavīra flowers, progeny with japā flowers, and houses and the like with jasmine (jātī) flowers. || 55 ||
With *yonipuṣpa* flowers one gains increase of lineage; with *vakula*, a joyful mind;
with *kiṃśuka*, the destruction of disease; and with *kuṭaja*, the elimination of enemies. (56)
O Bhārgava, having worshipped in this manner according to the prescribed rite with other flowers and leaves rich in fragrance, one shall obtain great fruit.
One should worship with fruits and grains according to the prescribed path,
or one should worship the Mother Tripurā with hundred-thousand wick-lamps.
In that case, one who is capable should provide lamps using two wicks, whether by ten, a hundred, or even a thousand. || 59 ||
One should offer fifty, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand lamps,
each filled with ghee, while reciting the names one by one.
By means of the thousand names of the Goddess, or indeed by the hundred names, whether through ten recitations or even a single recitation; || 61 ||
In that manner, one should offer a lamp to the Goddess after five hundred repetitions;
at the end, there should be nine pairs of wicks made of gold or silver.
Having placed [the vessel] in a copper lamp brightly illuminated by a ghee wick,
one should offer it into the jar and likewise perform the oblation with milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should indeed perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the Mistress of the Śrīcakra with the Śrīsūkta,
using one hundred thousand, one thousand, or one hundred recitations.
Either by oneself or by means of Brāhmaṇas, with milk, sugarcane juice, clarified butter, honey, fruit juices, or fragrant curds; || 65 ||
O Rāma, with water or with substances produced from sacred fords (tīrtha), according to the previously mentioned method,
one should finally offer oblations into the fire in sequence, using milk-rice (pāyasa) in a quantity ten times [the previous amount].
One should conclude the Śrīsūkta by reciting it verse by verse as before;
it is declared that the great fruit is obtained even through the consecration with the Rudra-mantras.
Thus, O Bhārgava! it has been declared that while the wealthy perform auspicious means through their riches, those without wealth must perform auspicious means with their very bodies. (68)
One who is capable should bring about his own welfare by undertaking a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrtha), or else he should perform service at the abode of the deity. 69.
Or one should serve those who are devoted to that worship, being free from longing;
for one who is extremely dull-witted, this alone is declared to be the duty.

Through the recitation of the Prajāpati-mantra, through the proclamation of stories and the like, and through the reading and teaching of the scriptures concerning the deities, the wise man shall attain the highest good. (71)
He who properly expounds the scripture on the worship of deities to those who are worthy shall dwell for a long time within the enclosure of Indra at the end of his body.
He who, with great devotion, should paint various [images] of the Goddess upon her palaces,
shall dwell for a long time in Vāsantavapra with his inner self filled with joy. (73)
One who cleanses the temple and sprinkles it with cool water, and likewise sprinkles it with well-perfumed cool water as well, [attains merit]. (74)
He who illuminates his residence with lamps at night shall dwell on the edge of Candra-vapra, free from all affliction. (75)
Having obtained enjoyments according to his desires, he shall dwell at the edge of Sūryavapra;
for in this manner, whoever performs service here in the temple [shall attain such a state]. 76.
At the end of his body, he attains such a station in Śrīpura;
even by giving gifts to worshippers, one may attain that station. || 77 ||

He who, with devotion, gives a book of the deity to a worthy person shall obtain the state of a Siddha, which brings great happiness. Furthermore, he who should give articles for worship to an excellent practitioner...
He shall indeed dwell in the precincts of the lords of the directions and obtain happiness. || 79 ||
Thus, whatever one may offer with devotion to this most excellent object of worship, one shall attain a residence equal to that very thing; of this there is no doubt. || 80 ||
Now I shall fully describe to you the supreme and highest among gifts:
the gift of the Śrīcakrarāja, which bestows great fruit.
Having duly worshipped the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja) with gold,
at the conclusion of the worship, [he should honor] a Brahmin of auspicious marks who is devoted to the worship of Tripurā. (82)
Having worshipped him together with his consort using special materials and offerings,
such as garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
Together with the pedestal, the ritual implements, and the materials for the sādhana,
he should place the general arghya water into the hand of the brahmin.
Then the Brahmin should perform the dismissal of that worship, beginning with the ritual of dismissal (udvāsana), and feed the invited Brahmins according to the prescribed rules. || 85 ||
One should feed married women while reciting the sixteen eternal names,
or else one should diligently feed Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Alternatively, one should always feed sixteen auspicious women with their husbands, and having honored twelve Brahmins, one should feed them as well. (87)
Thus, whoever gives a gift to the Wheel-King with devotion,
the Great Goddess, being pleased with him, bestows upon him union with her own self.
He has bathed in all sacred fords; by him every vow has been performed;
by him every gift has been given, and likewise by him all sacrifices have been offered.
Indeed, he has performed great penance and studied all the scriptures;
yet even Tripura is not a fit object for his deeds, and there is truly no fruit [to be gained from them].
Thinking thus, he quickly bestows upon him union with himself;
for, O Rāma, the wheel is the likeness of the form of the entire universe.
p.813) By him the world has been given; how could it be that nothing was given?
If one should perform [this rite] with desire, whatever desire one may wish for, [that shall be attained]. (92)
He attains each of those states suddenly and shall attain liberation in the end;
such is the stationary yantra, which is provided with a necklace in front.
Even an infinite being would not be capable of describing the merit of that man who gives a gift endowed with great generosity to a Brahmin. (94)
One should devoutly offer either an image, or [an amulet from] the Narmadā river, or the name of Śiva, or a śāligrāma stone, or indeed Kuṇḍalinī itself.
Having resided for a long time in Śrīpura, one shall be liberated at the end of the body;
likewise, he who repairs a dilapidated temple of the Cakrarāja and other deities shall make it new again. (96)
The merit from that would be a hundredfold greater than the construction of a new temple for one who, moreover, restores worship that has been long discontinued. (97)
By the gift of wealth and land, even that yields a hundredfold fruit.
Furthermore, O Bhārgava, listen as I speak of that which is the most secret of all. (98)
But he who, out of regard for wealth, honor, and the like, should bestow the tradition upon worthy devotees according to the method of the *Kramadīkṣā* and other such rites— || 99 ||
O Rāma! Its fruit is infinite—who is capable of describing it?
One may dwell as one desires within the circle of the Lord, and at the end, one is liberated. 100.
But he who, out of desire, delusion, negligence, or even out of dispassion, forbids one who is worshipping while seeking a worthy tradition, [is at fault]. (101)
And whoever should impart the scripture to an unworthy person out of greed for wealth and the like—for those two, no higher world exists, as they shall both attain a low state of existence. || 102 ||
Therefore, he who, out of foolishness and driven by greed for wealth, does not establish the tradition for his devotees, he too goes to the lowest state. (103)
Therefore, one should by no means refuse another—one's own disciple or someone else—who is disciplined, endowed with devotion, and desirous of knowing the tradition. (104)
This, O Rāma, yields great fruit; there is nothing else equal to it.
Any other gift, even that which is called "non-self," would result in bondage. (105)
Indeed, this is the supreme self-surrender specifically in the gift of knowledge;
even by the gift of written knowledge, that fruit shall be infinite.

He who, due to incapacity arising from dullness of intellect, is unable to bestow knowledge—especially in its oral transmission—may nevertheless obtain that same fruit by the gift of written knowledge. || 107 ||
This which has been extremely well-guarded has been explained to you out of affection;
thus is the attainment of great fruit in the ritual of the worship of Tripura. 108.
O Bhārgava, this majesty and power of Tripurā has been declared to you in its secret essence; by hearing it, one becomes possessed of devotion. (109)
O divine sage! This section concerning the majesty of Tripurā has indeed been heard by me with an attentive mind within the secret [teachings]. (110)
Whoever hears this is completely liberated from all sins;
for this is the supreme means for the liberation of the self from bondage. 111.
For devotion is said to be the progenitor of liberation; and since that devotion never arises without hearing about the Great Soul (Mahātman), [one must hear it]. 112.
Therefore, indeed, the first step of the staircase to that palace known as Parā is the hearing of its majesty in this world; this is remembered as the gateway to liberation.
Without hearing of his greatness, how could devotion arise here?
Without devotion, how could there be supreme bliss through the highest deity? (114)
Without devotion, nothing whatsoever is a means to liberation;
just as the beauty of a young woman utterly perishes without youth, so it is in this case. (115)
Just as a seed cannot produce a sprout without soil, so knowledge never produces fruit without devotion. (116)
For one who lacks devotion, there is no ritual action, no prayer, and no discernment;
therefore, for one devoid of devotion, there can be no steadfastness anywhere.
O Nārada, since the hearing of its greatness is its very root, one should therefore listen to this section known as the Māhātmya. 118.
For those who hear or even read it, this is the destroyer of great sins;
this chapter, or even a single verse from it, should be recited daily. (119)
For one who desires the grace of Tripurāśakti and every kind of auspiciousness, this [text] generates long life and increases well-being. 120.
The barren woman shall have sons, and the sonless woman shall become a mother of sons;
for by his mere hearing, whatever is desired is indeed attained. (121)
When written down and worshipped, it bestows knowledge; when desired, it grants one's wishes;
and when reflected upon, it bestows upon men wisdom, devotion, detachment, and so forth. (122)
May she who obtained the nectar of devotion from the churning of the ocean of all scriptures—
by whom Śiva and the other gods became immortal— be that very Mother Tripurā, who is *hrīṃ*.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Chief Devotees," in the Māhātmya-khaṇḍa of the glorious Tripurā-rahasya, the best of histories.
May it be offered to Tripurāmbā.
Om Tat Sat.
Thus concludes the *Māhātmyakhaṇḍa* within the *Tripurārahasya*.
To Śrīvidyā, with respectful devotion:
she whose indescribable [splendor] floods all directions with the mass of moonbeams consisting of the nectar of awakened consciousness.
Free from the stain of parts (*kalā*), she traverses the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*);
uniquely skilled at shattering the darkness of wretchedness, spreading her supreme speech, may that eternal Mistress of the World (*Bhuvaneśvarī*) sport in my mind like a swan.

The secret of Tripurā consists of the triad of gods, the triad of sacrificial fires, the three powers, the three vowels, the triple world, the three steps, the three Puṣkaras, and likewise the three Vedas and the three letters.
Whatever exists in the three worlds, regulated in its threefold nature— be it the three aims of life or anything else— all that truly corresponds, O Blessed One, to your name "Tripurā."

(Laghustava composed by Laghvācārya) I bow to her whose body is crimson like vermilion, who has three eyes, whose crest is the shimmering leader of stars upon a crown of rubies, whose face is smiling, and whose breasts are full.
One should meditate upon the supreme Mother, who is gentle, holding in her two hands jeweled goblets filled with wine and a red lotus, and whose feet are red and rest within a jeweled vessel.

One should meditate upon the visualization of Śrīvidyā, seated in the lotus posture with a blossoming countenance, her eyes as broad as lotus petals, golden-hued and clad in yellow garments, her beautiful limbs holding a radiant golden lotus in her hand.

[I bow to] Bhavānī, who is adorned with every ornament, who is eternally free from old age, who is accessible through devotion, who is Śrīvidyā of peaceful form, who is praised by all the gods, and who bestows all prosperity.

O Dark One, may all success be attained by those living among mortals who offer you as an oblation during worship even a hair, a bone, a piece of meat, a cat, a camel, a sheep, a man, a buffalo, or even a goat.
A unique power arises at every step.
(This is a verse from the *Karpūrastava*.
The worship of Tripurasundarī.
O Mother Tripura! I take refuge in you, the source of bliss, the abode of the Vedas, whose body consists of pure consciousness,
whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu, and who are the dwelling place for the birth of all good fortune.
Truly, for those who daily recite your name as "Hrīm," "Hrām," and "Hraum"—what indeed is difficult to attain in this world?
What is the greatness of the syllable *hrīṃ*? *Hrām*, *Hraum*. For those reciting your name every day, what here is truly hard to obtain?
In the city called Tripura,
Lakṣmī herself serves those who are worthy of honor— their garlands, crowns, and rutting elephants— by means of her own sweetness.
